articles.title: Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo y Morgan Stanley consideran la tokenización como una oportunidad de crecimiento, no como una amenaza
articles.text:
Goldman, Wells Fargo, Morgan Stanley consideran la tokenización como una oportunidad de crecimiento, no como una amenaza
Los bancos más grandes del mundo están observando nuevas oportunidades de negociación, acelerando los pagos y un papel para los asesores a medida que la tokenización se arraiga en Wall Street.
- Goldman Sachs considera la tokenización como una forma de expandir su negocio de trading.
- Wells Fargo afirma que su sistema de depósitos tokenizados ya está procesando pagos transfronterizos en dos minutos o menos.
- Morgan Stanley está recurriendo a la tokenización para generar una mayor demanda de asesoramiento en gestión patrimonial, mientras los inversores disponen de nuevas formas de mover activos.
La tokenización, o el proceso de incorporar activos financieros y del mundo real a una blockchain, ha estado generando titulares en los últimos meses, con un número creciente de empresas que afirman estar ofreciendo, o planean ofrecer, versiones de acciones, bonos y materias primas que pueden ser negociados las 24 horas del día con pocas, si es que existen, restricciones geográficas.
No es sorprendente que los bancos más grandes de Wall Street también estén examinando la tecnología, y las llamadas de resultados del tercer trimestre de esta semana brindaron a los ejecutivos la oportunidad de expresar una visión más clara sobre la dirección que creen que tomará el negocio, aunque ninguno cuantificó la oportunidad en términos de ingresos.
Goldman Sachs (GS), Wells Fargo (WFC) y Morgan Stanley (MS) se centraron en diferentes aspectos del proceso: oportunidades de trading, transmisión de dinero y servicios de asesoría.
Para Goldman Sachs, todo se trata de trading. Al CEO David Solomon se le preguntó si la tokenización, las finanzas descentralizadas (DeFi) y los mercados de predicción podrían afectar los ingresos por trading de la firma. Su respuesta fue que podrían hacer lo contrario.
Solomon señaló el cambio hacia la negociación electrónica de acciones hace casi 50 años, que en su momento generó preocupaciones similares sobre el futuro de las mesas de negociación de Wall Street. Goldman se adaptó a ese cambio y su negocio de acciones creció. La tokenización, dijo, podría seguir un camino similar.
"Los desarrollos están evidentemente creando más productos, mayor actividad, potencialmente nuevos clientes, canales de distribución más amplios," dijo Solomon en la llamada del martes con analistas.
Tokenización, compensación y liquidación
El banco ha dedicado años a invertir en infraestructura de activos digitales, aunque quizás de manera más discreta que la mayoría de sus competidores. Construyó GS DAP, su propia plataforma para activos tokenizados, como ya en 2022 y ha trabajado en la tokenización de bonos, fondos del mercado monetario y bienes raíces.
En julio, el banco participó en una jornada de medio día de un servicio de tokenización de la Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), que gestiona gran parte de la infraestructura detrás de los mercados de valores de EE. UU. y procesa cuadrillones de dólares en transacciones cada año.
Goldman está ahora explorando formas de utilizar ese servicio a una escala mayor, con Solomon afirmando que la tokenización podría ayudar a reducir costos, automatizar transacciones y facilitar la negociación de activos. Pero fue cauto respecto a la cantidad de negocios que representa actualmente.
"Diría que la actividad hasta ahora es pequeña y marginal," dijo.
Wells Fargo, por su parte, ya está procesando pagos transfronterizos utilizando depósitos tokenizados, con el dinero llegando a las cuentas de los beneficiarios en dos minutos o menos.
"Esto está en producción, por cierto, y hasta ahora tiene un volumen pequeño," dijo el CFO Michael Santomassimo.
La mayor oportunidad para Wells Fargo podría ser geográfica. A diferencia de algunos de sus rivales globales, el banco no cuenta con una amplia red de sucursales internacionales. Santomassimo señaló que los depósitos tokenizados podrían ayudarle a ganar más negocio de pagos transfronterizos sin necesidad de construir dicha red.
El banco también ve otros posibles usos para la tecnología, incluyendo valores tokenizados, activos del mundo real y comercio de criptomonedas para clientes de patrimonio. Santomassimo no indicó cuándo podrían estar disponibles esos servicios.
Para Morgan Stanley, el énfasis radica menos en mover dinero y más en lo que ocurre cuando los inversionistas pueden transferir activos con menos demoras.
Si bien la tecnología podría hacer que la transferencia de inversiones sea más rápida y sencilla, eso no significa que los clientes dejarán de necesitar asesoramiento, afirmó la directora financiera Sharon Yeshaya.
"El mundo tokenizado implica que es más rápido y fácil mover activos, y necesitará asesoramiento," dijo ella.
Morgan Stanley ha estado invirtiendo en capacidades digitales en sus negocios de gestión de patrimonio y valores institucionales. Yeshaya no anunció un nuevo producto, simplemente identificó la tokenización como otra oportunidad para la firma.
Diversified RWA stablecoins sustain 5-7% yield from real credit as crypto funding compresses to ~4%. GENIUS pushes yield off-chain; TAM grows to $4B in 3 years.

articles.title: Citrini predice un auge en la tokenización de RWA. La pregunta más difícil es quién se beneficia
articles.text:
Citrini prevé un auge en la tokenización. La pregunta más difícil es quién se beneficia
La influyente firma de investigación afirma que los activos del mundo real podrían finalmente otorgar a las cadenas de bloques un papel claro en las finanzas. Para los inversores, el próximo desafío es determinar qué empresas, redes y protocolos capturan los ingresos.
Este es un extracto de la nueva ‘" de CoinDeskTokenización Semanal’ boletín que se lanzará pronto. Los detalles para suscribirse serán aquí cuando se active.
Los entusiastas de las criptomonedas han pasado años afirmando que las finanzas –acciones, bonos y otros activos financieros– eventualmente se trasladarían a las cadenas de bloques.
Ahora, una firma de investigación influyente a la que prestan atención los inversionistas de Wall Street ha presentado argumentos a su favor.
Citrini Research, conocido principalmente por su trabajo en tecnología general, IA y tendencias del mercado más que por promover el cripto, dirigió su atención la semana pasada sobre la tokenización en un informe de 79 páginas titulado Rompiendo el Muro.
El informe en sí ya no es noticia, pero el argumento que lo sustenta merece ser considerado detenidamente porque marca el avance de la conversación.
Durante años, el sector criptográfico construyó una infraestructura cada vez más sofisticada para el comercio, el préstamo y la transferencia de dinero, mientras que la mayoría de los activos que los inversores realmente querían poseer —acciones, bonos, crédito y materias primas— permanecían dentro del sistema financiero tradicional. Ahora, esos activos están comenzando a migrar hacia las vías que la criptomoneda tardó más de una década en construir.
Citrini lo resumió en una línea:
“Las blockchain finalmente han encontrado su razón de ser.”
Por qué es importante
Para bien o para mal, una de las críticas más antiguas hacia las criptomonedas y las cadenas de bloques era que parecían una solución en busca de un problema.
Existían intercambios descentralizados, protocolos automatizados de préstamo, billeteras criptográficas y una infraestructura financiera cada vez más elaborada, pero si todo ello se utilizaba principalmente para intercambiar una criptomoneda por otra, la pregunta obvia seguía siendo: ¿para qué se construyó realmente la infraestructura?
La tokenización podría finalmente ofrecer una respuesta convincente.
Los bonos del Tesoro de EE. UU., el crédito, las acciones, los fondos y otros activos están migrando cada vez más hacia la cadena de bloques, y una vez que están allí, el objetivo no es simplemente que un inversor pueda negociar Nvidia a las 2 a.m. en un domingo.
El argumento más interesante que presentó Citrini es que la tokenización puede hacer que los activos financieros se comporten más como software: moviéndose entre aplicaciones, sirviendo como garantía, siendo prestados o integrados en otros productos financieros sin que cada plataforma tenga que reconstruir la custodia y la liquidación desde cero.
Esos elementos también están comenzando a unirse. Las stablecoins ponen efectivo en la cadena. Las billeteras, los intercambios y los protocolos DeFi han madurado. Las plataformas de trading orientadas al consumidor minorista como Robinhood (HOOD), Coinbase (COIN) y otras proporcionan distribución. Y los reguladores – en el EE.UU. y alrededor el globo – están comenzando a ofrecer a los valores tokenizados un camino más claro hacia los mercados.
Por qué esto es un gran acontecimiento
Citrini no está descubriendo la tokenización. Los inversores nativos de criptomonedas han hablado sobre activos del mundo real (RWA) durante años.
Lo que cambia es ver a una firma de investigación ampliamente seguida fuera de la burbuja cripto traducir la tesis al idioma que más importa a los grandes inversores: ¿dónde se gana realmente dinero?
Eso no es tan evidente como parece.
Citrini argumentó que la tokenización podría impulsar el ecosistema cripto en general, pero que más activos en la cadena no significa automáticamente que bitcoin , ether  o cualquier blockchain que los aloje sea la mejor opción de inversión.
Arthur Hayes, cofundador de BitMEX y director de inversiones de Maelstrom, planteó ese problema de manera más directa.
La tokenización de RWA se ha discutido durante una década, dijo él en un entrevista reciente con The Rollup, y simplemente tomar un activo que ya se encuentra en una base de datos digital y registrarlo en otro lugar no crea necesariamente mucho valor.
“Está bien, llevando una mejor contabilidad. Gracias,” dijo Hayes. “¿Dónde van a generar realmente ingresos en la tokenización?”
Existen varias respuestas posibles.
Las acciones tokenizadas pueden generar comisiones por emisión, ingresos por trading, demanda de stablecoins, actividad de préstamos y uso de colateral, pero dichas economías pueden ubicarse en lugares muy distintos.
Christian Magoon, CEO de Amplify ETFs, que gestiona el enfoque en la tokenización TKNQ el fondo, considera que los proveedores de infraestructura podrían convertirse en “peajes en las autopistas de peaje blockchain”, mientras que la distribución podría ser igual de valiosa: Coinbase, Robinhood, bancos y plataformas de gestión patrimonial que ya cuentan con las relaciones con los clientes.
Jeff Dorman, director de inversiones de la firma de inversión Arca, dijo a CoinDesk que espera que el proceso real de tokenización se vuelva cada vez más estandarizado a medida que crece la competencia.
La economía más persistente, dijo, surge después de que un activo está en cadena: cuando comienza a negociarse, a prestarse o a servir como garantía para préstamos. Por eso, él ve beneficiarios potenciales que van desde Securitize (SECZ) hasta protocolos criptográficos como la plataforma de negociación basada en blockchain Hyperliquid, el prestamista descentralizado Aave  y el intercambio descentralizado Aerodrome (AERO).
Zach Pandl, jefe de investigación de activos digitales en Grayscale, dijo a CoinDesk que la apuesta más sencilla podría ser las redes que están debajo de todo esto.
"La forma más directa de posicionar una cartera para la megatendencia de la tokenización es poseer las redes que alojan activos del mundo real (RWA) y procesan transacciones," dijo. "Los líderes de la industria hoy en día son Ethereum , BNB Chain  y Solana (SOL)"
Otras redes podrían desempeñar roles distintos. Avalanche (AVAX) y Canton , por ejemplo, han adoptado enfoques más enfocados en instituciones para el manejo de activos tokenizados y podrían experimentar una demanda creciente a medida que bancos y gestores de activos trasladan más actividad a la cadena, afirmó.
Y ahí es donde Hayes ve una historia aún mayor que podría convertir la tokenización en mucho más que una mejor contabilidad: agentes de IA gestionando servicios financieros.
“Creo que la mejor historia que quiero contar es que los agentes de IA gestionarán todos tus servicios financieros,” dijo Hayes.
Piense en un software que reajusta continuamente su cartera, moviendo efectivo ocioso hacia rendimientos más altos, encontrando un préstamo más barato o cambiando garantías conforme cambian las condiciones del mercado. Esos agentes necesitarían dinero e inversiones a los que puedan acceder programáticamente, las 24 horas del día, sin que un humano tenga que hacer clic en cada transacción.
Eso resulta ser muy parecido a la infraestructura que las criptomonedas han estado construyendo durante años: activos programables, mercados siempre activos, préstamos con contratos inteligentes y liquidación casi instantánea.
Citrini llegó a un argumento similar, afirmando que los activos tokenizados traducen efectivamente los productos financieros a un formato nativo para máquinas con el que los agentes de IA pueden trabajar.
Aun así, hay mucho espacio para que esos ganadores cambien. Magoon de Amplify destacó que el mercado sigue siendo “extremadamente temprano,” con activos tokenizados que aún son diminutos en comparación con los mercados financieros globales.
“El amplio periodo por delante aumenta la probabilidad de que los ganadores futuros puedan ser diferentes de los líderes actuales,” dijo.

articles.title: Polygon Labs completa la adquisición de Coinme para desafiar a Visa y Stripe en pagos globales
articles.text:
Polygon considera la adquisición de Coinme como su entrada al sector de pagos dominado por Visa y Stripe
El CEO Marc Boiron declaró que la adquisición de Coinme ayudará a Polygon a controlar las relaciones con los clientes y a capturar ingresos que anteriormente se dirigían a intermediarios de pagos.
- Polygon Labs espera que su negocio de pagos regulados se vuelva rentable el próximo año a medida que se expande más allá de la infraestructura blockchain hacia el procesamiento de pagos.
- La adquisición de Coinme permite a Polygon gestionar conversiones entre criptomonedas, stablecoins y monedas tradicionales, mientras mantiene las relaciones con los clientes y cobra comisiones de pago.
- Polygon ingresará a una industria dominada por empresas como Visa y Stripe, y su plataforma unificada de pagos se encuentra en vista previa técnica con un pequeño grupo de usuarios tempranos.
Polygon Labs espera que su negocio de pagos regulados sea rentable en 2027, a medida que avanza más allá de la infraestructura blockchain para ingresar en la industria de procesamiento de pagos dominada por empresas como Visa (V) y Stripe, afirmó el CEO Marc Boiron a CoinDesk.
La empresa, desarrolladora de la cadena de bloques Polygon, declaró el miércoles que completó el adquisición de Coinme, un proveedor de pagos criptográficos regulado por EE. UU., que ofrece Empresa con sede en las Islas Caimán con la capacidad de manejar conversiones entre criptomonedas, stablecoins y dinero tradicional utilizando sus propios recursos.
El acuerdo forma parte de un cambio en el negocio de Polygon que incluye la introducción en enero del Open Money Stack, un marco para apoyar los pagos basados en stablecoins y optimizar las transferencias transfronterizas. Ahora, además de proporcionar la tecnología para mover dinero, también puede cobrar tarifas por la conversión y transferencia de ese dinero, una fuente de ingresos que anteriormente correspondía a otras empresas, dijo Boiron en una entrevista en video.
"No he considerado que compitamos con las blockchains desde hace un tiempo, para ser franco," dijo Boiron. "Somos, más bien, una empresa centrada en pagos que simplemente utiliza blockchains para mover dinero, y en particular, Polygon."
Aun así, la empresa está lejos de ofrecer una competencia seria a los líderes del mercado. El volumen de pagos de Visa en el año fiscal 2025 superó los $12.3 billones, mientras que Stripe alcanzó los $1.9 billones. Polygon apenas está comenzando su trayectoria.
La adquisición de Coinme aborda un problema de larga data para las redes blockchain: ellas proporcionan la tecnología detrás de las transacciones, pero a menudo tienen poco control sobre las empresas que las generan. La incorporación de Coinme permitirá a Polygon gestionar una mayor parte del proceso de pago, en lugar de derivar a los clientes a un tercero cada vez que se necesite que el dinero entre o salga de una blockchain.
"No tenemos esa relación con el cliente; no nos corresponde decidir lo que sucede", dijo Boiron, quien afirmó que blockchains rivales han ofrecido incentivos financieros a las empresas de pago para desviar sus transacciones de Polygon.
"Ahora, cuando somos nosotros quienes gestionamos el negocio regulado, nadie puede obligarnos a mover flujos a ningún lugar que no deseemos, porque realmente tenemos esas relaciones con los clientes."
Nueva fuente de ingresos
Polygon Labs genera ingresos a partir de sus servicios de pago. Las tarifas por transacción en la blockchain de Polygon son independientes, y las tarifas de prioridad se distribuyen entre validadores y stakers. Boiron señaló que las tarifas de transacción ya compensan sus emisiones de tokens, y evaluó que millones de dólares en tarifas adicionales se destinan a validadores y stakers de tokens.
A diferencia de las tarifas de transacción en blockchain, que pueden ser fracciones de un centavo, el negocio de pagos puede obtener comisiones basadas en el valor del dinero transferido.
Sin embargo, es probable que Polygon enfrente cierta competencia desde la dirección opuesta, ya que las empresas tradicionales de pagos se expanden hacia las transferencias de dinero basadas en blockchain.
Stripe ha estado desarrollando pagos con stablecoins, mientras que Swift, el servicio mundial de mensajería interbancaria, está desarrollando infraestructura blockchain con grandes bancos. Visa, mientras tanto, ha amplió su red de liquidación de stablecoins para incluir la blockchain de Polygon, entre otras, mientras lanzando una plataforma que permite a los bancos y fintechs emitir, gestionar y liquidar stablecoins.
Para Polygon, el desafío ya no es simplemente persuadir a las empresas para que utilicen su blockchain. Es convencerlas de que usen Polygon Labs para mover su dinero.
Los usuarios tempranos de la plataforma incluyen a Tazapay, un proveedor de pagos transfronterizos; Mesh, una red de pagos en criptomonedas; Toku, una plataforma global de nómina; y Kira, una empresa de infraestructura de pagos. La integración unificada de la plataforma se encuentra en vista previa técnica, lo que significa que aún no está disponible de forma general para los clientes.

articles.title: Claude de Anthropic resuelve un misterio de 25 años sobre una curva de la NSA, qué significa para bitcoin
articles.text:
‘Vaya, es un verdadero descubrimiento’: Claude resuelve un misterio de un número de la NSA de 25 años
Los números que la agencia de espionaje entregó en la década de 1990, largamente sospechados de ocultar una puerta trasera, resultaron provenir de un programa informático básico. Bitcoin nunca estuvo en esa lista, y su problema cuántico no ha desaparecido.
- Un modelo de IA de Anthropic tardó menos de 30 minutos en rastrear cinco semillas inexplicables para curvas elípticas NIST suministradas por la Agencia de Seguridad Nacional a un generador de números aleatorios común utilizando marcas de tiempo de 1997 y 1998.
- El hallazgo hace que una puerta trasera oculta de la NSA sea menos probable y no requiere que los usuarios de las curvas NIST tomen medidas, aunque quedan preguntas sobre cómo se seleccionaron algunos elementos.
- Bitcoin no se vio afectado porque utiliza secp256k1, una curva más simple con poco margen para ocultar una debilidad, aunque las computadoras cuánticas lo suficientemente potentes podrían eventualmente representar una amenaza distinta.
Un modelo de inteligencia artificial de Anthropic ha resuelto uno de los misterios más prolongados de la criptografía, rastreando números que la NSA entregó al gobierno de EE. UU. a finales de la década de 1990, los cuales durante mucho tiempo se sospechó que ocultaban una puerta trasera, hasta un programa ordinario de números aleatorios alimentado con marcas de tiempo de 1997 y 1998.
Al modelo le tomó aproximadamente media hora desarrollar una solución, una que los criptógrafos habían estado buscando durante 25 años.
Un candado con un diseño inexplicado
Gran parte de internet depende de la criptografía de curva elíptica, la familia de matemáticas que también se utiliza para proteger las billeteras de bitcoin. Permite que alguien demuestre que posee una clave secreta sin revelar los detalles de la clave en sí.
Piense en la curva como un diseño de cerradura que cualquiera puede inspeccionar. Cada persona que la utiliza tiene su propia clave secreta, pero todos dependen de que el diseño sea difícil de vulnerar.
Pero, ¿quién eligió las matemáticas en las que todos confiarían?
En 2000, el Instituto Nacional de Estándares y Tecnología de EE. UU., o NIST, adoptó un conjunto de curvas proporcionadas por la Agencia de Seguridad Nacional. La NSA facilitó esos diseños sin explicar el origen de algunos de los números utilizados para generarlas.
La secretividad se volvió aún más difícil de ignorar después de la Las revelaciones de Snowden vinculadas a la NSA a los esfuerzos para debilitar los estándares criptográficos. NIST posteriormente se eliminó esa herramienta, el generador de números aleatorios Dual EC, de sus recomendaciones.
Esos números iniciales, llamados semillas, eran públicos. Pero la NSA nunca explicó cómo los eligió, lo que alimentó años de sospechas de que había probado muchas alternativas hasta encontrar una curva con una vulnerabilidad que solo ella sabía cómo explotar. La teoría conspirativa era que la NSA tenía una puerta trasera en cada sistema que la utilizaba.
Los criptógrafos Neal Koblitz y Alfred Menezes examinaron la controversia en su artículo de 2015, “Un enigma envuelto en un misterio.” Menezes había ayudado a redactar el estándar original y recordó haber recibido las semillas del matemático de la NSA Jerry Solinas en 1997.
El investigador de seguridad Steve Weis pasó años buscando una explicación, incluyendo la presentación de solicitudes de registros públicos en 2018. NIST declaró que no tenía documentación, mientras que la NSA dejó de responder. Una pista prometedora sugería que los números provenían de una frase humorística que Solinas había olvidado, enviando a los investigadores a buscar entre posibles combinaciones de palabras.
En 2023, el ingeniero en criptografía Filippo Valsorda y otros colaboradores ofreció una recompensa de $12,288 en busca de una respuesta, aumentando a más de $36,000 si el ganador lo donaba a la caridad. Solinas había fallecido a principios de ese año, dejando a los investigadores trabajar a través de viejos recuerdos y los números en sí sin obtener resultados.
Claude empieza a indagar
Hasta que Claude entró en escena. Este mes, un empleado de Anthropic pidió a un modelo interno de investigación que analizara, sin compartir la antigua teoría de que las semillas provenían de una frase olvidada.
Al modelo le tomó menos de media hora rastrear cinco semillas de la curva NIST hasta lrand48, un generador de números aleatorios que se encuentra en bibliotecas de software C más antiguas.
Claude reprodujo la secuencia detrás de P-256, una curva ampliamente utilizada, y encontró una coincidencia exacta para su semilla publicada en el candidato número 1,842.
“Esto es asombroso: resuelve el misterio de 25 años,” escribió el modelo en su razonamiento registrado, después de cuestionar brevemente si estaba trabajando dentro de una prueba simulada. “Hmm, ¿es plausible en la realidad? Según mi conocimiento … la recompensa estaba sin resolver. … Todos los bits superiores claros—20 bits, oportunidad 1e-6. Así que realmente es del mundo real.”
“Vaya, es un verdadero descubrimiento.”
Cualquier persona ahora puede ejecutar nuevamente el programa y obtener los números proporcionados por la NSA. Anthropic afirma que eso hace que una debilidad oculta sea mucho menos probable, aunque el equipo aún no puede explicar por qué el programa descartó algunos candidatos utilizables o cómo se eligieron otras partes de las curvas.
Esa previsibilidad es lo que permitió a Claude reconstruir los números, y sería un desastre dentro de una cartera. Una clave secreta generada con lrand48 podría ser recreada por cualquiera que determinara aproximadamente cuándo fue creada, proporcionándoles todo lo necesario para vaciar los fondos.
Las semillas de la NSA fueron públicas desde el primer día, por lo que nunca hubo un secreto que robar.
Dónde encaja bitcoin
Bitcoin nunca formó parte de este juego de adivinanzas. Sus monederos funcionan con secp256k1, una curva construida a partir de una ecuación más sencilla.
La versión de Bitcoin está definida por dos números pequeños y fijos que dejan casi nada por ajustar, mientras que la versión P-256 lleva un número de 77 dígitos que proviene de la semilla inexplicada de la NSA.
Con tan pocos parámetros para ajustar, hay poco espacio para que alguien haya insertado discretamente una vulnerabilidad en la curva de bitcoin, y los criptógrafos han señalado durante mucho tiempo eso como un punto a su favor.
El creador Satoshi Nakamoto nunca explicó públicamente por qué la eligió, y la curva se utilizaba rara vez antes de que bitcoin la hiciera famosa. Ethereum también la adoptó posteriormente, y bitcoin la mantuvo cuando su actualización Taproot de 2021 introdujo un estilo de firma más reciente.
Una potente computadora cuántica traería un peligro diferente, ya que CoinDesk exploró anteriormente este año. Podría funcionar hacia atrás desde una clave pública visible en la cadena de bloques de Bitcoin hasta la clave secreta detrás de ella, sin importar cómo se haya elegido la curva.
Los avances en hardware continúan reduciendo la brecha entre esa teoría y un ataque efectivo. Google declaró esta semana su chip Willow redujo los errores aproximadamente 40 veces en uno de los pasos más costosos que una máquina de este tipo necesitaría.
Sin embargo, nadie ha construido hasta ahora una computadora cuántica lo suficientemente grande o fiable como para descifrar una clave de bitcoin, y no existe un calendario claro sobre cuándo podría llegar una.
Mientras tanto, Anthropic indicó en su blog que las personas que utilizan las curvas NIST no necesitan cambiar nada. Después de décadas de preguntas sobre el origen de las semillas, ahora cualquiera puede ejecutar el programa y retraçar su camino hasta los números publicados.
La búsqueda también tenía un premio. Su recompensa de $36,864 será entregada al Internet Security Research Group, la organización sin fines de lucro detrás de Let’s Encrypt, que proporciona certificados de seguridad gratuitos a sitios web.

articles.title: TRON moved $2.2 trillion in stablecoins while TRX supply grew for 108 straight days
articles.text:
Quick Take
- TRX recorded positive net issuance on all 108 days from July 1 through October 16, adding 148.6 million tokens.
- Staked or delegated resources recover over time, allowing network use without burning the underlying TRX committed to staking.
- October 1–16 balance required 57.5% more burn with issuance fixed, or 36.5% less issuance with burns fixed.
TRON’s stablecoin settlement business grew in the third quarter of 2026, while the supply of its native TRX token increased on every day from July 1 through October 16. The blockchain added 125.8 million TRX in Q3 and another 22.9 million over the first 16 days of October, after subtracting tokens burned.
TRON can handle more dollar transfers without destroying more of its native token than it creates. TRON DAO Research reported $2.2126 trillion in Q3 stablecoin settlement, up 5.1% from Q2. TRX supply nevertheless kept expanding into October.
TRON’s design allows these outcomes to coexist: reusable resources can cover network activity, while block-production and voting rewards continue to mint TRX. October’s measured shortfall shows how far the network was from supply balance and how closing the gap would affect resource payers and reward recipients.
TRONSCAN’s July, August and September daily records contain 92 observations covering the full third quarter. Issuance exceeded burns on every date. The October 1–16 records add another 16 positive readings, bringing the sample to 108 consecutive days.
| Period in 2026 | TRX issued | TRX burned | Net TRX issued | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Q3: July 1–Sept. 30, 92 days | 360,217,352 | 234,453,624 | 125,763,728 | 
| Oct. 1–16, 16 days | 62,650,984 | 39,778,374 | 22,872,610 | 
CryptoSlate’s sums of the daily issuance and burn records show 148.6 million TRX added over the window. The figures were retrieved on October 17 and exclude that incomplete day.
The scale was modest. Q3’s net addition amounted to approximately 0.133% of an opening supply of about 94.850 billion TRX.
Stablecoin supply is a separate stock. The quarterly report puts combined USDT and USDD balances on TRON at $93.88 billion, up 5.5% from Q2. Those dollar tokens and TRX perform different roles, so growth in one supply does not determine the direction of the other.
Settlement measures value transferred. Its 5.1% quarterly increase differs from the report’s 3.9% increase in daily average settlement because Q3 had 92 days and Q2 had 91.
How reusable resources and rewards affect TRX supply
TRON’s resource rules meter transaction size and computation. Bandwidth covers the bytes recorded on the blockchain; Energy covers smart-contract execution. The dollar value of stablecoins moving through a transaction does not, by itself, set either cost.
Users can obtain resources by committing TRX through staking, or receive delegated resources from another account. TRON’s documentation describes Bandwidth and Energy recovering over a rolling 24-hour window. Resources used at one time fully recover after 24 hours without further consumption; additional activity changes the recovery schedule.
Using those resources does not destroy the underlying staked TRX. The stake supports access that can be used repeatedly as capacity recovers. Delegation allows a receiving account to use resources supplied through someone else’s stake.
The fallback rules differ by resource. For an ordinary Bandwidth charge, the network first tries staked or delegated quota, then free quota. Each must cover the transaction’s entire byte cost. If neither can, TRX is burned for the full Bandwidth charge.
Energy can cover part of the caller’s smart-contract execution cost, with TRX burned for the caller-side remainder within the applicable fee limit. Resource provision therefore matters alongside activity when assessing burns.
On the issuance side, TRON pays block producers and voters with newly minted tokens. Its documented consensus rewards list 8 TRX per block for production and 128 TRX per block for voter rewards. Governance can change these parameters.
Distribution also matters. Under TRON’s staking and voting reward model, voters can receive a share after the representative retains its brokerage cut. Simply holding unstaked TRX does not confer the same reward claim.
A resource user, a staker and a passive token holder can therefore experience the network’s economics differently. One uses transaction capacity, another supplies stake and may vote for rewards, while an unchanged token balance receives no automatic increase merely because the network issues more TRX.
October’s gap to supply balance
Over October 1–16, burns offset approximately 63.5% of new issuance. Average daily issuance was 3.916 million TRX, compared with 2.486 million burned, leaving a daily average gap of 1.430 million TRX.
Holding issuance at the observed 62,650,984 TRX, aggregate burns would have needed to increase from 39,778,374 TRX to 62,650,984 TRX to reach balance. The additional 22,872,610 TRX represents a 57.5% increase over observed burns.
Holding burns fixed instead, issuance would have needed to fall by 22,872,610 TRX, or 36.5% of the observed issuance total. The percentages differ because each uses a different starting denominator.
These are separate arithmetic comparisons for the same 16-day window. Aggregate burn depends on both resource use and charging, so a 57.5% increase in total burn need not mean a 57.5% increase in each transfer’s fee.
At supply balance, new tokens could still be issued and destroyed in equal amounts. Deflation would require burns to exceed issuance over the measured period.
Holding issuance and other conditions fixed, a route that closes the gap entirely through more burn requires more TRX to be destroyed through resource payments or other burn charges. That cost falls on the accounts funding those charges.
A route that closes it entirely through lower issuance reduces the aggregate newly minted reward pool, holding other conditions fixed. Individual allocations depend on the reward rules and brokerage.
For holders whose balances remain unchanged, positive net issuance increases the supply against which their tokens are measured. Q3’s roughly 0.133% expansion provides the scale of that effect. Reward recipients may add tokens to their balances, while staked resources provide utility through recurring access to network capacity.

articles.title: Who opened your crypto wallet before it reached your hands?
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Ledger confirmed a hidden implant that stole recovery phrases during wallet setup.
- The spy chip transmitted stolen recovery words over a mobile connection.
- Bitquery estimates $102 million was stolen across 324 wallets.
In early October, customers in Southeast Asia discovered that their crypto had disappeared from Ledger hardware wallets that still seemed to be working normally.
They bought the devices through CryptoBilis, an authorized reseller, and believed their private keys were protected inside a device built for that purpose. What they couldn't see was a second piece of hardware, hidden inside the casing, that could steal the information needed to empty the wallet.
On Oct. 10, Ledger confirmed an unauthorized implant in one affected customer's device. Three days later, its security team explained that the added electronics had read the wallet's 24 recovery words as they appeared on the screen during setup and sent them over a mobile connection.
The protected chip, operating system, and transaction signatures were unchanged.
Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery estimates that attackers stole $102 million from 324 wallets across six networks, although Ledger hasn't confirmed that total or established that every loss came from an implanted device.
The moment the secret leaves the chip
Hardware wallets don't actually hold crypto. The coins remain on their networks, so the device only protects the private keys used to authorize transactions, keeping those secrets away from malware on an internet-connected phone or computer.
When an owner approves a payment, the wallet signs the transaction without giving the computer those keys. That separation is the product's main promise, but one exception appears before every owner makes a first payment.
During setup, a Ledger wallet displays 24 recovery words, which can recreate the wallet and its keys if the device is lost. Owners are told to write the phrase down, keep it offline, and never share it. Anyone who copies it can restore the same accounts on another device, and the original wallet's PIN will not stop them.
The CryptoBilis implant was designed for that brief moment when the words appeared on the screen. According to Ledger, a small controller intercepted the information being sent to the display, reconstructed the phrase, and transmitted it over LTE using an embedded SIM card.
It didn't need to break the protected chip or trick the owner into entering the words on a fake website.
The owner could finish setup, use the wallet, and approve legitimate transactions, while someone else had an identical way to access the funds. An optional additional passphrase can protect accounts created with it, but for ordinary accounts the recovery words alone are enough.
A real check with a real blind spot
Ledger's Genuine Check verifies that a device contains an authentic Secure Element, the chip responsible for sensitive security operations. It can identify a counterfeit chip, but it can't inspect every component inside the casing or prove that nothing has been added since manufacture.
Ledger's security documentation warns that physical modifications may escape detection when the original chip remains intact. That's the weakness the implant exploited: the device could truthfully report on its Secure Element while failing to reveal the extra circuitry beside it.
Tibane Labs examined modified Ledger Nano X devices fitted with electronics that monitored signals between the secure chip and the screen. A more sophisticated specimen used a custom board hidden beneath the display and kept the device's original battery, so casual inspection couldn't find it.
Those specimens were separate from the CryptoBilis investigation and don't prove that the same devices or attackers were involved. They do, however, explain why an authentic chip, correct signatures, and a normal-looking wallet are not the same as proof that the entire device is untampered.
The weak point was the journey to the buyer
CryptoBilis was an authorized reseller operating in Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Customers weren't taking a reckless shortcut by buying there, as Ledger itself recommends buying through authorized sellers.
That's what makes the case more consequential than a counterfeit wallet bought from an anonymous seller. The question was whether the product could be trusted after passing through distributors, retailers, and anyone else with access to the stock.
In an Oct. 15 update, Ledger said attackers bought genuine devices over several months, opened them, fitted custom components, and returned them to distribution through Southeast Asian resellers.
The company described the incident as an attack on the distribution channel and said samples checked in warehouses and stores showed no tampering.
Ledger also said it had asked authorized resellers and distributors in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to suspend sales. It's tightening controls on returned products and asking sellers to keep devices off display shelves, measures that acknowledge how important physical access becomes when attackers can modify a product without changing the software inside it.
Germany's MediaMarktSaturn suspended Ledger sales following a report of a tampered device, while rival wallet maker Trezor moved to reduce its reseller network despite finding no evidence that its own products were compromised.
Bitquery found that 25 Tron wallets signed the same approval within three seconds, a pattern consistent with someone already controlling multiple accounts.
But blockchain records can't identify who opened a package, installed a component, or returned a device to a shop. That requires hardware examinations and distribution records.
A new device is not enough
For anyone who may have received a compromised wallet, the important difference is between the device and the recovery phrase. A PIN protects the original device from unauthorized use, but it does nothing to stop someone from restoring the same keys elsewhere.
Buying new hardware and entering the old 24 words recreates the same risk. The assets need to move to accounts generated from a fresh recovery phrase on a trusted device, using carefully verified addresses and instructions.
Ledger has told people who bought from CryptoBilis not to initialize unused devices and advised those who already set them up to move funds to a new signer with a new phrase. Affected owners should use official support channels, preserve potentially relevant evidence, and never provide recovery words to someone claiming they can help recover the money.
The incident shows that the security boundary people think they are buying extends beyond the chip inside the device. It extends through the screen, casing, packaging, and distribution chain, all the way to the moment the recovery words first appear.
Self-custody removes the need to trust an exchange to hold the keys, but not the need to trust the hardware that creates and displays them. In the CryptoBilis case, the attackers didn't have to wait for an owner to make a mistake after opening the box, because they gained access long before the owner even arrived.

articles.title: Ethereum sets October 26 for Hoodi’s 200 million gas test
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Ethereum scheduled Hoodi’s Glamsterdam activation for October 26 at 17:42:48 UTC, creating a software deadline for testnet operators.
- Hoodi operators must update execution and consensus clients; validators must also upgrade their beacon node and validator client.
- The 200 million gas target guides a gradual block-limit adjustment under existing rules; mainnet activation timing remains undecided.
Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade is scheduled for Hoodi, a test network, on Oct. 26, 2026, at 17:42:48 UTC, giving its node operators a deadline to upgrade software. The test pairs changes to block production and validation with a scheduled 200 million gas target.
The Ethereum Foundation’s Oct. 16 announcement fixes the next testnet deployment after Glamsterdam’s Oct. 6 activation on Sepolia. Mainnet timing remains undecided. ETH holders and mainnet operators have no action to take as a result of this Hoodi announcement.
All Hoodi operators must update their execution and consensus clients before activation. Validators must update both the beacon node and validator client, and review new duties, builder-tooling compatibility and gas-limit settings to follow the upgraded testnet.
The Foundation’s confirmed Hoodi releases, as checked Oct. 17, are:
| Layer | Client | Listed release | 
|---|---|---|
| Execution | Besu | 26.10.0 | 
| Execution | Ethrex | 30.0.0-rc.2 | 
| Execution | Nethermind | 2.2.0 | 
| Consensus | Lodestar | 1.50.0 | 
| Consensus | Nimbus | 26.10.1 | 
| Consensus | Prysm | v7.3.0 | 
| Consensus | Teku | 26.10.1 | 
Ethrex’s listed version is a release candidate. Grandine, Lighthouse, Erigon, go-ethereum and Reth remain unlisted; operators should use releases whose notes confirm this Hoodi activation.
Besu 26.10.0 migrates Bonsai code storage on first startup and retains more history when pruning. Downgrading requires the documented besu storage revert-code-format command before an older version can reopen the database.
What the scaling test changes
Hoodi’s 200 million gas target is a planned budget for computational work per block. The gas-limit schedule sets client defaults and recommendations while preserving operator preferences. The actual block limit adjusts gradually under existing rules, so the target is not an instantly enforced ceiling.
Throughput depends on transaction complexity, while fees also depend on demand.
Glamsterdam combines Amsterdam on the execution layer with Gloas on the consensus layer. Enshrined proposer-builder separation moves the exchange between block proposers and builders into the protocol and gives validators more time to check execution. Block-level access lists record accessed accounts, storage and state changes so clients can perform more work in parallel.
Developers also have testing to do: changed gas pricing can affect contracts that rely on fixed stipends, hardcoded limits or remaining-gas assumptions. The Foundation advises testing contracts and gas estimation under the new rules.

articles.title: Crypto Super PAC Fairshake Pours Millions More Into Defeating Sherrod Brown - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- A new FEC filing shows Fairshake affiliate Defend American Jobs disclosed spending to oppose the Ohio Democrat has increased to about $46.66 million—the industry’s most expensive 2026 target.
- Brown, a longtime crypto skeptic, chaired the Senate Banking Committee before losing in 2024, a race Fairshake spent ~$40 million to influence.
- The blitz follows Fairshake’s Oct. 5 move to back 32 House incumbents with $6 million committed to six.
Crypto’s biggest political spender is turning up the pressure on one of the industry’s fiercest critics. Fairshake has reported fresh spending to defeat Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown in Ohio, pushing its total outlay against the former Senate Banking Committee chairman well past the $40 million mark.
A filing with the Federal Election Commission, signed Oct. 15, shows Defend American Jobs, the Fairshake affiliate that spends in Republican-friendly races, disclosed a $5.2 million media buy opposing Brown, followed by another roughly $1.95 million buy days later, plus media-production costs.
The filing lists Brown’s calendar-year-to-date total at about $46.66 million, cementing the Ohio contest as the most expensive target of the crypto industry’s 2026 campaign. The same filing showed parallel spending supporting Brown’s Republican opponent, Jon Husted, who inherited the seat after being appointed last year.
The sums dwarf what Fairshake is deploying elsewhere, underscoring how personal the Ohio race has become for the industry. The PAC earlier signaled plans to spend at least $30 million against Brown, a figure this filing shows it has already blown past.
Brown’s return to the Senate would hand crypto skeptics a powerful voice on the Banking Committee, the same perch from which he stalled market-structure legislation before losing his seat in 2024, a defeat Fairshake spent roughly $40 million to help engineer.
The renewed Senate blitz comes days after Fairshake broadened its map to the House. On Oct. 5, the PAC network announced it would back 32 House incumbents, 19 Republicans and 13 Democrats, framing itself as an issue-focused group that supports “pro-crypto candidates who support American innovation in both parties.”
It committed an initial $6 million, or $1 million each, to six of them: Republicans French Hill, Bill Huizenga and Bryan Steil, and Democrats Janelle Bynum, Steven Horsford and Derek Tran. All 32 voted to advance the Clarity Act when it passed the House in July 2025.
Fairshake, funded largely by Coinbase, Ripple, and Andreessen Horowitz, entered September with roughly $120 million in cash and is expected to spend more than $100 million across House and Senate races this cycle. Its push runs alongside the Coinbase-backed advocacy group Stand With Crypto, which has rolled out its own slate of midterm endorsements.
The spending reflects the industry’s hardened resolve after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate, channeling its considerable war chest into reshaping the Congress that will decide crypto’s rules.

articles.title: Crypto Firms Launch Quantum Alliance as 6 Million Bitcoin Sit Exposed - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Nine blockchain organizations launched the Quantum Alliance, an open standards body to define what “quantum-ready” means and create a common way to test and verify quantum-resistance claims across networks, wallets and infrastructure.
- The group warns that elliptic-curve signatures leave roughly 6.04 million BTC (~30% of supply) quantum-exposed, citing forecasts pointing toward the late 2020s.
- Modeled on the IETF, it will work in four groups—migration, zero-knowledge systems, wallet security and cross-chain compatibility.
A group of crypto companies is trying to settle one of the industry’s murkiest questions: what it actually means for a blockchain network to be safe from quantum computers.
Executives from nine organizations launched the Quantum Alliance on Thursday, an open standards body that will set criteria for judging quantum-resistance claims and create compatibility rules for networks as they migrate to new cryptography.
The founding contributors span base-layer protocols, privacy networks, rollups, hardware wallets and security auditing, including Quantus, Postquant Labs, Midnight Foundation, Keystone, Abelian and security firm Hacken.
Modeled on the Internet Engineering Task Force, the Alliance said proposals will advance on public evidence and working implementations rather than corporate size or token holdings, and everything it produces will be published openly.
Its work will run in four groups: blockchain migration, post-quantum zero-knowledge systems, wallet security and cross-chain compatibility. “In the future, ‘post-quantum cryptography’ will just be called ‘cryptography’ and everything else will be in a museum,” said Quantus founder and CEO Christopher Smith.
The problem it’s tackling is that there’s no agreed definition of “quantum-ready,” and no standard way to test one. A network can call itself quantum-resistant today with no shared understanding of what the claim covers or what evidence should back it, a gap the Alliance was formed to close.
The stakes are familiar to anyone following the beat. Nearly every major blockchain secures accounts with elliptic-curve signatures, and once an account’s public key is exposed on the ledger, a sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could theoretically reverse-engineer the private key and seize the funds.
The same cryptography guards stablecoin minting keys, bridges, oracles, and governance contracts, meaning one cracked privileged key could cascade across platforms. By the Alliance’s count, roughly 6.04 million BTC, about 30% of supply, sit quantum-exposed at rest.
The timelines keep tightening. The Quantum Alliance cites a cluster of recent forecasts pointing toward the late 2020s, including a model co-built by two Alliance contributors that flags March 2028 as an early window, and a Google Quantum AI study that slashed the estimated qubits needed to break Bitcoin’s cryptography to under 500,000.
No machine can do it yet. Google has also chipped away at key quantum bottlenecks, while figures like famed investor Kevin O’Leary have flagged the quantum threat as a catch hanging over Bitcoin’s long-term case.
The newly formed Quantum Alliance joins a widening industry scramble to address the risk. Coinbase recently urged Bitcoin developers to start the quantum migration now, suggesting preparations could take years. Meanwhile, a consortium backed by BlackRock, Strategy, and Coinbase has committed $15 million to the problem.

articles.title: Stablecoin cards are booming, but who makes money when you swipe?
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Stablecoin cards let users spend USDC while merchants receive local currency.
- Multiple providers split fees while covering settlement, fraud and support costs.
- Adoption depends on whether rewards and convenience outweigh fees and currency conversion.
Someone paying for lunch with a stablecoin card doesn't need the restaurant to know what USDC is. The card works like any other at the terminal, with the customer's digital dollar balance funding the purchase while the merchant receives regular dollars through its usual payment provider.
That leaves several companies to collect fees for connecting the two.
Visa enables this arrangement through its partnership with Bridge, which allows customers in Colombia to spend stablecoins while merchants receive Colombian pesos.
Bridge handles the conversion, so neither the restaurant nor its payment provider needs to accept cryptocurrency, letting customers spend stablecoins without first withdrawing them to a bank account.
On Oct. 1, Visa reported more than 160 stablecoin-linked card programs, with payment volume up nearly 200% from the previous year, creating a growing business for companies such as Bridge, Wirex, and Rain that provide the infrastructure behind those cards.
Much of their revenue comes from payment fees, with additional opportunities in currency conversion, settlement financing, and customer subscriptions. The new funding source hasn't removed the traditional costs of running a card program, which still need to be covered every time someone makes a purchase.
The card still runs on familiar fees
The name printed on a stablecoin card rarely identifies every company involved in processing the payment.
The consumer app manages the customer relationship, the regulated issuer provides the card, the payment network connects participating institutions, and the merchant's provider handles acceptance, with conversion or settlement services sometimes supplied by another business.
Those responsibilities can overlap, but funding the purchase with USDC doesn't eliminate them, and each participant needs enough revenue to cover its part of the transaction.
| Participant | Role in the payment | Potential revenue | 
|---|---|---|
| Card issuer | Issues the card and manages issuing responsibilities | Interchange | 
| Wallet or card brand | Provides the app and customer relationship | Interchange share, subscriptions, transaction fees | 
| Card network | Connects financial institutions and processes payments | Network and processing fees | 
| Merchant's payment provider | Enables the merchant to accept cards | Merchant service charges | 
| Settlement lender, where used | Advances money for payment obligations | Interest | 
Companies can perform more than one role, and these aren't separate fees necessarily charged on every transaction.
Interchange matters because the merchant's bank or payment provider pays it to the card issuer, usually as part of the broader fees merchants pay to accept cards.
Visa earns money from its network and related services, while the issuer's agreements determine how much revenue it can share with the company operating the customer-facing card.
Bridge, which Stripe acquired in 2025, advertises a card product that allows program operators to retain 100% of interchange and charge additional transaction fees.
That gives crypto wallets and financial apps a way to earn money when customers spend their balances, although the amount retained after processing costs, fraud prevention, compliance, and other expenses depends on each program's arrangements.
Those expenses don't end when a payment is approved. Disputed purchases can produce chargebacks weeks later, fraudulent transactions require investigation, and customer support costs continue regardless of whether the provider earns enough from an individual purchase to cover them.
Pavel Matveev, Wirex co-founder and CEO, told CryptoSlate that programs using the company's infrastructure process more than $200 million in monthly spending, including partner activity.
The company hasn't provided the requested breakdown of transaction fees and revenue sharing, so its reported processing volume can't establish how much of it Wirex retains.
Someone has to fund the stablecoin payment
Card payments also create obligations that aren't always settled when a customer taps the terminal. Authorization lets the merchant accept the purchase, while the financial institutions involved must later settle what they owe one another, sometimes before the customer's funds have completed their journey through the system.
Stablecoins can move around the clock, but card programs still need access to money when settlement obligations come due, which creates demand for short-term financing even when the underlying transaction begins with digital dollars.
Rain, a provider of stablecoin-linked card infrastructure, uses a revolving credit facility from Credit Coop to meet its Visa settlement obligations. Under the arrangement, Rain draws on the facility to fund payments, then directs incoming cardholder proceeds through smart contracts that help repay the borrowing and interest.
Credit Coop earns income for supplying money during the interval between payment and repayment, allowing Rain to support transactions without keeping enough idle cash to cover every settlement obligation entirely from its own resources.
Borrowing $1 million at an annual rate of 10% would cost approximately $274 for one day, compared with about $68 for six hours. Those aren't Rain's disclosed borrowing terms, but they show why faster settlement can reduce financing costs without changing how much customers spend.
Revolving credit also lets the same capital fund successive batches of payments as earlier advances are repaid, so cumulative processing volume can far exceed the amount borrowed at any given moment.
Credit Coop's financing model allows card operators to cover Visa settlement obligations with borrowed stablecoins rather than tying up their own cash. Visa claims the arrangement has reduced borrowing costs by as much as 30% for some participants, although the underlying terms and allocation of credit risk remain undisclosed.
The potential benefit is lower funding costs for card operators, but no evidence yet shows those savings are being passed on to customers through lower fees.
Visa also supports USDC settlement between participating financial institutions, allowing stablecoins to move further through the payment system without requiring the merchant to receive them.
The currency a customer spends, the currency institutions use to settle, and the money ultimately deposited into the merchant's account can all be different.
Stablecoin cashback has to survive the math
Rewards introduce another cost, and the fee income available to cover them can be much smaller than the advertised cashback rate.
Britain's Payment Systems Regulator sets interchange caps of 0.2% for covered domestic consumer debit transactions and 0.3% for covered consumer credit transactions. On a qualifying £100 debit purchase, that leaves at most 20 pence in interchange before the issuer's operating expenses or any share paid to a card partner.
Offering 2% cashback on the same purchase would cost £2, leaving a £1.80 gap that would need to come from another revenue source or a promotional budget.
The UK caps don't apply to every stablecoin card or international transaction, but they show why generous rewards can't always be funded from ordinary payment fees. Providers can cover the difference through subscriptions, conversion charges, income from other services, or subsidies designed to attract new customers.
Those arrangements become more important when the advertised cashback depends on maintaining a qualifying token balance, joining a paid plan, or meeting minimum spending requirements.
With the Wirex card, higher cryptoback rates are tied to subscription tiers and token lockups, and rewards vary by market and customer plan.
The customer's return depends on the entire arrangement. Cashback loses much of its appeal when a monthly subscription, conversion spread, or foreign-transaction charge eats into the benefit, especially for customers who don't spend enough to justify an upgraded plan.
For the operator, a customer who makes one purchase to collect an introductory bonus has different economics than someone who uses the card for groceries, travel, and bills every month.
Revenue from repeat spending can help cover the cost of acquiring and supporting customers, but that depends on how much the program earns after rewards and its partners' fees.
The customer may save money, but not always
Stablecoin cards offer their best advantage to people who already receive or hold digital dollars.
For example, freelancers paid in stablecoins can spend their earnings without repeatedly transferring money through a crypto exchange and a local bank, avoiding some of the steps and charges involved in accessing those funds.
Whether that convenience translates into savings depends on the customer's alternatives and the transaction's total cost.
Someone earning and spending euros faces a different calculation because converting euros into dollar stablecoins and then back into euros at checkout can introduce currency costs that wouldn't arise with an ordinary euro-denominated bank card.
Even someone paid directly in stablecoins needs to consider conversion spreads, card fees, and the exchange rate applied when spending in local currency.
Dollar-linked tokens aim to maintain a stable value against the dollar. Their purchasing power in euros, pesos, or pounds can change with foreign-exchange rates, regardless of whether the token maintains its dollar peg.
Those differences make it hard to estimate typical customer savings from card-spending totals alone. Wirex hasn't supplied transaction-level fee figures or retention data that would let its reported payment activity connect to individual customer economics, while public spending dashboards don't show how much of each purchase stays with the companies operating the cards.
Despite the rapid growth in stablecoin-card spending, the volume moving through these products doesn't establish whether customers keep using them after introductory incentives end or whether providers consistently earn more than they spend serving those customers.
Stablecoin cards made digital dollars easier to use at ordinary businesses without asking merchants to change how they accept payments. The companies making that possible now earn money from the same services that have supported card payments for decades, with blockchain-based settlement potentially reducing some costs.
For people paying with stablecoins, the benefit comes down to the money left after every fee, conversion, and reward is counted. For the companies behind the cards, it comes down to whether enough customers find that benefit worth returning for.

articles.title: Crypto Today: tablecoin Savings, Solana, OpenAI
articles.text:
Here’s what happened in crypto today
Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
Today in crypto, Stablecoin issuer Circle is seeking to enter about 40 developing markets, according to CEO Jeremy Allaire. and a new report highlighted substantial cost savings from stablecoin remittances, especially in emerging markets. Meanwhile, Solana postponed its Shanghai event after registrations exceeded local capacity limits.
Circle’s Allaire says stablecoin issuer looking to enter 40 developing markets: Report
Stablecoin issuer Circle is seeking to enter about 40 developing markets, according to the company’s CEO and chairman, Jeremy Allaire.
“We’re kind of going through an inflection point...a transition right now, and that transition is essentially moving from the early adopter phase of blockchain technology into the mainstream scaling phase,” Allaire told Reuters, speaking Friday on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok.
Markets in Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa and the Middle East are experiencing increasing demand for stablecoins as businesses and individuals seek to enter the internet-based economic system, Allaire reportedly said.
Stablecoin remittances cost 84% less than traditional transfers, Borderless finds
Stablecoin-funded remittances cost roughly 84% less than traditional money transfers, according to a new third-quarter report from payments network Borderless.xyz.
Sending $200 through stablecoin payment networks costs a median of $2, or 1%, compared with $12.72, or 6.36%, for conventional remittances. The comparison uses Borderless pricing from the third quarter of 2026 and World Bank data from the same period last year.
Savings were particularly pronounced in emerging markets. In Sub-Saharan Africa, stablecoin remittances cost 2.9%, compared with 8.46% for traditional transfers. In Latin America, the respective costs were 1.25% and 5.64%.
Businesses also stand to benefit. A $10,000 stablecoin-funded transfer to the eurozone costs as little as $26, compared with $135 to $150 for an international bank wire, including foreign-exchange costs.
Stablecoin payouts also settled faster in several markets, with a median of two minutes in Brazil and Colombia and three minutes in Mexico. Traditional SWIFT transfers typically settled the next business day.
However, reliability varied. Payment completion rates reached 98.6% in Mexico but fell to 73% in Costa Rica, highlighting differences in local payment infrastructure.
Solana’s Liu says Shanghai event postponed over registration surge
The Solana Accelerate event in Shanghai was postponed after pre-registration exceeded the event cap set by local authorities, according to Lily Liu, president of the Solana Foundation.
Event registration quadrupled overnight following publicity for the event, Liu wrote in a Friday X post, adding that organizers decided to postpone the event to “comply with local requirements.”
Earlier on Friday, X users claimed that the event was “abruptly suspended” as law enforcement officers were stationed at the venue.
In October 2025, a Solana event in Shenzhen was also cut short due to venue capacity and public-safety concerns, Solana’s Chinese-language community account announced then on X.
Shanghai was scheduled to open Solana’s four-city Accelerate China tour, followed by Hangzhou on Sunday, Shenzhen on Tuesday and Beijing on Thursday, according to the event’s website.
The postponement followed Solana executives’ promotion of a new Shanghai office earlier this week.

articles.title: Chinese Startup StepFun Launches a Phone Built Around an AI Agent, Not Apps - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- StepFun launched the STEPX Neo on Oct. 13, a 3,999-yuan phone, about $560, running its Step AOS 1.0 operating system with a built-in AI agent called Amoo.
- Pre-orders opened on JD.com, Tmall and Douyin, and the price includes 12 months of AI access at 100 billion tokens a month.
- Nearly 100 partners including Alipay and Tencent have signed on, after ByteDance's Doubao phone agent drew blocks from major Chinese apps in December.
StepFun, a Chinese AI startup backed by Tencent, launched the STEPX Neo, a phone whose AI agent is built into the operating system itself instead of sitting in an app.
The operating system is the core software that runs a phone, like iOS or Android. Pre-orders opened that evening at 3,999 yuan, about $560, with a first sales event on Oct. 16.
Instead of opening a ride-hailing app, typing an address and picking a car, you tell the phone where you want to go, and its agent—software that takes a goal and carries it out on its own—handles the remaining steps.
StepFun told the launch audience that in the agent era AI is no longer an add-on to a smartphone but the product itself.
StepFun first showed the agent, the operating system, and the STEPX brand in Shanghai on July 13, without a price or sales date. The company said at the time that conventional smartphone software was never built for autonomous task execution.
Siri and Gemini are assistants that live inside iOS and Android. StepFun says its Step AOS 1.0 was instead built from scratch for the agent, with long-term memory, task scheduling, and security controls in the base layer. The company describes the system as a mix of Android, Linux, and real-time operating system components.
Step AOS breaks phone functions such as messaging, apps, files and settings into small blocks the agent can call directly, using Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a shared standard that lets AI programs plug into other software. Users get two entrances: the familiar app grid and a separate space for the agent.
The agent, called Amoo, keeps one memory for the user's facts, habits, and preferences and another for what it has learned about carrying out tasks. Simple commands like setting an alarm run on a small model inside the phone, some of them offline, while harder requests that span several apps go to a larger model in the cloud. A second MiniLED screen on the back shows what Amoo is doing.
Nearly 100 companies and products, including Alipay, Tencent, Ctrip, Didi and Meituan, have signed on to Amoo, and payments, travel bookings and content creation are still completed by their own platforms. That is StepFun's alternative to the screen-reading and simulated-click approach Doubao used.
StepFun, founded in 2023 by former Microsoft vice president Jiang Daxin, builds its own large language model, or LLM, the kind of AI system behind ChatGPT. Its flagship, Step 5 Preview, arrived in September with 600 billion parameters, the internal numbers a model adjusts while training, of which 27 billion are active at a time.
Step 5 Preview can take in up to 1 million tokens, the chunks of text AI services count and bill by, at once. The smaller Step 3.5 Flash, released earlier this year, is open-source under an Apache 2.0 license.
The 3,999-yuan price includes 12 months of the STEPX Token Plan, which provides 100 billion tokens a month, and StepFun has not said what the AI costs after the first year.

articles.title: Binance Pool shuts on November 10, with record access ending two weeks later
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Binance Pool will stop accepting mining shares at 07:00 UTC on November 10, requiring miners to switch pools beforehand.
- Account steps are requested by 23:59 UTC that day, while final rewards and settlements remain subject to eligibility.
- Binance Pool’s historical pages close at 07:00 UTC on November 24, leaving users a limited window to save records.
Miners connected to Binance Pool need to redirect their equipment before 07:00 UTC on Nov. 10, 2026, when Binance will shut the service and stop crediting new mining work.
Binance set out the timetable in an Oct. 13 closure notice. The shutdown also covers Pool Savings, Cloud Mining and Transaction Accelerator, alongside Telegram hashrate alerts, email notifications and mining-pool API services.
Binance will disable its Stratum URLs and mining endpoints at the cutoff. Later hashrate submissions and mining shares will not be accepted, processed or credited.
Eligible shares submitted before the deadline will still enter the final reward calculation under Binance Pool rules.
A mining share is proof of work submitted while contributing computing power to a pool, according to Binance’s Mining Pool Product Terms.
Users with active Pool Savings positions should also review them and unsubscribe or redeem before the service ends. The product terms make redemptions subject to daily limits and available liquidity, with requests processed in the order received. They provide for transfers within one business day, or up to 90 days in exceptional circumstances.
Final payments and records have separate deadlines
Eligible outstanding rewards, balances, refunds or settlements, where applicable, will be processed after the mining cutoff. Product rules, account status, risk controls, compliance checks and applicable law still govern eligibility.
Binance asks users to ensure their accounts can receive any eligible remainder, including completing required identity checks where applicable, by 23:59 UTC on Nov. 10. That is a deadline for necessary account steps; it does not extend mining operations or promise a payout that evening.
Under the existing product terms, users must meet platform requirements and keep account details current to remain eligible for rewards. Selected assets may also require a valid designated third-party wallet address.
Binance Pool pages will remain accessible until 07:00 UTC on Nov. 24 for historical data, account records and payout status, where available. Binance asks users to save relevant records before those pages become permanently inaccessible.

articles.title: Solana resilient but observation warranted
articles.text:
Solana shows resilience, but some areas need continued observation, Fidelity says
Solana has had no reported mainnet outages in two years, but concentrations in stake, hosting and client software should be monitored, according to a report.
Solana has made significant progress in terms of network health across resilience, economic security and performance indicators, according to a Fidelity report.
Solana has had no reported mainnet outages in two years, but concentrations in stake, hosting and client software could threaten this, according to the report by Fidelity’s Center for Applied Technology (FCAT).
The report said economic security was supported by substantial staking participation and incentives that reward validator performance. Low latency, expanded capacity and inexpensive transactions also support practical use at scale.
Related: Solana Foundation hires ex-Binance CMO and payments exec as new partnerships expand
Still, it noted that several areas surrounding decentralization and resilience warrant continued observation, including stake concentrates among a small number of validator identities and operators.
Cointelegraph reported on Aug. 21 that Solana had reduced its slot time to 350 milliseconds, marking the first such reduction since the inception of the network, according to the Solana Foundation’s vice president of technology, Jacob Creech.
In June, the Solana Foundation shared plans to reduce slot times to 200ms, arguing that it would improve latency and accelerate confirmations on the blockchain network. Three further 50ms reductions are planned.
