articles.title: Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
articles.text:
Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Edinburgh
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills.
- Share:
Brain cells that normally help protect the brain may play an unexpected role in cognitive decline as we grow older. Scientists have discovered that cells responsible for maintaining the protective coating around nerve fibers can become dysfunctional with age, potentially contributing to the gradual loss of memory and thinking abilities.
The research, published in Nature Medicine, challenges the long-held belief that these cells are always beneficial. By examining human brain tissue and conducting experiments in mice, researchers found evidence that problems with these normally supportive cells can damage nerve fibers and interfere with cognitive function.
The discovery also points to a possible new approach for protecting the aging brain. Drugs that act on the biological pathway involved are already being used to treat other neurological conditions, raising hopes that existing treatments could eventually be adapted to combat age-related cognitive decline.
Scientists Discover Changes in the Aging Brain
The study was led by researchers from the University of Edinburgh and the UK Dementia Research Institute, who investigated how changes in the brain relate to declining cognitive abilities later in life.
Their research focused on the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936, a group of people whose cognitive abilities have been tracked from childhood into old age. This unusually extensive record allowed scientists to investigate how thinking and memory changed over decades.
Between ages 70 and 82, participants underwent assessments measuring memory, the speed at which they processed information, and their ability to understand spatial relationships.
Of the 1,091 people enrolled in the cohort, 866 completed additional cognitive testing after age 70. Nearly everyone experienced at least some decline, but the rate varied considerably. These differences gave researchers an opportunity to investigate what might distinguish brains experiencing faster deterioration from those aging more gradually.
When scientists examined brain tissue collected after death from a subset of participants, they discovered a striking pattern. Individuals who had experienced greater cognitive decline tended to have fewer large nerve fibers, along with an abnormal buildup of unhealthy myelin.
Myelin is the protective coating that surrounds nerve fibers, helping electrical signals travel efficiently through the brain. Although this insulation is essential for normal brain function, the findings suggest that excessive or abnormal myelin may become part of the problem.
The changes were especially pronounced around the large nerve fibers that remained. Importantly, these abnormalities were associated with how quickly cognitive abilities declined, rather than how well someone performed on cognitive tests at a particular age.
A Protective Brain Cell May Have a Hidden Weakness
To understand what might be causing these changes, the researchers turned their attention to oligodendrocytes, specialized brain cells responsible for producing and maintaining myelin.
Oligodendrocytes have traditionally been regarded as beneficial because they help keep nerve fibers insulated and functioning properly. However, the new findings suggest that these cells can become dysfunctional during aging and may contribute to the very problems they normally help prevent.
The researchers discovered that people with more severe cognitive decline had lower levels of a protein called NRF2 inside their oligodendrocytes.
NRF2 plays an important protective role in cells by regulating hundreds of genes involved in defending against damage and maintaining normal cellular function. When its activity decreases, cells may become less capable of protecting themselves and performing their usual jobs.
To investigate whether this protein was directly involved in the brain changes, the team conducted experiments in mice.
When researchers specifically reduced NRF2 in oligodendrocytes, the animals developed excessive myelin and lost large nerve fibers, closely resembling the abnormalities observed in human brain tissue. The mice also showed reduced improvements in cognitive performance as they aged.
These experiments provided evidence that declining NRF2 activity can directly disrupt oligodendrocyte function, potentially triggering changes in myelin and nerve fibers that contribute to cognitive decline.
Existing Drugs Could Offer a New Treatment Strategy
The findings may have important implications for developing treatments that help preserve cognitive abilities in older adults.
One particularly promising aspect is that the NRF2 pathway is already a target of medications used for other conditions, including a drug prescribed to treat multiple sclerosis (MS).
Previous studies have found that increasing NRF2 activity can improve cognitive function in people with MS. That raises the possibility that medications acting on the same pathway might eventually be repurposed to address oligodendrocyte dysfunction and age-related cognitive decline.
Although further research is needed to determine whether such treatments would benefit older adults experiencing cognitive decline, the discovery identifies a potentially valuable therapeutic target.
Veronique Miron, MRC Senior Non-Clinical Fellow and UK Dementia Research Institute Group Leader at the University of Edinburgh and St. Michael's Hospital, part of Unity Health Toronto, said:
"As the prevalence of cognitive decline is rising with an aging population and no current treatments exist, we are excited about this work as it points to a potential strategy for new therapeutic strategies to preserve cognitive ability in aging."
A New Understanding of Cognitive Decline
Beyond its potential medical applications, the research changes how scientists understand the role of oligodendrocytes in the aging brain.
Rather than simply providing support for healthy nerve function throughout life, these cells appear capable of becoming dysfunctional and contributing to cognitive problems.
Georgina Craig, the study's first author and a Postdoctoral Fellow at St Michael's Hospital in Toronto and the UK Dementia Research Institute, said:
"This study has fundamentally shifted how we think about these brain cells in aging. We have always considered oligodendrocytes as purely beneficial, yet here we surprisingly find that they can become dysfunctional and contribute to cognitive impairment in aging."
The findings suggest that maintaining healthy oligodendrocyte function could become an important strategy for protecting memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.
Published in Nature Medicine, the study was funded by the UKRI Medical Research Council (MRC) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR). The research also involved scientists from the University of Edinburgh's Lothian Birth Cohort studies and Northwestern University.

articles.title: NASA’s Webb reveals the wild weather of a mysterious world 20 light-years away
articles.text:
NASA’s Webb reveals the wild weather of a mysterious world 20 light-years away
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- Trinity College Dublin
- Summary:
- NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed that a turbulent world 20 light-years away has a surprisingly orderly weather system, with three recurring atmospheric states driven by temperature changes and shifting clouds. The breakthrough gives scientists a powerful new tool for uncovering weather patterns on distant worlds and understanding the conditions that shape their atmospheres.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a powerful new way to decode the weather on distant worlds, revealing surprisingly organized patterns hidden within the turbulent atmosphere of a mysterious object 20 light-years from Earth.
Researchers at Trinity College Dublin used observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to investigate SIMP 0136, a brown dwarf previously associated with phenomena resembling the northern lights. They found that its complex weather is largely governed by just two factors: changes in temperature and the vertical structure of its clouds.
The discovery offers a new way to understand the atmospheric conditions of distant worlds and could help astronomers investigate planets far beyond our Solar System.
How NASA's Webb Telescope Decoded Alien Weather
To investigate SIMP 0136, the researchers analyzed observations collected by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) using a mathematical technique called Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
This technique helps scientists make sense of large, complicated datasets by identifying the strongest patterns within them. In this case, the team examined how the brown dwarf's light changed as it rotated, looking for subtle variations that could reveal what was happening in its atmosphere.
Rather than beginning with detailed assumptions about how the atmosphere should behave, the researchers allowed the observations to reveal the most important processes. The method also helped separate genuine atmospheric changes from minor fluctuations and random noise in the measurements.
Webb's exceptionally sensitive instruments made this possible by detecting extremely small changes in the object's brightness as different parts of its atmosphere rotated into view.
Scientists Discover Hidden Order in Chaotic Alien Weather
The results revealed something unexpected. Although SIMP 0136 appears to have a highly complicated atmosphere, nearly all of its observed atmospheric variability could be explained by just two dominant components, consistent with temperature fluctuations and changes in the vertical arrangement of clouds.
Even more remarkably, the researchers identified three recurring weather states that appear and disappear from view as the brown dwarf rotates.
Together, these states create a shifting atmospheric patchwork. Some regions are hotter and have thinner clouds, while others are cooler and contain thicker cloud layers that extend farther vertically through the atmosphere.
Instead of constantly changing in an unpredictable way, these weather patterns appear to follow an underlying structure.
The findings, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, suggest that the seemingly chaotic atmosphere of SIMP 0136 is actually governed by a remarkably consistent set of processes.
Brown dwarfs occupy an unusual place between planets and stars. SIMP 0136 is larger and hotter than a typical gas giant planet, but it lacks the mass needed to shine like a star. Its atmosphere contains enormous cloud systems that evolve rapidly, making its weather more comparable to an extreme version of Jupiter's than anything experienced on Earth.
These immense weather systems can span planetary scales, continually changing the appearance of the distant world.
"We also discovered that these drivers of the weather patterns on SIMP-0136 persist over time, even as the detailed appearance of the atmosphere evolves over more than a dozen rotations," said first author Merle Schrader, a PhD candidate in Trinity's School of Physics.
"In relative terms, SIMP 0136 is one of the easier brown dwarfs for us to capture high-quality data from. These data have been studied before by established methods, allowing us to compare some of the results from this new technique to what we already know about this object. The technique has also helped us develop a better understanding of what drives the weather on this faraway world and how these weather patterns interact and co-exist, but perhaps even more importantly, it shows how this approach can be further refined and applied to other, less well-known brown dwarfs in different parts of space."
A Remarkable Connection Across 20 Light Years
For Schrader, the research also revealed an extraordinary personal connection to the distant object.
SIMP 0136 is located approximately 20 light years from Earth, meaning its light takes about two decades to reach us. The light captured by Webb in 2023, which provided the observations used in the study, had actually left the brown dwarf during the year Schrader was born.
"Light travels at around 300,000 km/s but, even at that speed, it took two decades to reach us, peering through the JWST lenses," she said.
"When you consider light takes just over a second to reach the Moon after leaving Earth, that gives a sense of how far away SIMP 0136 is, and how incredible astrophysical progress has been. I think it's amazing that we have been able to discern the intimate weather patterns of a distant world and map their interactions from our cozy little corner of the universe, when all we observe directly of these objects is a single pixel spread across the light spectrum."
The achievement highlights how much information astronomers can extract from seemingly tiny amounts of light. Even though SIMP 0136 appears as little more than a single point in telescope observations, changes in its brightness at different wavelengths can reveal detailed information about its atmosphere.
What This Discovery Means for Distant Planets
The new technique could have implications far beyond SIMP 0136.
Brown dwarfs are particularly valuable for investigating the atmospheres of giant exoplanets, which are planets orbiting stars outside our Solar System. Because brown dwarfs can often be observed directly, they give scientists an opportunity to study atmospheric processes that are much harder to investigate on most exoplanets.
By examining these objects, researchers can test how clouds form, how heat moves through an atmosphere, and how atmospheric circulation behaves under extreme conditions.
The technique developed by the Trinity team could make those investigations considerably more efficient. By quickly identifying the processes responsible for most of the observed atmospheric changes, astronomers can better determine which features deserve closer examination using more complicated computer models.
Professor Johanna Vos, Associate Professor in Trinity School of Physics, explained the potential significance of the findings.
"Our findings will transform how astronomers analyze future JWST observations. Since our approach rapidly identifies the dominant components of the atmosphere it offers an efficient first step before we begin computationally intensive modeling.
"Applying this technique to a wide range of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets will help us better understand the diverse weather systems that shape worlds far beyond our Solar System."
Ultimately, understanding weather on distant worlds is about more than identifying clouds and temperature changes. Atmospheric behavior can provide important clues about a planet's chemical composition, physical conditions, and overall environment.
Those insights are also relevant to one of astronomy's biggest questions: which planets beyond our Solar System might have conditions capable of supporting life?
By revealing how complex alien atmospheres can be understood from faint changes in light, this new approach could help scientists take another step toward answering that question.

articles.title: A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
articles.text:
A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
Forest soils may be quietly helping fight climate change more effectively than scientists expected.
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Göttingen
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.
- Share:
Forest soils are playing a surprisingly powerful role in removing methane from the atmosphere, and new findings suggest that certain effects of climate change could make them even better at it. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming, but microorganisms living in the soil can break it down before it builds up in the air.
Scientists from the University of Göttingen and the Baden-Württemberg Forest Research Institute (FVA) analyzed the world's most comprehensive collection of long-term measurements of methane absorption by forest soils. Their findings revealed an unexpected trend: under certain climate conditions that could become more common in the future, forest soils can actually increase the amount of methane they remove from the atmosphere.
The researchers examined measurements collected from 13 forest sites in southwestern Germany over periods of up to 24 years. On average, the amount of methane absorbed by the soils increased by approximately 3% annually. The researchers linked this rise to declining rainfall and warmer temperatures, which create conditions that make it easier for methane to enter the soil and be broken down by microorganisms.
The findings, published in Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, challenge previous research suggesting that climate change is generally reducing the ability of forest soils to absorb methane.
How Scientists Measured Methane Absorption Over 24 Years
To understand how methane absorption changes over time, the researchers examined an extensive collection of soil gas measurements gathered through the FVA's long-running monitoring program.
The measurements included soil gas profiles, which reveal the chemical composition of gases trapped in the soil at different depths. Every two weeks, researchers collected air samples through thin tubes installed beneath the ground and analyzed them in a laboratory. This repeated sampling allowed scientists to track changes in methane concentrations over many years.
To confirm their findings, the team also used an independent measurement technique involving airtight chambers placed directly on the soil surface. By monitoring how gas concentrations changed inside these chambers, the researchers could determine whether the soil was absorbing methane and calculate how much was being removed.
Combining these methods gave the scientists a detailed picture of methane uptake across the forest sites and how it responded to changing environmental conditions.
Why Warmer, Drier Forest Soils Absorb More Methane
Although methane absorption varied considerably between the 13 locations, a clear overall pattern emerged. Forest soils in southwestern Germany were particularly effective at removing methane from the atmosphere during periods of lower rainfall and higher temperatures.
"Our long-term data shows that climate change does not necessarily have a negative impact on how much methane forest soils absorb. While the largest study to date from the US found a decline in methane uptake of up to 80 percent due to increasing rainfall, our significantly more comprehensive field study in south-western Germany found the opposite, " explains Professor Martin Maier at Göttingen University's Department of Crop Sciences, who led the study and was previously involved in the FVA's soil gas monitoring program.
"We observed a significant long-term increase in methane uptake in the forest areas we studied."
The explanation lies partly in how water moves through the ground. When soil becomes saturated with moisture, water fills many of the tiny spaces between soil particles, making it more difficult for gases to move through them. Drier soil contains more pores filled with air, allowing atmospheric methane to travel deeper into the ground.
Once methane enters the soil, microorganisms use it as an energy source, breaking it down in the process. Rising temperatures can slightly accelerate this microbial activity, allowing the organisms to consume methane more quickly.
Together, these two effects help explain why warmer temperatures and reduced rainfall were associated with greater methane absorption in the forests studied.
Findings Challenge Previous Climate Change Research
The results offer a different perspective from several major international research reviews. These analyses, known as meta-analyses, combine findings from numerous individual studies to identify broader patterns. Many have concluded that methane absorption by forest soils is declining.
However, the German study suggests that the relationship between climate change and methane uptake is more complicated than those overall trends indicate. While increasing rainfall can reduce methane absorption by limiting the movement of gas through soil, drier conditions can produce the opposite effect.
The findings do not mean that climate change is beneficial for forests overall. Instead, they demonstrate that its effects on methane absorption can differ considerably depending on local temperatures, rainfall patterns, and soil conditions.
The researchers emphasize that these regional differences make long-term monitoring especially important. Shorter studies or analyses that combine measurements from widely different environments may miss gradual changes that only become apparent after years of observation.
"Our results make it clear that taking a series of measurements over many years and running monitoring programs are indispensable for assessing the real effects of climate change," says Maier.

articles.title: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
articles.text:
Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
Scientists have uncovered a hidden brain circuit linking deep sleep, growth hormone, and wakefulness, revealing why a good night's sleep is essential for both body and brain health.
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.
- Share:
A good night's sleep does much more than leave you feeling refreshed. During deep sleep, the body releases growth hormone, a powerful chemical messenger that helps build muscle, strengthen bones, and regulate fat metabolism. For teenagers, getting enough sleep is especially important because growth hormone plays a major role in reaching their full height potential.
Scientists have long known that insufficient sleep can interfere with growth hormone production. What remained unclear was exactly how the brain controls this process, particularly during non-REM sleep, the deep, restorative stage that typically dominates the earlier part of the night.
Now, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have uncovered the brain circuitry behind this relationship. In a study published in the journal Cell, the team identified the neurons that regulate growth hormone release during sleep and discovered a previously unknown feedback system that helps maintain a delicate balance between hormone levels and wakefulness.
The discovery reveals that the relationship works in both directions. Sleep stimulates growth hormone production, but growth hormone also sends signals back to the brain that influence when we wake up.
The findings could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to treating sleep disorders associated with metabolic diseases such as diabetes, as well as neurological conditions including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.
"People know that growth hormone release is tightly related to sleep, but only through drawing blood and checking growth hormone levels during sleep," said study first author Xinlu Ding, a postdoctoral fellow in UC Berkeley's Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute. "We're actually directly recording neural activity in mice to see what's going on. We are providing a basic circuit to work on in the future to develop different treatments."
Why Deep Sleep Matters for Growth and Metabolism
Growth hormone is best known for its role in childhood development, but its importance extends well into adulthood. It supports the maintenance of muscle and bone, helps the body regulate how it uses stored fat, and influences blood sugar levels.
When sleep is consistently disrupted, growth hormone regulation can suffer. Because this hormone helps control glucose and fat metabolism, inadequate sleep may contribute to an increased risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.
To understand how the brain coordinates these processes, the Berkeley researchers focused on a region called the hypothalamus. Located deep within the brain, this small but essential control center helps regulate hunger, body temperature, hormone production, and the daily cycle of sleeping and waking. Its basic functions have been preserved throughout mammalian evolution.
Within the hypothalamus, the researchers examined neurons that produce growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) and two distinct types of neurons that produce somatostatin.
These chemical messengers have opposing functions. GHRH encourages growth hormone secretion, while somatostatin suppresses it. Together, they help control how much growth hormone enters the bloodstream, largely by regulating its release from the pituitary gland, a small hormone-producing structure at the base of the brain.
The scientists also investigated how growth hormone influences the locus coeruleus, a region in the brainstem involved in alertness, attention, thinking, and the drive to explore new or unfamiliar experiences.
Disruptions in the activity of this region have been linked to several psychiatric and neurological disorders.
"Understanding the neural circuit for growth hormone release could eventually point toward new hormonal therapies to improve sleep quality or restore normal growth hormone balance," said Daniel Silverman, a UC Berkeley postdoctoral fellow and study co-author. "There are some experimental gene therapies where you target a specific cell type. This circuit could be a novel handle to try to dial back the excitability of the locus coeruleus, which hasn't been talked about before."
Scientists Map the Brain Circuit That Controls Growth Hormone
The research was conducted in the laboratory of Yang Dan, a professor of neuroscience and of molecular and cell biology at UC Berkeley.
To investigate how the circuitry works, the team studied mice using electrodes implanted in their brains. The scientists recorded neural activity while using light to stimulate specific neurons in the hypothalamus, allowing them to observe how different parts of the system responded.
Mice are particularly useful for studying sleep regulation because their sleep patterns differ significantly from those of humans. Rather than sleeping through one long stretch each night, mice typically sleep in brief episodes lasting only several minutes, scattered throughout the day and night.
This gave the researchers repeated opportunities to examine how neural activity and growth hormone regulation changed as the animals moved between sleeping and waking.
Using advanced techniques to trace connections between brain cells, the team discovered that GHRH and somatostatin behave differently depending on the stage of sleep.
During rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, the stage commonly associated with vivid dreaming, activity involving both GHRH and somatostatin increases. Although these hormones normally exert opposing effects, their coordinated activity during this stage contributes to increased growth hormone release.
During non-REM sleep, the pattern changes. Somatostatin activity decreases, reducing its inhibitory influence, while GHRH activity rises moderately. This combination also promotes growth hormone secretion.
The discovery helps explain how different sleep stages can support the release of the same essential hormone through distinct patterns of brain activity.
Growth Hormone Also Helps Control When We Wake Up
Perhaps the most surprising finding was that growth hormone does not simply respond to signals from the sleeping brain. It also influences the brain circuits that control wakefulness.
As growth hormone gradually builds up during sleep, it stimulates neurons in the locus coeruleus, increasing their activity and helping promote the transition toward waking.
This creates a feedback loop in which sleep encourages growth hormone release, and the resulting hormone activity helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.
The researchers also identified an unexpected complication. Although greater activity in the locus coeruleus generally promotes alertness, excessive stimulation can have the opposite effect.
In an earlier study published the same year, Silverman demonstrated that when neurons in this region become overexcited, they can paradoxically promote sleepiness rather than wakefulness.
Together, these findings reveal a carefully regulated system in which the brain must balance competing signals to maintain healthy sleep and hormone activity.
Scientists describe this type of self-regulating process as homeostasis, the body's ability to maintain stable internal conditions even as its environment and physiological demands change.
"This suggests that sleep and growth hormone form a tightly balanced system: Too little sleep reduces growth hormone release, and too much growth hormone can in turn push the brain toward wakefulness," Silverman said. "Sleep drives growth hormone release, and growth hormone feeds back to regulate wakefulness, and this balance is essential for growth, repair and metabolic health."
A Surprising Connection Between Sleep and Brain Health
The newly identified feedback system may have implications that extend beyond physical growth and metabolism.
Because the locus coeruleus helps regulate attention, alertness, and cognitive function, growth hormone's influence on this region suggests it could also play a role in how effectively the brain functions after waking.
This raises the possibility that maintaining healthy sleep and growth hormone rhythms may support both physical recovery and mental performance.
"Growth hormone not only helps you build your muscle and bones and reduce your fat tissue, but may also have cognitive benefits, promoting your overall arousal level when you wake up," Ding said.
By identifying the specific brain cells and signaling pathways involved, the researchers have provided a foundation for exploring therapies that target disrupted sleep and hormone regulation.
Such approaches could eventually prove useful for people with sleep disturbances related to metabolic disorders or neurological diseases. However, the experiments were conducted in mice, and additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans and whether they can be safely targeted with treatments.
The findings underscore a fundamental principle of sleep biology: Rest is not simply a period when the brain switches off. It is an active, carefully coordinated process in which hormones and neural circuits constantly communicate to support growth, repair, metabolism, and wakefulness.
Research Funding and Contributors
The research was supported by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI), which supported Dan as an HHMI investigator until the year of the study's publication, and the Pivotal Life Sciences Chancellor's Chair fund.
Dan holds the Pivotal Life Sciences Chancellor's Chair in Neuroscience.
Additional co-authors include Peng Zhong, Bing Li, Chenyan Ma, Lihui Lu, Grace Jiang, Zhe Zhang, Xiaolin Huang, Xun Tu, and Zhiyu Melissa Tian of UC Berkeley, along with Fuu-Jiun Hwang and Jun Ding of Stanford University.

Neuroendocrine circuit for sleep-dependent growth hormone release. Cell, 2025; 188 (18): 4968 DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2025.05.039

articles.title: Scientists predicted doomsday for November 13, 2026. Should we be worried?
articles.text:
Scientists predicted doomsday for November 13, 2026. Should we be worried?
- Date:
- October 16, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- In 1960, scientists predicted that runaway population growth would bring humanity to the brink of destruction on November 13, 2026, and their mathematical forecasts remained surprisingly accurate for decades. But as birth rates declined and population growth slowed, the terrifying prediction unraveled, revealing how even convincing scientific models can fail when human behavior changes.
- Share:
In 1960, Science, one of the world’s leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026. It predicted that on this future date — less than a month from today — the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself.
The outlandishness of the claim landed the article widespread public attention. More surprisingly — because its underlying research and math seemed sound — it also received careful and sustained scientific attention.
The authors — Heinz von Foerster, an Austrian-American professor and cybernetics expert and two of his students, Patricia M. Mora and Lawrence W. Amiot — argued that human populations are exceptional and might grow beyond an exponential rate, at an ever-increasing one.
“Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve,” they argued. “They will be squeezed to death.”
The article was regularly cited, and its predictions appeared remarkably accurate — until around 1993, halfway to the predicted “doomsday,” when the global population began falling behind its forecasts.
Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half what it was in 1960. Hopefully, we will all wake up on Nov. 13 to an ordinary day. Nonetheless, this article remains exemplary for blending rigorous science with the art of stagecraft to staggering effect.
Unique human capacities
The mid-20th century saw increasing societal concern about global population growth and its potential to lead to resource scarcity and geopolitical conflict. Underlying much of this concern was implicit or explicit acceptance of the Malthusian idea that whereas population has the potential to grow exponentially, it is kept constantly under check by its capacity to feed itself.
In their article, however, von Foerster and his co-authors argued that as far as populations go, humans may be exceptional.
Given our capacity to communicate and form “coalitions” that help us resolve problems, rising population density might simply mean more opportunities for collaboration, so that our numbers might grow not only beyond an exponential rate but at an ever-increasing one.
They then used 24 estimates of the world population stretching across the past 2,000 years to show that human numbers have in fact continually outpaced expectations. All this was presented in calm, scientific prose and aided by dense mathematical equations.
‘Squeezed to death’
Von Foerster and his co-authors then projected these historical figures into the future, calculating that thanks to ever-increasing growth, in the year 2026 our numbers would near infinity.
Thankfully, the same capacity for collaboration that assisted our species’ development throughout history could now avert this catastrophe. Since we are unlikely to want to reduce our life spans, they concluded, we should work together to reduce the global birth rate by half.
This publication caused an immediate stir. There were stories in Time and The New York Times. It became the subject of a series of Pogo comic strips and many commentators took the article as strictly a tongue-in-cheek comment on population fears.
A population explosion
Rather than the story dying out, a funny thing happened. When Science published letters to the editor from mathematicians and demographers attacking von Foerster and his colleagues’ work — calling it “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd” — the authors responded with spirited defenses that doubled down on the underlying math and its conclusions.
Throughout the 1960s through to the 1980s, the “doomsday” equation became regularly cited — usually at face value — in textbooks on genetics, ecology and demography.
It appeared in stranger places, too. In a 1963 Canadian Parliamentary committee, for example, a witness from the chemical industry prominently cited it as reason chemical pesticides were required: to feed the approaching population explosion. In a 1971 U.S. Supreme Court abortion case leading up to Roe v. Wade, it was cited as why there was no compelling reason for the government to favor increased population.
The doomsday idea persisted in part because its predictions for future populations turned out to be highly accurate — at least for a while. Its core equation yielded projections that were better than those of most demographers throughout the 1970s and 1980s.
Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter and the global population began falling behind the forecasts — because the world began to do what von Foerster and his colleagues recommended it do. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.
Science and stagecraft
We will probably not all wake up on Friday, Nov. 13 “squeezed to death.” But before simply moving on — prepping for the next doomsday scenario — it is worth asking what we can learn from this one.
For me, the lesson is in how we present our beliefs to the world. Heinz von Foerster was, at one point in his life, a stage magician. Borrowing the classic language of stagecraft, an effective illusion relies on three parts: the setup, the extraordinary turn and the final reveal that returns the situation to normal.
Von Foerster and his co-authors’ article gained attention because it was an ordinary scientific article wrapped in an extraordinary title and conclusion. It retained significance because it was firmly grounded in research and argument.
To draw the world’s attention to a serious matter by way of absurdity — that’s a good trick.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Alan MacEachern, Professor, History, Western University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before
articles.text:
Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before
- Date:
- October 16, 2026
- Source:
- Stanford University
- Summary:
- Stanford scientists have developed a revolutionary microscope that reveals the hidden inner workings of living cells in real time, without the fluorescent labels that can interfere with observations. The breakthrough could provide new insights into cancer, infectious diseases, and how drugs interact with cells.
- Share:
A new microscope developed at Stanford University allows scientists to watch the tiny structures inside living cells move and interact in real time, providing an exceptionally detailed view without the fluorescent labels typically used to make these structures visible.
Researchers at Stanford have created a powerful new imaging system that reveals the inner workings of living cells with remarkable clarity. By combining two advanced microscopy techniques, the instrument achieves a resolution of approximately 120 nanometers, an unprecedented level of detail for an approach that does not require fluorescent labels.
Known as Interferometric Image Scanning Microscopy (iISM), the technology makes it possible to observe multiple cellular structures simultaneously while they move, change, and respond to their surroundings. Scientists can also investigate what happens when cells encounter drugs or disease causing organisms, potentially uncovering biological processes that have been difficult to study.
The breakthrough, described in the Nature portfolio journal Light: Science and Applications, could lead to advances in cancer research, drug development, infectious disease studies, and investigations of how plants interact with microorganisms.
"This new microscope provides a fantastic new view into the cell, where you can see the tiny structures and machines in the cell moving, changing, and interacting without having to add fluorescence to observe them," said senior author W.E. Moerner, the Harry S. Mosher Professor of Chemistry in Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences. "It's a wonderful look into these complex little cellular boxes that drive our life."
Seeing Inside Living Cells Without Fluorescent Labels
One of the most important advantages of the new microscope is its ability to reveal cellular activity without relying on fluorescent markers.
Many existing microscopy techniques use fluorescent substances to highlight specific structures inside cells. Although these methods have transformed biological research, they come with limitations. Researchers can generally label only a small number of structures at once, making it difficult to observe how different components interact across an entire cell.
Fluorescent signals can also fade during observation through a process known as photobleaching. In addition, introducing the labels can be challenging, and some markers may alter the behavior of the very structures scientists want to study.
The Stanford system avoids these problems by imaging cells without fluorescent labels. This allows researchers to follow numerous cellular components over extended periods while observing their activity in a more natural setting.
Another advantage is that iISM requires substantially less illumination power than comparable label-free methods that produce high-contrast images. Lower light exposure reduces the possibility of photodamage, which occurs when the light used for imaging harms living cells or interferes with their normal functions.
Although other specialized microscopes can achieve finer resolution, the combination of detailed imaging, gentle illumination, and extended observation makes iISM particularly valuable for studying living biological systems.
The researchers emphasize that their technology is intended to complement fluorescence microscopy rather than replace it.
First author Michelle Kueppers, a postdoctoral scholar in Moerner's laboratory, explained that combining the strengths of different imaging approaches could help scientists answer previously inaccessible questions.
"Every method has its advantages and disadvantages, and we believe in a complementary implementation in the future," Kueppers said. "If we use the strengths of fluorescence for molecular specificity and the strength of iISM for label-free context and dynamics, we can really start tackling questions that have been difficult to address before."
How the New Microscope Achieves Unprecedented Detail
The breakthrough comes from bringing together two different microscopy technologies, each with its own advantages.
Moerner received the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his pioneering contributions to super-resolution fluorescence microscopy. He specifically recruited Kueppers to Stanford because of her doctoral research involving a technique called "interferometric scattering microscopy."
This method relies on a familiar property of light: scattering.
Light changes direction when it encounters tiny particles. The same basic phenomenon explains why the sky appears blue. As sunlight passes through Earth's atmosphere, molecules, dust, and water droplets scatter its different wavelengths. Shorter blue wavelengths scatter more strongly than longer red wavelengths, producing the blue color we see overhead.
Interferometric scattering microscopy takes advantage of this behavior on a much smaller scale.
A laser illuminates a cell, causing tiny structures inside it to scatter some of the incoming light. Because the scattered signal is extremely weak, a second laser beam is used to amplify it through interference, allowing the microscope to detect structures that would otherwise be difficult to observe.
The Stanford team improved this approach by combining it with technology adapted from advanced confocal microscopes.
Traditional confocal microscopes use a small opening called a pinhole and a single detector to isolate light from a selected area. More advanced versions replace that arrangement with camera-based detector arrays capable of collecting multiple views of the same region.
The researchers incorporated an array detector into their new microscope, allowing it to collect more light than a conventional system built around a pinhole and single detector.
Hundreds of Views Combined Into One Sharper Image
The advantage of collecting multiple perspectives is similar to the way human vision works.
Our two eyes observe the world from slightly different positions, helping the brain distinguish nearby objects from those farther away. The Stanford microscope uses a related principle, but instead of relying on just two perspectives, its detector array gathers tens to hundreds of views.
The researchers developed a computational method that combines these measurements to generate images with improved sharpness, contrast, depth information, and precision.
By merging the strengths of interferometric scattering microscopy and advanced detector arrays, the team created an instrument capable of resolving structures as small as approximately 120 nanometers.
For perspective, a nanometer is one billionth of a meter. At this scale, researchers can examine extremely small cellular structures and follow their movements and interactions.
Crucially, the microscope achieves this resolution without sacrificing imaging speed or requiring intense laser illumination. Scientists can therefore observe living cells for longer periods while minimizing the risk of disturbing or damaging them.
From Cancer Drugs to Malaria: New Possibilities for Research
Moerner and Kueppers are continuing to refine the instrument, with the goal of eventually making it accessible to scientists across many areas of biology.
Three collaborations with other Stanford research groups are already underway or in development, demonstrating the range of questions the technology could help investigate.
One project uses the microscope to observe interactions among plant cells, fungi, and bacteria as they happen. By watching these organisms interact in real time, researchers hope to gain a clearer understanding of the complex relationships between plants and microbes.
Another collaboration focuses on cancer treatment. Scientists are using iISM to investigate how a cancer drug enters a cell, potentially providing valuable information about how medications interact with their targets.
A third project, still in the planning stages, will examine how red blood cells change shape when exposed to malaria infection. Observing these physical changes could offer new insights into how the disease affects blood cells.
These applications illustrate why the researchers believe their microscope could become a useful tool across numerous scientific disciplines rather than serving only a narrow area of research.
"This is not a niche technique," Kueppers said. "It has broad applications, and we hope the life science community will be well served by it, leading to many new discoveries."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Stanford University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Michelle Küppers, W. E. Moerner. Interferometric Image Scanning Microscopy for label-free imaging at 120 nm lateral resolution inside live cells. Light: Science, 2026; 15 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41377-026-02210-y

articles.title: SpaceX just delivered some very strange cargo to the International Space Station
articles.text:
SpaceX just delivered some very strange cargo to the International Space Station
- Date:
- October 16, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- SpaceX just delivered some surprisingly strange cargo to the International Space Station, including tiny brain models, 3D heart tissue, and technology for making artificial retinas in space. Scientists hope these experiments could unlock new ways to treat devastating brain diseases, restore eyesight, and test future medicines. The shipment also includes materials for creating unusual glass in near weightlessness and the station’s final upgraded solar arrays.
- Share:
SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft arrived at the International Space Station at 10:27 a.m. EDT on October 15, docking at the space-facing port of the station's Harmony module. The spacecraft delivered more than 6,300 pounds of food, essential supplies, and scientific equipment for the Expedition 75 crew.
The arrival marks SpaceX's 35th commercial resupply mission to the orbiting laboratory under its contract with NASA. Along with everyday necessities for the astronauts, Dragon brought an unusual collection of scientific experiments that could help researchers develop new medical treatments and better understand how materials behave in space.
Artificial Retinas, Brain Research, and New Solar Arrays
Among the most important items aboard Dragon is the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, known as IROSAs. These solar panels are designed to expand the station's ability to generate electricity, providing additional power for its operations and scientific research. Installation is planned for later this fall.
The spacecraft also delivered equipment for manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity, the condition of near weightlessness experienced aboard the space station. Researchers hope that producing these structures in space could eventually lead to technologies that help restore vision for people on Earth.
Other experiments include 3D heart tissue models, which recreate important features of human heart tissue. Scientists plan to use these models to advance methods for testing large numbers of potential drugs during future space missions.
Dragon also transported materials for investigating how a new type of glass forms in microgravity. Studying the process without the usual influence of Earth's gravity could provide insights into how the material develops and behaves.
Another experiment involves brain organoids, tiny three-dimensional models of brain tissue grown from cells. These miniature models allow scientists to investigate aspects of brain biology that can be difficult to study directly in humans. Researchers hope the findings will reveal potential targets for treating neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis.
Dragon's Return to Earth
Dragon is expected to remain docked at the space station until mid-November. After completing its stay, the spacecraft will carry time-sensitive research materials and other cargo back to Earth, ending its journey with a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean off the California coast.
The mission began on October 13 at 6:33 a.m. EDT, when a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

articles.title: James Webb reveals a strange bulge in an alien planet's atmosphere
articles.text:
James Webb reveals a strange bulge in an alien planet's atmosphere
- Date:
- October 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of Bristol
- Summary:
- Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered that a distant alien planet's atmosphere is surprisingly lopsided. Located 1,300 light-years away, the scorching gas giant WASP-17b experiences powerful winds that redistribute heat, causing one side of its atmosphere to bulge outward. A groundbreaking new mapping technique revealed these hidden distortions, confirming predictions about how extreme temperatures and winds shape alien worlds.
- Share:
Astronomers have long depicted distant exoplanets with smooth, circular outlines. But new observations reveal that the atmospheres surrounding some of these scorching alien worlds can have surprisingly uneven shapes.
Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), researchers have discovered that the atmosphere of WASP-17b, a giant planet roughly 1,300 light-years from Earth, extends farther outward on one side than the other. Although its overall outline remains approximately circular, its atmosphere is noticeably asymmetrical. The distortion provides new evidence of how extreme temperatures and powerful winds reshape the atmospheres of distant planets.
The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, comes from a study jointly led by Cornell University in the United States and the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom. Researchers used an innovative technique called 'transmission strings', developed by Bristol astrophysicists Dr. David Grant and Dr. Hannah Wakeford, to investigate the planet's atmospheric structure in unprecedented detail.
James Webb Reveals the 3D Structure of an Alien Atmosphere
WASP-17b belongs to a class of planets known as 'hot Jupiters', enormous gas giants that orbit close to their host stars and experience intense heating. Its unusual atmospheric shape offers a new perspective on how heat moves around these extreme worlds.
Lead author Dr. Lili Alderson, a Klarman Postdoctoral Fellow at Cornell University, began the research while studying at the University of Bristol, where she earned her doctorate in physics.
"This is proof of concept that planets are in fact 3D objects, and that consistently, as they go around their star, what we predict should be happening is happening. To move beyond computational exercises and see it for real is a different matter."
The observations provide valuable information about WASP-17b's atmospheric chemistry and temperature variations, including differences between its equator and poles and between its permanently illuminated and dark hemispheres.
These results closely match earlier theoretical predictions and computer models. Together, they offer one of the most detailed three-dimensional pictures of an exoplanet's atmosphere yet produced, establishing a useful reference point for studying the more than 6,000 exoplanets confirmed so far.
Co-author Dr. Hannah Wakeford, Associate Professor in Astrophysics at the University of Bristol, said: "Planets are temperamental, their atmospheres complex and chaotic. The fact that all of these numbers came together and showed us this very structured, dynamical picture of this giant world over 1,000 light-years away was just really exciting."
A New Technique Uncovers Hidden Atmospheric Features
James Webb's extraordinary sensitivity has already enabled scientists to investigate alien atmospheres using a method called eclipse mapping. This approach examines subtle changes in light as a planet moves behind its parent star, helping researchers determine how conditions vary across the planet.
The new "transmission strings" technique, also called transit mapping, examines the opposite part of the planet's orbit. As an exoplanet passes in front of its star, some starlight travels through the outer edges of its atmosphere before reaching the telescope.
By analyzing that light from different angles, scientists can investigate the atmosphere's composition and determine how far it extends at different locations around the planet. This outer atmospheric boundary is known as the limb.
Traditional methods generally combine light measurements from the entire limb into a single average spectrum. The new approach instead separates information from different regions, allowing researchers to identify atmospheric variations that would otherwise be concealed.
"Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet," Dr. Alderson said. "We're able to go around the edge. So, we've gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak."
Powerful Winds Create a Lopsided Atmosphere
The new measurements revealed a particularly interesting feature near WASP-17b's equator, precisely where previous models predicted it would appear.
The distortion occurs on the planet's "evening" side, where powerful atmospheric winds carry heat away from the hemisphere that permanently faces its star and toward the hemisphere locked in darkness.
This movement of hot gas causes the atmosphere on the evening side to expand farther outward than it does on the cooler "morning" side. As a result, the planet's atmospheric outline is not perfectly symmetrical.
The findings confirm a major prediction about the temperature differences between these regions. The transit mapping measurements also supported other previously identified characteristics of WASP-17b.
Dr. Alderson added: "Theory predicts that the morning and the evening sides should have a strong temperature difference, and WASP-17b fits really nicely in that trend -- pretty much bang-on what we thought it would be."
A Breakthrough for Mapping Weather on Distant Planets
Successfully applying transmission strings to WASP-17b demonstrates that the technique could be used to study the atmospheres of many other exoplanets.
Until recently, much of what astronomers could determine about these distant atmospheres came from measurements averaged across large regions. The new method offers a way to distinguish conditions at different latitudes, as well as between the day and night sides of a planet.
Eventually, this approach could help scientists investigate atmospheric structures on smaller scales, bringing them closer to mapping weather patterns on worlds far beyond our solar system.
Dr. Wakeford said: "Having this very robust mathematical model that we can apply to this state-of-the-art data is incredibly exciting. The results are a really beautiful demonstration of the dynamics that are going on in these multidimensional and multifaceted worlds."
The study used observations gathered through JWST's Telescope Scientist Deep Reconnaissance of Exoplanet Atmospheres through Multi-instrument Spectroscopy (TST DREAMS) Guaranteed Time Observations program.

articles.title: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
articles.text:
USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
Scientists have created a potentially renewable source of engineered immune cells that fight cancer, offering a promising path toward longer-lasting, ready-made immunotherapies.
- Date:
- October 16, 2026
- Source:
- Keck School of Medicine of USC
- Summary:
- USC scientists have discovered a way to create a potentially renewable supply of genetically engineered immune cells that can attack cancer and strengthen the body's natural defenses. By growing and modifying immature immune cells rather than mature ones, researchers developed a system that can continuously produce tumor-fighting cells inside the body.
- Share:
Scientists at the University of Southern California (USC) have discovered a way to produce a potentially renewable supply of cancer-fighting immune cells, opening a promising new direction for cancer treatment. By working with immature cells that can develop into powerful immune defenders, the researchers have created a system capable of generating large numbers of genetically engineered cells that recognize tumors and help activate the body's natural defenses.
The breakthrough, described in a study published in Cell, could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles facing cancer immunotherapy, including the difficulty of manufacturing enough immune cells and keeping them active in the body. In experiments involving mice, the engineered cells established themselves in bone marrow, produced new immune cells, and slowed the progression of both blood cancers and solid tumors.
The USC Stem Cell-led team focused on a type of immature immune cell called granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs). These cells normally develop into macrophages and other immune cells that protect the body from infections and participate in immune responses. The researchers found that GMPs could be grown extensively in the laboratory while retaining their ability to develop into functioning immune cells. They could also be genetically modified to recognize specific cancer markers and strengthen broader immune responses.
"The study establishes a scalable and engineerable GMP platform for cellular immunotherapy and introduces concepts that we believe could have broad implications for both cancer immunotherapy and stem cell biology," said the paper's corresponding author Qi-Long Ying, MD, PhD, professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC.
Scientists Discover a Surprising Ability in Immune Cell Precursors
Beyond its potential applications in cancer treatment, the discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of how blood and immune cells develop.
Stem cells are known for their ability to self-renew, meaning they can repeatedly divide while maintaining their original properties. In the blood-forming system, this ability has traditionally been associated primarily with hematopoietic stem cells, which can produce all the major types of blood and immune cells.
Progenitor cells, by contrast, are further along in development and are already committed to producing a more limited range of cells. They are generally thought to have less capacity for long-term self-renewal.
The USC researchers demonstrated that GMPs can retain this ability under carefully controlled laboratory conditions. Rather than quickly maturing into other cell types, the progenitors continued multiplying while preserving their identity and their capacity to generate functional immune cells.
"The prevailing view has been that long-term self-renewal in the blood system is primarily a property of the hematopoietic stem cells that can generate any type of blood or immune cell," said Ying. "We found that, under the right conditions, GMPs can also self-renew, dividing extensively while keeping their identity and ability to produce functional immune cells. That gives us a scalable starting point for engineering cell therapies for cancer, infectious disease and potentially many other conditions."
This finding could be especially important for developing treatments that require large, reliable supplies of genetically engineered immune cells.
Why Macrophages Could Be Powerful Weapons Against Cancer
Macrophages are among the immune system's most versatile defenders. Their name comes from Greek words meaning "big eaters," reflecting their ability to surround and engulf bacteria, damaged cells, and other unwanted material.
They also help coordinate immune responses by sending signals that influence the behavior of other immune cells. Some macrophages can enter tumors and attack cancer cells, making them attractive candidates for cancer immunotherapy.
One particularly promising application involves solid tumors, which include cancers that form masses in organs and tissues. Existing therapies based on engineered T cells have achieved their greatest successes against certain blood cancers, but treating solid tumors has proven more difficult.
Macrophages offer a potentially different approach because they naturally migrate into tissues and can penetrate tumors. However, turning them into practical treatments presents several challenges.
Once macrophages have fully matured, they are difficult to multiply in large quantities outside the body. They are also challenging to modify genetically and can be damaged during freezing and storage, complicating the production and distribution of cell therapies.
Another problem occurs after administration. Mature macrophages often collect in organs such as the lungs and liver instead of spreading widely throughout the body. Their relatively rapid disappearance can also limit how long a treatment remains effective.
To work around these limitations, the scientists decided to begin at an earlier stage of immune cell development.
Creating a Renewable Supply of Cancer-Fighting Immune Cells
Rather than trying to manufacture large numbers of mature macrophages, first author Shi Yue, MD, of Ying's laboratory and his colleagues concentrated on GMPs, the progenitor cells that can produce macrophages.
The researchers developed a precisely defined mixture of chemicals that allowed GMPs to survive and multiply for extended periods in the laboratory. The mixture prevented the cells from prematurely developing into mature immune cells, preserving a renewable population of progenitors.
Even after extensive laboratory expansion, the GMPs maintained the molecular characteristics that defined them. Importantly, they also retained the ability to develop into functional macrophages and other related immune cells when needed.
This approach could make it possible to manufacture large numbers of engineered immune cells from a starting population that can be continually expanded, instead of repeatedly collecting and preparing mature cells.
To confirm that the method could be reproduced, collaborators in the laboratory of Ravi Majeti, MD, PhD, at Stanford University independently demonstrated that GMPs could be maintained for extended periods and genetically engineered. Their results provided additional support for the reliability of the technique and its potential use in future cell therapies.
Majeti, Director of the Institute for Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine at Stanford University, noted: "This method for the expansion and engineering of GMPs opens the door to numerous translational applications, much like T cell expansion and engineering. We have already demonstrated engineering of these cells to drive multiple potent functions, and there is a lot more to be explored."
Engineering Immune Cells to Recognize and Attack Tumors
The team next investigated whether these expandable progenitor cells could be programmed to fight cancer.
They genetically engineered GMPs to carry a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. This engineered receptor allows immune cells to identify a particular molecular marker on the surface of cancer cells, helping direct their activity toward tumors.
CAR technology is already an important part of cancer immunotherapy, particularly in treatments that modify a patient's T cells to recognize and attack cancer. The USC researchers explored whether a similar strategy could be applied to GMPs, allowing them to generate engineered macrophages and other immune cells.
The scientists also equipped some of the progenitor cells with an additional immune-activating signal. This modification was designed to recruit and stimulate nearby immune cells, including T cells, which can help mount a stronger attack against cancer.
The added signal offered another potentially important advantage. It remained effective even when the immune characteristics of donor cells did not match those of the recipient.
That finding raises the possibility of developing off-the-shelf treatments using cells manufactured in advance from donors. Unlike personalized cell therapies, which must be prepared separately using each patient's own cells, such products could potentially be produced in larger batches and made available to multiple patients.
Engineered Cells Slow Cancer Progression in Mice
After successfully expanding and engineering GMPs from both mice and humans, the researchers investigated their therapeutic potential in mouse experiments.
When administered to mice, the progenitor cells established themselves in the bone marrow and other locations responsible for blood cell production. These environments provided places where the GMPs could generate additional engineered macrophages and related immune cells.
This was an important difference from treatments using mature macrophages. Instead of relying solely on immune cells that may disappear relatively quickly, the progenitors could provide a continuing source of replacement cells from within the body.
The strategy may therefore help overcome the rapid clearance that has limited macrophage therapies, including approaches evaluated in recent clinical trials.
The researchers tested the engineered cells in mice with blood cancers and solid tumors. GMPs carrying CAR receptors slowed disease progression in both types of cancer.
The effects were even stronger when the progenitors carried both CAR receptors and the additional signal designed to activate other immune cells. This combination improved the treatment's ability to stimulate a broader antitumor response.
Although these findings are encouraging, the cancer-treatment results remain preclinical. Further research will be needed to establish whether engineered GMPs can be used safely and effectively in people, particularly if they are intended to persist and produce immune cells over extended periods.
Potential Applications Beyond Cancer Treatment
The scientists also explored whether their approach could help treat conditions involving defective immune defenses.
In a separate mouse experiment, they studied chronic granulomatous disease, an inherited disorder that interferes with the ability of certain immune cells to kill harmful microbes. People with this condition are particularly vulnerable to recurrent bacterial and fungal infections because their immune cells cannot eliminate some pathogens effectively.
When the researchers administered GMPs to mice with the disorder, the cells restored the animals' ability to fight bacterial infection.
This result suggests that renewable, genetically engineered immune cell progenitors might eventually have applications beyond cancer, including treatments for inherited immune deficiencies and potentially infectious diseases.
The broader lesson, according to the researchers, is that the developmental stage of an immune cell may be just as important as the genetic modifications used to turn it into a treatment.
By engineering cells before they fully mature, scientists may be able to create therapies that are easier to manufacture, more adaptable, and capable of maintaining a continuing supply of specialized immune defenders.
"Our study suggests that the future of immunotherapy may depend not only on designing better CAR receptors, but also on choosing the right developmental stage of the cell," said Ying.
About the Research
The study, published in Cell, is titled "Expansion and CAR engineering of granulocyte-monocyte progenitors for cellular immunotherapy."
Along with Ying, Yue, and Majeti, the research team included Zheng Guo, Crystal Pan, Xueyuan A. Jing, Tai Nguyen, Jiaqi Tang, Yanpui Chan, Humberto Contreras-Trujillo, Du Jiang, Xue Yan, Hang Xiang, Xugeng Liu, Xiao Wang, Ziyuan Wang, Natalie Shu, Daniel B. McKim, Rong Lu, and Chao Zhang of USC; Litao Tao and Celia Bloom of Creighton University; Asiri Ediriwickrema and Sebastian Koschade of Stanford University School of Medicine; and Yingxiao Shi of Harvard Medical School and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.
Financial support came from the Chen Yong Foundation of the Zhongmei Group, a sponsored research project from Myelogene Inc., the L.K. Whittier Foundation, the Eli and Edythe Broad Innovation Award, the Ming Hsieh Institute for Research on Engineering Medicine for Cancer Award, the USC SBIR/STTR Planning Award, the Xia Research Fund, and the Wu & Jiang Research Fund.
Majeti also reported support from the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research. Guo received funding through the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine Predoctoral Training Fellowship.

articles.title: The uranium cubes that exposed Nazi Germany’s nuclear failure
articles.text:
The uranium cubes that exposed Nazi Germany’s nuclear failure
- Date:
- October 16, 2026
- Source:
- PNAS Nexus
- Summary:
- Scientists investigating Nazi Germany's secret nuclear program have uncovered evidence that its final experimental reactor was nowhere near as close to working as previously claimed. Analysis of surviving uranium cubes and wartime documents reveals that Germany lacked the enormous quantities of uranium and heavy water needed to make its reactor operational.
- Share:
During World War II, the United States raced to develop the atomic bomb partly out of fear that Nazi Germany might build one first. But how close did Germany actually come to achieving that goal? A new scientific investigation suggests the Nazi nuclear program was much further from success than its leading physicist claimed.
By examining surviving uranium cubes and previously documented historical evidence, researchers have uncovered major limitations in Germany's final experimental nuclear reactor. Their findings indicate that the project was not simply missing a few materials. The reactor would have required far more uranium and heavy water than Germany had available during the war.
The Race to Build an Atomic Bomb
The Manhattan Project, the secret American effort to develop nuclear weapons during World War II, was driven partly by the possibility that Nazi Germany might achieve a similar breakthrough first. Scientists knew that whoever succeeded could gain an unprecedented military advantage.
One possible route to an atomic bomb involved building a nuclear reactor capable of producing plutonium, a radioactive element that can be used in nuclear weapons. Inside a reactor, uranium atoms undergo nuclear fission, a process in which their nuclei split apart and release energy along with additional particles called neutrons. Under the right conditions, those neutrons trigger further fission reactions, creating a sustained chain reaction.
Although Nazi Germany pursued nuclear research through a program known as the Uranprojekt, historians have long debated how close its scientists came to developing a functioning reactor.
Germany's final attempt was an experimental reactor known as the B8 pile, constructed in 1945 under the direction of physicist Werner Heisenberg. The device used cubes of natural uranium suspended in heavy water, a specialized substance that played an essential role in controlling the nuclear reaction.
Why Heavy Water Was Essential to Nazi Germany's Reactor
Heavy water looks much like ordinary water, but its hydrogen atoms contain an additional neutron. This subtle difference makes it particularly useful in certain nuclear reactors.
In a reactor, heavy water serves as a neutron moderator, meaning it slows down the neutrons released during fission. Slower neutrons are more likely to trigger additional fission reactions in uranium, helping sustain the chain reaction needed for a working reactor.
For Germany, however, obtaining enough heavy water was a major obstacle.
During the war, the only European facility capable of supplying the heavy water needed by the German program was the Norsk Hydro plant in Vemork, Norway. Germany gained control of the facility after occupying Norway in April 1940.
Recognizing its importance to Germany's nuclear ambitions, Allied forces targeted the plant through sabotage and bombing operations. A major American bombing raid struck Vemork on November 16, 1943, contributing to the eventual end of heavy water production there.
Scientists Reexamine Hitler's Final Nuclear Reactor
When American forces discovered and dismantled the B8 reactor in 1945, it had never achieved criticality. In nuclear physics, criticality refers to the point at which a chain reaction becomes self-sustaining, with each generation of fission reactions producing enough neutrons to maintain the next.
Reaching this threshold is a fundamental requirement for operating a conventional nuclear reactor. Despite its name, criticality does not mean that a reactor is about to explode. It simply means the nuclear chain reaction can continue without relying on an external neutron source.
Heisenberg, who led the German reactor effort, maintained that the B8 experiment had come close to reaching this milestone. He argued that the device needed only a relatively modest increase in its uranium supply to become operational.
But a new study led by Timothy Koeth and his colleagues challenges that assessment.
The researchers examined two surviving cubes of natural uranium that had been used in the German nuclear project. They also studied historical records, technical reports, correspondence, and other archival documents to reconstruct the reactor's capabilities and determine what would have been required for it to work.
Their findings paint a very different picture of Germany's nuclear progress.
A Massive Uranium and Heavy Water Shortage
According to the researchers' calculations, the B8 reactor would have needed approximately twice as much uranium and more than twice as much heavy water as it actually contained to achieve a sustained nuclear chain reaction.
The required quantities exceeded the materials available to Germany during the war. In particular, the heavy water needed for a functioning reactor was far beyond the amount the German program could obtain from its Norwegian supply.
The researchers also examined whether German scientists could have avoided the heavy water shortage by using graphite, a form of carbon that can also slow neutrons in nuclear reactors.
This approach had worked for American scientists, who achieved the world's first controlled, sustained nuclear chain reaction using a graphite-moderated reactor in 1942.
However, the graphite available in German-controlled territory contained impurities that made it unsuitable for the same purpose. In particular, traces of boron could absorb neutrons that would otherwise help sustain the reaction, preventing the reactor from reaching criticality.
That meant Germany could not simply substitute graphite for heavy water to overcome its supply problems.
Why Nazi Germany's Nuclear Program Was Doomed
The findings suggest that Heisenberg significantly underestimated how much additional material his reactor would have required.
Rather than standing on the verge of a functioning nuclear reactor, the German scientists faced shortages they could not overcome with the resources available to them.
The research also provides a clearer explanation for why Germany's nuclear program failed to make the transition from experimental reactor designs to a working reactor capable of producing material for an atomic bomb.
Based on the designs and materials available during World War II, the researchers conclude that Nazi Germany lacked the resources necessary to make either its heavy water reactor or a graphite-based alternative operational.
More than eight decades after the war, the surviving uranium cubes have helped resolve a longstanding historical question, revealing just how far Nazi Germany remained from achieving a critical step toward building an atomic bomb.
