articles.title: A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
articles.text:
A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- University College London
- Summary:
- A 120-million-year-old fossil forgotten in a museum for nearly a century has revealed a terrifying new dinosaur that may have been more dangerous to humans than a T. rex. The tiger-sized predator also provides the first evidence of megaraptorans in Europe, helping explain how these mysterious dinosaurs eventually became gigantic hunters.
- Share:
A dinosaur fossil that spent nearly a century overlooked in a museum collection has turned out to belong to an entirely new species of prehistoric predator. About the size of a large tiger and armed with enormous curved claws, the animal roamed what is now Britain approximately 120 million years ago.
The discovery was made by researchers led by University College London (UCL), who examined a fossil skull fragment originally found on the Isle of Wight. Their findings, published in the journal Royal Society Open Science, identify the dinosaur as Invictibellatrix amberina, the first known European member of a mysterious group of carnivorous dinosaurs called megaraptorans.
These agile predators walked on two legs and were closely related to tyrannosaurs, including the famous Tyrannosaurus rex. However, their hunting equipment was strikingly different. Rather than relying primarily on massive jaws, megaraptorans had relatively narrow skulls, powerful arms, and huge curved claws that helped them seize their prey.
Some members of this group eventually became enormous predators, rivaling tyrannosaurs in size. Invictibellatrix, however, was among the earliest and smallest megaraptorans discovered so far.
Its name translates to "unconquered female warrior," a reference to the powerful predators that later emerged from this evolutionary lineage.
A Forgotten Dinosaur That Could Have Hunted Humans
The fossil consists of part of the rear of the dinosaur's skull. Although the Natural History Museum acquired it in 1924, its scientific importance went unrecognized for generations.
By comparing the fragment with fossils from related dinosaurs, researchers were able to estimate what this long-extinct animal might have looked like and how it lived.
Lead author Dr. Cassius Morrison (UCL Earth Sciences) said: "Based on what we know about its closest relatives, Invictibellatrix would have been three to four meters long and just over a meter and a half in height -- about as tall as a human. It would likely have had feathers and its claws might have been about 10cm to 20cm long. It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals -- occupying a similar role in the food chain to the hyena today.
"It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small.
"It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years. Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight -- who knows what else is waiting to be discovered."
Although humans never encountered these dinosaurs, Morrison's comparison highlights an intriguing difference between predators of different sizes. A relatively small carnivore might have regarded a human as worthwhile prey, whereas an enormous hunter such as T. rex may have preferred much larger animals.
Discovery Solves a Mystery About Dinosaur Evolution
Beyond identifying a previously unknown species, the fossil provides an important missing piece in the evolutionary history of megaraptorans.
These dinosaurs remain among the least understood groups of large meat eaters because their fossils are exceptionally rare. Scientists have long suspected that they first evolved in Asia before spreading through Europe and eventually reaching the southern supercontinent of Gondwana (including present-day Africa, South America and Antarctica).
There was one major problem with that explanation: Until now, no megaraptoran fossils had been identified in Europe.
The discovery of Invictibellatrix provides the evidence researchers needed to support that proposed migration route.
Co-author Charlie Scherer, a PhD student at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south."
The finding suggests that Europe was an important part of the journey that eventually brought these predators to the southern continents, where some of their descendants became dominant hunters.
CT Scans Reveal the Dinosaur's Hidden Anatomy
To determine exactly what kind of dinosaur they were examining, the scientists used CT scanning technology to investigate the fossil in detail.
The scans allowed them to build a three-dimensional reconstruction of the skull fragment, along with a model of its internal cavity. This provided clues about the shape of the space that once housed the dinosaur's brain.
The team then compared its anatomy with fossils from several other groups of meat-eating dinosaurs, including tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs, raptors, and other predators that walked on two legs.
Several unusual features helped distinguish the specimen from known species. These included an oval opening where the spinal cord connected to the brain and a distinctive crest shaped like an hourglass.
Together, these anatomical characteristics indicated that the fossil represented a previously unidentified dinosaur.
The researchers also used computer algorithms to compare its skeletal features with those of other dinosaurs. These analyses consistently placed Invictibellatrix within the megaraptoran group, providing further support for the identification.
How Giant Megaraptors Conquered the Southern Continents
The team went beyond examining the fossil itself, using mathematical models to reconstruct how megaraptorans spread and evolved over millions of years.
Their analysis combined the available fossil record with evolutionary relationships among dinosaurs, ancient geography, and climate conditions.
The results suggest that megaraptorans were distributed widely around the world during the Early Cretaceous (i.e., at the time of Invictibellatrix).
However, their fortunes appear to have changed dramatically as the Cretaceous continued.
By the Late Cretaceous, tens of millions of years later, megaraptorans had probably disappeared from the northern supercontinent of Laurasia (including modern-day Europe).
In the south, the story was very different. Megaraptorans continued evolving across Gondwana, eventually becoming some of the largest and most formidable predators in their ecosystems.
Some developed claws measuring up to 35cm (14") long. One particularly impressive example, Maip macrothorax, lived in what is now Argentina and is estimated to have reached nine to 10 meters in length, with a body weight comparable to that of an elephant.
Exactly why megaraptorans apparently vanished from northern regions remains uncertain. The researchers suggest several possibilities, including changes in climate, shifts in environmental conditions, and competition from other large carnivorous dinosaurs such as tyrannosaurs.
A Century-Old Museum Fossil Finally Reveals Its Secret
The fossil that made this discovery possible was originally collected by amateur paleontologist Reginald Walter Tooley near the base of a cliff on the southwestern coast of the Isle of Wight.
Tooley discovered more than 1,000 fossil specimens during his lifetime. Following his death, the Natural History Museum acquired his collection, including the skull fragment that would eventually be identified as Invictibellatrix.
The discovery highlights how important fossils can remain unrecognized even after spending decades in museum collections.
Professor Paul Barrett, the study's senior author from the Natural History Museum, said: "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Invictibellatrix, have been particularly elusive.
"Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made."
The researchers also gave the dinosaur's name a deeper meaning.
In their paper, they explained that Invictibellatrix was chosen to "give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in face of such odds."
The second part of its name, amberina, honors both the amber found in the rock layers where the fossil originated and the female name Amberina.
The study received funding from the Palaeontographical Society, the Royal Society, and UKRI.
With a single forgotten skull fragment revealing an entirely new dinosaur and helping reconstruct the ancient movements of giant predators, the findings demonstrate that some of paleontology's most intriguing discoveries may already be sitting in museum drawers, waiting for someone to take a closer look.

Royal Society Open Science, 2026; 13 (10) DOI: 10.1098/rsos.260937

articles.title: Cancer is rising in younger adults, and scientists can't fully explain why
articles.text:
Cancer is rising in younger adults, and scientists can't fully explain why
Cancer rates are rising among younger adults despite improvements in several lifestyle risk factors, and scientists say obesity alone can't explain why.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- BMJ Group
- Summary:
- A major study found that several cancers are rising faster among younger adults in England, even as smoking, diet, and other established risk factors have generally improved. Excess weight explains only part of the increase, leaving scientists searching for other possible causes, including changes in the gut microbiome and early-life exposures.
- Share:
Cancer rates are increasing among adults of different ages in England, but a new study has uncovered a particularly concerning pattern among younger people. Rates of bowel and ovarian cancer have risen among younger adults (under 50), while the same increases have not been observed in older age groups.
The findings, published in the open-access journal BMJ Oncology, also show that several other cancers are becoming more common at a faster pace among younger adults than among those aged 50 and older.
Although excess body weight appears to play an important role, researchers say obesity alone cannot account for the increases. The findings suggest that additional factors may be contributing to the growing burden of cancer in younger generations.
Similar increases in cancer among people under 50 have been reported outside England. However, scientists still do not fully understand whether changing lifestyle habits and other established risk factors can explain these trends.
Cancer Rates Rise Across Multiple Age Groups
To investigate, researchers examined cancer incidence records collected by England's National Disease Registry Service between 2001 and 2019. They compared trends in more than 20 cancer types among men and women aged 20 to 49 and adults aged 50 or older.
The team also analyzed national health survey data to track changes in established cancer risk factors. These included smoking, alcohol consumption, diet (high red/processed meat, low fiber intake), excess body weight (BMI), and insufficient physical activity. The researchers assessed how these factors changed across age groups and sexes and estimated how much they contributed to cancer cases.
The results revealed widespread increases in cancer incidence. Among younger women, 16 of the 22 cancer types examined showed statistically significant increases. Among younger men, rates rose significantly for 11 of 21 cancers.
Of particular concern were 11 cancers associated with known behavioral risk factors that became significantly more common among adults under 50. These included cancers of the thyroid, liver, kidney, gallbladder, bowel, pancreas, mouth, breast, and ovary, along with multiple myeloma and cancer of the uterine lining (endometrial).
Most of these cancers also increased significantly among adults over 50. However, bowel and ovarian cancers stood out because their incidence rose significantly among younger adults but not among older people.
The researchers also identified several cancers whose incidence increased more rapidly in younger women. These included endometrial, kidney, pancreatic, multiple myeloma, and thyroid cancers. Among men, multiple myeloma was the only cancer found to be increasing significantly faster in the younger age group.
Obesity Is a Major Factor, but It Doesn't Explain Everything
The researchers examined how established lifestyle risks might help explain the increases. Of the 11 cancers of particular interest, 10 were associated with obesity, with mouth cancer being the exception.
Six cancers (liver, bowel, mouth, pancreas, kidney, and ovary) were linked to smoking, while four (liver, bowel, mouth, and breast) were associated with alcohol consumption. Three (bowel, breast, and endometrial) were connected to physical inactivity, and one (bowel) was linked to dietary factors.
Yet the findings revealed an important contradiction. Apart from excess weight, most of these established risk factors either remained relatively stable or improved among younger adults over the previous one to two decades.
Red meat consumption, for example, showed some of the largest reported improvements, with reductions of around 7% in the survey trends examined. Among younger men, average daily consumption fell from 38 grams in 2008 to 17 grams in 2018. Among younger women, it dropped from 22 grams to 10 grams over the same period.
Younger women also consumed substantially less processed meat than younger men, averaging about 10 grams per day compared with approximately 20 grams.
Fiber intake remained a concern, with more than 90% of younger adults failing to consume enough fiber in 2018. Nevertheless, average intake was generally stable or improved slightly among both sexes between 2009 and 2019. Older adults showed broadly similar dietary trends.
These findings raise questions about why cancer incidence continued to increase even as several recognized lifestyle risks were moving in a more favorable direction.
How Much Cancer Is Linked to Known Risk Factors?
Despite these improvements, established behavioral risk factors were still associated with a substantial proportion of cancer cases.
For men in 2019, the researchers estimated that these factors accounted for 68% of mouth cancer cases among younger adults and 65% among older adults. The corresponding figures were 42% and 48% for liver cancer, 49% and 53% for bowel cancer, 29% and 33% for kidney cancer, and 36% and 34% for pancreatic cancer.
Among women, the estimated proportions attributable to these risks were 52% for younger adults and 45% for older adults for mouth cancer. For endometrial cancer, the figures were 35% and 42%, while liver cancer accounted for 44% and 46%.
The corresponding estimates were 38% and 42% for bowel cancer, 33% and 37% for kidney cancer, 31% and 28% for pancreatic cancer, and 19% and 24% for gallbladder cancer.
Excess body weight was associated with more of the cancer types examined than any other individual risk factor. In 2019, the estimated proportion of cases attributable to excess weight varied considerably, from 5% for ovarian cancer to 37% for endometrial cancer.
Even so, the researchers found that increases in obesity could not fully account for the broader cancer trends.
"These patterns suggest that while similar risk factors across ages are likely, some cancers may have age-specific exposures, susceptibilities, or differences in screening and detection practices," write the researchers.
Scientists Search for Other Explanations
The study was observational, meaning it could identify associations and trends but could not determine whether particular risk factors directly caused the increases in cancer incidence.
The researchers also acknowledged several limitations. Reliable national data covering long periods were unavailable for some risk factors, and the analysis focused exclusively on England rather than the entire United Kingdom.
In addition, their calculations assumed a 10-year delay between exposure to a risk factor and the development of cancer.
"The observed increasing cancer incidence despite declining trends in several behavioral risk factors may reflect the net effect of multiple influences operating in different directions. Other contributing factors not evaluated here, for example, reproductive history, early-life or prenatal risk factors, and changes in cancer diagnosis and detection practices, may also play a role," they explain.
The researchers emphasized that obesity remains important, but increases in cancer cases cannot be attributed to weight alone.
"Although overweight and obesity are linked to 10 of the 11 cancers evaluated and account for a substantial proportion of cancer cases, both BMI-attributable and BMI-non-attributable incidence rates have increased -- though the latter more slowly -- suggesting other contributors," they add.
Other potential explanations have been proposed for the increase in cancers among younger adults. These include greater consumption of ultra-processed foods and sugary drinks, childhood obesity, physical inactivity/sedentary behavior, antibiotic exposure, and air pollution.
However, many of these possible contributors have not shown the increases that might be expected if they were solely responsible for rising cancer rates.
"While these factors are common in England, most have shown stable or declining trends in the last decade," the researchers note.
One possibility that deserves closer examination is disruption of the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive system. Changes in these microbial populations have been suggested as a potential influence on cancer risk, although further research is needed to establish their role.
Cancer Remains More Common in Older Adults
While the rise in cancer among younger people is concerning, the researchers cautioned against overlooking the much greater number of cases that still occur among older adults.
The findings highlight the need to investigate cancer risk throughout life, including the possibility that exposures during childhood or even before birth may influence disease decades later.
"Although increases in cancer in younger adults are concerning, the absolute burden remains far higher in older adults, underscoring the public health and clinical importance of studying risk factors across all ages," they conclude.

articles.title: Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
articles.text:
Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Ice baths, massages, compression garments, and recovery supplements promise faster muscle recovery, but research suggests their benefits are often overstated, and some techniques may even undermine long-term gains. Scientists say the most effective recovery methods are far simpler and cheaper: getting enough sleep, eating well, and giving muscles time to rebuild.
- Share:
Finishing a tough workout always feels good. That is, until a few hours later when those uncomfortable muscle aches start setting in. This discomfort can linger for days – making easy, everyday tasks a challenge.
In search of relief, some recreational gym-goers are adopting the kind of recovery techniques once reserved for elite athletes. Social media and professional sport have helped popularize everything from ice baths and compression garments to massage and recovery supplements.
While many of these products promise faster recovery, reduced soreness and improved performance, the science is often more nuanced.
Ice baths
Few recovery strategies have received as much attention as ice baths. This involves immersing oneself in water that is below 15°C to boost recovery. But the evidence for this benefit is mixed.
Ice baths help ease inflammation, which research suggests can reduce muscle soreness and help athletes recover muscle function more effectively in a 24-hour period.
But there’s a catch. While inflammation causes soreness, it also triggers adaptations that build muscle. Dampening this response with ice baths may limit some of the long-term benefits of training – particularly if they’re used regularly.
When it comes to ice baths, side-stepping short-term pain may sacrifice long-term gains. It’s best to only use them when rapid recovery is vital.
Compression garments
Compression garments are commonly worn after exercise to speed recovery. The idea is that the external pressure they apply supports circulation, enhances blood flow to the muscles, and reduces swelling.
But while compression garments might make you think they’re helping as they reduce soreness, evidence showing they actually improve muscle recovery is generally less convincing.
A study from 2022 put them to the test. One group was given compression garments; the other group was given a placebo tablet that they were told was equally as effective as compression.
The compression garments were shown to improve circulation and muscle blood flow, while the placebo had no effect on these measures. This suggests the effects of compression garments on recovery are physiological and aren’t simply due to expectation or perception.
However, whether these changes meaningfully improve performance is less clear. Although emerging evidence suggests compression garments genuinely affect some markers of recovery, this is unlikely to directly restore muscle function.
So, compression garments may mainly help because they make you feel better recovered.
Massage
Massage is one of the few recovery interventions with relatively consistent scientific support. It can reduce soreness and improve perceived recovery after exercise.
It’s not currently clear what mechanisms actually trigger the recovery benefits of massage. But it could be due to the fact that massage reduces muscle stiffness, improves circulation and boosts relaxation.
But although athletes feel less sore and perceptions of recovery are improved after a massage, objective measures of performance and muscle function are modest and inconsistent.
Massage might ease the discomfort of training, but don’t expect miraculous performance restoration.
Recovery supplements
The nutrition supplement market is a big business, with hundreds of brightly coloured recovery drinks and capsules promising reduced soreness and faster recovery. But not all supplements are created equal. Some appear to confer small benefits, while some come with hype that science doesn’t back up.
Whey protein, for instance, is a well-researched supplement. Rich in amino acids (the building blocks of protein), it stimulates muscle protein synthesis – the process which helps your muscles grow. Whey protein is shown to have small-to-moderate benefits for muscle recovery – but evidence that it can alleviate soreness is inconsistent.
Branch chain amino acids (BCAAs) are widely-used supplements that typically contain a mixture of the amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine. BCAAs are popular because it’s believed the leucine they contain switches on protein synthesis.
Yet despite their popularity, BCAAs appear less effective than complete protein sources for muscle recovery. This is because muscle repair requires all essential amino acids – not just the ones found in BCAAs. Food sources such as chicken, beef, salmon and tofu contain all the essential amino acids.
Tart cherry juice is a relatively new supplement in the fitness world. It’s rich in polyphenols – plant compounds that are said to have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant (reducing or preventing cell damage) effects. It’s for these reasons that tart cherry juice is thought to help reduce muscle damage and soreness.
Although this is still an emerging area of research, evidence suggests these compounds have small-to-moderate effects on reducing soreness after workouts, and may also help restore muscular strength and power.
Omega-3 (fish oil) supplements are often championed as a way to reduce inflammation and accelerate recovery after exercise. While some research suggests they can modestly reduce muscle soreness and help preserve muscle function after strenuous exercise, results are far from consistent. As such, omega-3 supplements are unlikely to vastly improve recovery.
Importantly, all of these nutrients can be obtained from a healthy, balanced diet. Science also shows that it’s better to get these nutrients from whole foods over expensive supplements, as whole foods provide other important nutrients that may interact synergistically to support health.
What actually works?
Popular recovery techniques might have small benefits for reducing feelings of soreness, but they don’t actually tend to restore muscle function all that much. Instead, the strongest evidence for good recovery comes from the basics:
- Prioritize sleep: Get 7-9 hours of sleep per night so the body can conduct vital recovery and adaptive processes.
- Fuel properly: Consume 20-40g of protein after exercise for muscle repair and adequate carbohydrate intake to replenish energy stores.
- Train smart: Pair good sleep and nutrition with a sensible, well-structured training plan. This includes allowing rest days between sessions, challenging yourself a bit more each time, and scheduling easier sessions when needed to allow recovery.
So, perhaps the biggest lesson here is that recovery cannot be bottled and sold.

articles.title: Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
articles.text:
Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Cornell University
- Summary:
- Two unusually long-legged cats have helped scientists uncover the first genetically confirmed cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic felines. Researchers at Cornell University discovered that the brothers carried two altered copies of a gene linked to the rare connective tissue disorder, which can affect the eyes, heart, and blood vessels. Surprisingly, the cats survived into adulthood because their genetic mutation still allowed some normal function.
- Share:
Two brothers named Gary and Shaggy have helped Cornell University researchers make a rare genetic discovery. In a study published in Scientific Reports, scientists reported the first molecular characterization of Marfan syndrome in domestic cats, a condition primarily recognized in humans.
Gary and Shaggy first stood out as kittens because of their unusually long limbs. As they grew older, veterinarians also identified abnormalities in their eye structures and an enlarged aorta, the body's main artery. Together, these symptoms suggested Marfan syndrome, an inherited condition that weakens connective tissues throughout the body. The disorder affects approximately 1 in 4,000 people, but these brothers represented the first known documented feline cases.
"The findings provide a foundation for improved veterinary diagnostics," said senior author Dr. Jacquelyn Evans, assistant professor in the College of Veterinary Medicine and at the Baker Institute for Animal Health. "It can help veterinarians recognize similar cases in the future and may help develop genetic tests."
Scientists Uncover a Surprising Genetic Twist
To determine what caused the brothers' unusual symptoms, researchers from multiple disciplines conducted thorough medical examinations and analyzed their DNA. Their investigation identified changes in a gene called FBN1, which provides instructions for producing fibrillin-1. This protein is essential for healthy connective tissue, helping support structures throughout the body, including blood vessels, bones, ligaments, skin, and eyes.
Genetic testing revealed that Gary and Shaggy each had two altered copies of FBN1, having inherited one from each parent. This was especially notable because, in humans, a mutation in just one copy of the gene can be enough to cause Marfan syndrome. Having two altered copies is exceptionally uncommon and can severely disrupt the production of normal fibrillin-1.
Yet the brothers' genetic changes had an unexpected effect. Further analysis showed that their particular variant did not completely disable the gene. Instead, it interfered with how the gene's instructions were processed while still allowing some normal activity to continue. That remaining function helps explain why Gary and Shaggy were able to survive into adulthood, even though carrying two copies of such a mutation could otherwise have resulted in a much more severe form of the disorder.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cornell University. Original written by Teresa Griffin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Shawna R. Cook, Jessica J. Hayward, Soon Hon Cheong, Linda Impe, Ian R. Porter, Brian Lamendola, Gavin R. Hitchener, Urs Giger, Philip R. Fox, Jacquelyn M. Evans, Bart J. G. Broeckx. A homozygous hypomorphic FBN1 splice region variant in domestic cats with Marfan syndrome. Scientific Reports, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-70702-3

articles.title: The secret to easier exercise as an adult may start in childhood
articles.text:
The secret to easier exercise as an adult may start in childhood
A surprising new study suggests that staying active while growing up could make exercise easier and less exhausting for the rest of your life.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Penn State
- Summary:
- Exercise during childhood could have a surprising lifelong benefit, potentially making physical activity less exhausting in adulthood. In a study involving guinea fowl, researchers discovered that birds accustomed to carrying weights while growing up could carry those weights as adults without using extra energy, while untrained birds burned 23% more.
- Share:
How much energy your body needs to move as an adult could be influenced by how active you were during childhood. A new study led by researchers at Penn State suggests that physical activity early in life may have lasting effects on movement efficiency. Using birds as a model, the scientists provided the first direct evidence that experiences during development can change how much energy animals expend when moving as adults.
According to Jonas Rubenson, a professor of kinesiology at Penn State, the ability to move efficiently could play an important role in animal evolution. Animals that spend less energy getting around may have more resources available for essential activities such as finding food, hunting, and reproducing. The findings, published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, Biological Sciences, suggest that the energy demands of movement are more adaptable than scientists previously believed.
To investigate, the researchers attached small weights to one leg of young guinea fowl, birds closely related to chickens that walk on two legs like humans. They wanted to determine whether carrying extra weight during development would change how efficiently the birds moved once they matured.
The results revealed a striking difference. Birds that grew up carrying the weights could walk with the added load without expending additional energy. By comparison, birds raised without weights required 23% more energy when the same load was attached to their legs.
"This study showed how limb loading -- the application of mechanical stress on arms or legs, typically through weights or exercise -- during development can help an animal save energy during movement throughout its lifespan," said Rubenson, senior author of the study. "This is one of the first studies to indicate that animals' behaviors and environments in youth can affect how effortful moving is as adults."
Why Childhood Exercise Could Matter for Lifelong Health
Although the experiment involved birds, the findings raise important questions about human physical activity. One widely accepted scientific hypothesis proposes that people tend to avoid movement when it feels physically demanding or requires substantial energy.
If early activity influences movement efficiency in humans as it does in these birds, people who were less active during childhood might need to expend more energy to perform the same movements as adults. That additional effort could make them less inclined to exercise, potentially reinforcing a pattern of inactivity.
Rubenson believes the discovery could have broad implications for public health, particularly as children today are generally less physically active than those in earlier generations.
"Overall, children in the U.S. today are much less active than previous generations," Rubenson said. "This study suggests that more exercise through play and exercise during childhood could make it easier for people to remain or become more active as adults. If people do not need to exert as much energy to move as adults, then exercise -- and all its health benefits -- will be more accessible to them. This could have implications for many aspects of our nation's well-being, from heart health to mental health."
How Researchers Tested the Effects of Early Exercise
The experiment followed 12 guinea fowl from two weeks of age until they reached 16 weeks, when the birds were approaching their full adult size.
Half of the birds wore lead bands on one leg, with each band weighing 4% of the bird's body weight. The remaining six birds developed without any added weight. Apart from this difference, all 12 animals experienced the same living conditions and exercise routines.
When the birds reached nine weeks of age, the researchers began training them to walk on a treadmill.
At 16 weeks, the team assessed their energy expenditure using a flow-through metabolic chamber fitted to the treadmill. This equipment measured the oxygen each bird consumed, along with the carbon dioxide and water vapor it released. According to the researchers, this approach is considered the gold standard for determining how much energy an animal uses during a particular activity.
Each bird was tested under three conditions: standing still, walking on the treadmill without added weight, and walking while wearing a weight band on one leg. By comparing oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production across these conditions, the scientists could determine how the additional load affected energy use.
Early Training Produced a Surprising Energy-Saving Effect
The researchers found no differences in energy consumption when the birds were standing still. However, their responses changed considerably once they began walking with weights.
Birds that had not carried weights while growing up experienced a 23% increase in energy expenditure when walking with the added load compared with walking without it.
The birds that had worn weights throughout development showed a remarkably different response. Their bodies had adapted so effectively that walking with the extra load required slightly less energy than walking without it. This unexpected result surprised the research team.
"The birds became so efficient that they were not using any more energy to carry the weight than they needed to walk without the weight," Rubenson said.
Another unexpected finding emerged when the researchers compared the two groups. On average, birds accustomed to carrying weights throughout development used no more energy while walking with their bands than ordinary birds used when walking without any added weight.
Together, these observations suggest that experiences early in life can substantially influence how efficiently animals move as adults.
"This shows that animals -- and this probably includes humans -- can become more efficient based on their life experiences. So, when humans exercise regularly throughout our childhood and adolescence, it could build our capacity for exercise throughout our lives."
The findings provide new evidence that physical activity during development can have lasting effects on the energy required for movement. Whether the same adaptations occur in humans remains to be established, but the research suggests a potential mechanism through which childhood exercise could help support physical activity later in life.
Research Team and Funding
Stephen Piazza, a professor of kinesiology at Penn State, also participated in the research, along with several current and former graduate students working with Piazza and Rubenson.
The study's two co-first authors were Talayah Johnson and Kavya Katugam-Dechene. Johnson completed her master's degree at Penn State and is now pursuing a doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania. Katugam-Dechene received her doctorate from Penn State and currently serves as a research assistant professor of biomedical and rehabilitation engineering at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
Other contributors included Ian Dechene, who worked as research staff on the project and is now a software engineer, and Roberto Castro, a Penn State doctoral student jointly advised by Piazza and Rubenson.
Funding was provided by the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, part of the National Institutes of Health, through awards R21AR071588 and R01AR080711. The researchers are solely responsible for the study's content, which does not necessarily reflect the official positions of the National Institutes of Health.

articles.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
articles.text:
Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
A long-overlooked peptide once thought harmless could be a hidden contributor to Alzheimer's disease, challenging decades of research and opening new possibilities for treatment.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Santa Cruz
- Summary:
- For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.
- Share:
For decades, researchers have invested billions of dollars in Alzheimer's treatments designed to target amyloid beta, a peptide that forms harmful deposits in the brain. But a biochemist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, believes scientists may have overlooked another potential contributor to the disease: a smaller, closely related peptide that was long considered harmless.
In a new commentary published in ChemBioChem, UC Santa Cruz professor Jevgenij Raskatov highlights research suggesting that this lesser-known peptide, called P3, can form microscopic clumps and threadlike structures known as fibrils. Evidence also suggests that P3 may interact with amyloid beta (Aβ), potentially influencing how it accumulates in the brain and how toxic it becomes. These findings raise the possibility that P3 contributes to the nerve cell damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.
"The P3 peptide is, most likely, not the innocent bystander it was commonly thought to be. There's still more research to be done. But this could turn Alzheimer's research on its head," said Raskatov, whose laboratory investigates amyloid peptides in hopes of identifying ways to prevent their harmful effects and develop better Alzheimer's treatments. "P3 is a distinct aggregating peptide that is itself potentially neurotoxic and may be contributing to Alzheimer's disease."
Why Alzheimer's Treatments Have Had Limited Success
Alzheimer's is the most widespread neurodegenerative disease, affecting approximately 35 million people worldwide and generating annual costs exceeding $800 billion. The number of people living with the condition is expected to double by 2050.
Despite decades of intensive research, developing effective treatments has proved extraordinarily difficult. More than 400 clinical trials have investigated potential Alzheimer's drugs, with most focusing on amyloid beta. Many of these efforts have failed, while others have produced only modest benefits. Some treatments have also been associated with serious complications, including brain hemorrhages and strokes.
Amyloid beta originates from a much larger protein embedded in cell membranes called the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP). Two enzymes, β-secretase and γ-secretase, cut this protein in sequence, releasing amyloid beta peptides of different lengths.
Researchers have concentrated particularly on two versions, Aβ40 and Aβ42, which contain 40 and 42 amino acids, respectively. Aβ42 has attracted the greatest attention because it is especially prone to sticking together and forming toxic aggregates. As a result, it has remained a central target of Alzheimer's drug development for decades.
Existing medications, including cholinesterase inhibitors and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists, can temporarily ease certain symptoms but do not stop the disease from progressing. More recently, antibody treatments such as Lecanemab and Donanemab have been approved to help remove amyloid beta from the brain.
However, Raskatov argues that the benefits achieved so far remain limited, underscoring the need to investigate other biological processes involved in Alzheimer's.
"Progress has been extremely slow, and the current state of the art in Alzheimer's therapy leaves much to be desired," he said. "We need fundamentally new approaches to the problem."
The Overlooked Peptide That May Also Damage Brain Cells
Unlike amyloid beta, P3 forms when Amyloid Precursor Protein is processed through a different sequence of molecular cuts. In this pathway, an enzyme called α-secretase acts first, followed by γ-secretase.
Raskatov has proposed calling this peptide "Amyloid α," or Aα, to better distinguish it from amyloid beta and reflect its ability to form aggregates.
For years, scientists largely assumed that P3 was incapable of forming amyloid deposits, was not toxic to cells, and would remain soluble in water. Under that interpretation, the peptide would simply dissolve rather than accumulate in the brain.
These assumptions were never adequately verified, according to Raskatov. Nevertheless, they helped establish the view that P3 was unlikely to matter in Alzheimer's disease, leaving it largely absent from research efforts.
Raskatov, a specialist in peptide chemistry, and researchers in his laboratory decided to test those long-standing beliefs.
Over the past five years, the team has published three major studies demonstrating that P3 can form amyloid deposits at least as readily as amyloid beta. In fact, their experiments showed that P3 produces these aggregates more rapidly.
The researchers also found evidence that P3 itself may be harmful to neurons, although its toxicity appears lower than that of amyloid beta.
According to Raskatov, an independent research group in the United Kingdom has confirmed and expanded upon his team's findings. Other laboratories are now beginning to investigate how P3 and amyloid beta interact, including whether their relationship affects the accumulation and toxicity of these peptides.
Together, the results challenge the long-held assumption that P3 is biologically harmless and irrelevant to Alzheimer's. However, further research is needed to establish whether and how it contributes to the disease in patients.
Challenging Decades of Alzheimer's Research
For much of the past several decades, amyloid beta has dominated scientific explanations of Alzheimer's disease. David Teplow, an emeritus professor of neurology at UCLA and a prominent Alzheimer's researcher, said the peptide has long been regarded as a central cause of the condition.
But an independent evaluation of Raskatov's research led Teplow to conclude that scientists are beginning to reconsider this narrow focus.
"This reevaluation has far-reaching consequences for both basic science and clinical research into the causes and treatment of Alzheimer's disease," said Teplow, a founding editorial board member of the Journal of Molecular Neuroscience and the American Journal of Neurodegenerative Disease, as well as editor-in-chief of Progress in Molecular Biology and Translational Science.
Raskatov has also encountered a troubling problem while examining how other scientists have interpreted his team's discoveries.
He identified at least four papers published in respected, peer-reviewed journals that cited his laboratory's research as evidence that P3 was harmless and unable to form amyloid deposits. Yet his team's experiments had demonstrated precisely the opposite.
"This is exactly the opposite of what we have actually shown," Raskatov said. "We remain in the dark on how this sort of grand confusion may have come about. Clearly, there is more work ahead of us."
The emerging evidence suggests that understanding Alzheimer's may require looking beyond amyloid beta alone. By examining P3 and its interactions with other amyloid peptides, researchers hope to gain a more complete picture of the processes that damage brain cells and potentially identify new directions for treatment.

Materials provided by University of California - Santa Cruz. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

articles.title: Scientists may have finally solved the mystery of the Moon’s two faces
articles.text:
Scientists may have finally solved the mystery of the Moon’s two faces
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Science China Press
- Summary:
- Scientists may have solved a long-standing mystery about why the Moon’s two sides are so different, using samples collected from its farside for the first time. Their findings suggest that uneven heating from Earth's gravitational pull drove enormous flows of ancient magma, creating the dramatically different lunar landscapes we see today.
- Share:
Scientists investigating why the Moon's two sides look so different have uncovered new evidence that could help explain this long-standing mystery. A research team led by Professor Hejiu Hui of Nanjing University analyzed lunar rocks collected by China's Chang'e-6 (CE6) mission and found clues suggesting that enormous movements of molten rock shaped the Moon billions of years ago.
The researchers examined the chemical compositions of three types of lunar rock: anorthosites, Mg-suite rocks, and mare basalts. They compared these samples from the Moon's far side with material collected from the near side during the Apollo and Chang'e-5 missions. Their findings suggest that the Moon's striking differences emerged through large-scale heat-driven circulation within its ancient lunar magma ocean (LMO), after the Moon became tidally locked to Earth.
Why the Moon's Two Sides Are So Different
The side of the Moon facing Earth looks remarkably different from the hemisphere permanently turned away from us. The near side features vast plains of dark volcanic basalt and relatively high concentrations of potassium, rare earth elements, and phosphorus (KREEP). In contrast, the far side is dominated by ancient, heavily cratered highlands, with a much thicker crust and relatively few volcanic plains.
Scientists have debated the origins of this uneven structure for decades. Proposed explanations have included differences in how the Moon's original magma ocean circulated, a massive collision, heating caused by gravitational tides, and uneven development of the lunar crust. However, none of these ideas has gained universal acceptance.
Another important question has remained unanswered. Although the contrasts between the two hemispheres are clearly visible at the surface and within the crust, scientists have been uncertain whether similar differences extend deep into the lunar mantle.
Chang'e-6 Samples Reveal a Surprising Similarity
A major opportunity to investigate this mystery arrived in 2024, when Chang'e-6 became the first mission to return samples from the Moon's far side. For the first time, scientists could directly compare rocks collected from both lunar hemispheres.
The analysis revealed an important similarity beneath the Moon's contrasting surfaces. Basalts collected by Chang'e-6 show chemical signatures indicating that they originated from depleted mantle material, much like the low-Ti basalts brought back by Apollo astronauts. This suggests that the mantle cumulates, minerals that accumulated as the Moon's magma ocean crystallized, do not differ substantially in composition between the two hemispheres.
The researchers found additional support for this conclusion in Mg-suite rocks. These rocks form through interactions between the crust and mantle when portions of the accumulated mantle material partially melt. Their magnesium number (Mg#) provides an important indicator of the composition of the mantle material from which they originated.
Because Mg-suite samples from Chang'e-6 and Apollo have similar Mg# values, the researchers concluded that the mantle cumulates beneath both sides of the Moon share broadly similar chemical characteristics. In other words, the materials that crystallized from the Moon's original magma ocean show no significant compositional divide between the near side and far side.
The Moon's Crust Tells a Different Story
While the mantle appears relatively uniform in composition, the lunar crust reveals a much more pronounced contrast.
Anorthosite samples returned by Chang'e-6 have higher peak Mg# values than comparable Apollo samples, indicating that the far side's crust contains more magnesium-rich material. This agrees with earlier observations made by instruments studying the Moon remotely.
The researchers also identified important chemical differences in Mg-suite rocks. Samples from Chang'e-6 contain extremely low concentrations of rare earth elements and have lower thorium-to-samarium ratios, expressed as Th/Sm, than their Apollo counterparts.
These differences suggest two possible explanations. Either Mg-suite magmas formed on the far side without substantial involvement from KREEP-rich material, or the layer containing these elements developed unevenly across the Moon, leaving the two hemispheres with different chemical compositions.
How Earth's Gravity May Have Shaped the Moon
Combining these findings, the researchers developed a model that could explain how the Moon acquired its two dramatically different faces.
According to their proposed scenario, the Moon's early magma ocean initially cooled and crystallized in a relatively uniform manner. This process produced the first mantle cumulates and anorthositic crust, before the Moon became tidally locked to Earth.
The situation changed once the Moon settled into an orbit that kept the same hemisphere facing our planet. At that time, Earth and the Moon were much closer together, and gravitational tidal forces generated more heat on the lunar near side than on the far side.
This uneven heating created a temperature difference across the Moon's molten interior, setting off large-scale horizontal circulation. Hot magma moved from the near side toward the far side, carrying previously formed magnesium-rich anorthosite material with it.
Over time, this movement accumulated more crustal material on the far side, helping explain why that hemisphere developed a thicker crust with a higher magnesium content.
At the same time, the remaining molten material flowed preferentially toward the near side. As a result, the far side developed only relatively thin layers enriched in KREEP and ilmenite-bearing cumulates (IBC), while more of these late-stage materials became concentrated on the near side.
This model of heat-driven magma circulation provides a possible explanation for why the Moon has a chemically similar mantle but such dramatically different crustal compositions. By connecting the newly analyzed Chang'e-6 samples with the Moon's early thermal history, the findings offer fresh insight into the processes that shaped Earth's closest celestial neighbor.

articles.title: Ba "di vật" bí ẩn độc nhất chưa có lời giải, một cái mất dấu kỳ lạ
articles.text:
Mặc dù nhiều bí mật đã được kiểm chứng bằng các phương pháp khoa học tiên tiến hiện nay, nhưng vẫn có 3 câu đố lớn hiện vẫn chưa có lời giải, thậm chí có cái đột nhiên biến mất một cách kỳ lạ khiến giới khảo cổ học "đau đầu" hàng ngàn năm.
Trung Quốc vốn là một đất nước rộng lớn với diện tích 9,6 triệu km vuông, trên mảnh đất rộng lớn này vốn ẩn chứa rất nhiều bí mật. Mặc dù nhiều bí mật đã được kiểm chứng bằng các phương pháp khoa học tiên tiến hiện nay, nhưng vẫn còn đó nhiều điều chưa được giải đáp bí ẩn. Trong số đó có 3 câu đố lớn tới nay vẫn chưa có lời giải, một ở Bắc Kinh, một ở Tây An, và cái còn lại thậm chí còn khó hiểu hơn.
Trong địa phận cầu Bắc Tân, có một cái giếng vô cùng đặc biệt.
Tự cổ chí kim, mọi người đều biết Trung Quốc vốn là một quốc gia coi trọng văn hóa rồng phượng. Tại đây, rồng luôn tượng trưng cho địa vị tối cao, và chỉ có các bậc đế vương mới được sử dụng hoa văn rồng. Vì vậy, trong Tử Cấm Thành ở Bắc Kinh, du khách có thể thường xuyên nhìn thấy những kiến trúc rồng phượng. Và trong địa phận cầu Bắc Tân, có một cái giếng vô cùng đặc biệt, mặc dù bên ngoài không có gì nổi bật, nhưng trong giếng lại ẩn chứa huyền cơ.
Theo người dân địa phương, đây là một chiếc giếng rất đặc biệt. Tương truyền phía dưới giếng trấn áp một con rồng già, bị trói bởi một sợi xích sắt rất to. Nếu kéo sợi xích sắt lên miệng giếng thì nước sẽ phun ra, và khi kéo lên lên một độ cao nhất định, nó sẽ gây ra lũ lụt. Nguyên nhân là bởi đã làm kinh động tới con rồng dưới giếng, khiến nó giận dữ, có người còn nói rằng họ thậm chí nghe thấy cả tiếng gầm của rồng.
Trong thời kỳ Nhật xâm lược Trung Quốc, mọi người kể lại câu chuyện từng có lính Nhật không tin tà ma, bắt dân kéo sợi xích lên. Nhưng kéo một hồi lâu không hết nên lính Nhật tò mò lui tới miệng giếng kiểm tra. Lúc này, một dòng nước đen đột ngột phun lên và dưới giếng phát ra tiếng động lạ, khiến cho lính Nhật sợ hãi lần lượt bỏ chạy. Sau đó, người dân không có cách nào khác đành đặt sợi xích vừa kéo trở lại giếng.
Thực ra, khái niệm Tỏa long tỉnh (Tỏa nghĩa là khóa), còn được gọi là Tỏa giao tỉnh (giao trong tiếng hán ý chỉ con thuồng luồng – một loài vật trong truyền thuyết, giống con rồng không có sừng) – là một nội dung vật lý trong các câu chuyện và thần thoại Trung Quốc, phản ánh lý tưởng trị thủy của con người trong hàng nghìn năm và là một hiện tượng quan trọng trong văn hóa Trung Quốc.
Vào ngày 17/6, "Bắc Kinh Thanh niên báo" đăng một đoạn tin - "Đào được một giếng cổ trên đường số 5". Câu hỏi nó có phải là giếng Tỏa Long huyền thoại hay không đang được cục di tích văn hóa xác minh tìm câu trả lời. Công trường vì thế mà bị đình chỉ. Sau khi tin tức được đăng, nhiều người Bắc Kinh thốt lên rằng: "Không thể động đến giếng Tỏa Long, động vào bất đắc!". Quả nhiên tàu điện ngầm phải xây đường vòng qua chiếc giếng cổ này.
Hình minh họa chiếc giếng Tỏa Long. (Ảnh: Sohu).
Tương truyền, năm 1421, Minh Thành Tổ chính thức dời đô từ Nam Kinh về Bắc Bình (tên cũ của Bắc Kinh). Điều kỳ lạ là trong quá trình di dời, Minh Thành Tổ liên tục gặp phải trở ngại. Ví dụ một công trình vừa xây xong thì vài ngày sau bị sét đánh và gây ra hỏa hoạn. Lúc này các cận thần kinh hãi nên thuyết phục ông trở về Nam Kinh càng sớm càng tốt.
Có lời đồn rằng do Minh Thành Tổ kinh động tới một con rồng đang canh giữ kho báu ở Bắc Bình nên nó trừng phạt ông bằng một trận đại hồng thủy. Minh Thành Tổ không sợ hãi mà tìm đến “hắc y tể tướng” Diêu Quảng Hiếu để đối phó với con rồng này. Người này thông thạo tam giáo và có địa vị đáng kể vào thời điểm đó. Ngoài ra, ông còn được mệnh danh là hóa thân của “Hàng Long La Hán”.
Diêu Quang Hiếu giúp Minh Thành Tổ hàng phục con rồng già này. Ông đã ném nó xuống một cái giếng bên cạnh cầu Bắc Tân và “phong ấn” tại đó. Ông đã yêu cầu mang tới 1 sợi dây xích thật lớn để trói con rồng này dưới đáy giếng. Để đề phòng con quái thú có thể xổng ra, Diêu Quảng Hiếu cho người xây dựng trên giếng một ngôi đền có ba sảnh để trấn áp. Không biết thực hư thế nào nhưng quả thực, giếng Tỏa Long và đền Trấn Hải vẫn còn tồn tại tới ngày nay.
Sau này, các nhà khoa học sử dụng các dụng cụ hiện đại để khảo sát chiếc giếng kỳ quái này. Kết quả, họ nhận ra đây là giếng dựng đứng tự nhiên, đầu dưới thông với sông ngầm.
Tiếng động gọi là “rồng gầm” thực chất đó là âm thanh tạo ra do ma sát giữa xích sắt và thành giếng. Vì những người dân thường truyền tai nhau những câu chuyện bí ẩn nên tự nhiên sinh ra tâm lý sợ hãi. Họ cũng tìm thấy một mảnh sắt có mùi tanh. Tuy nhiên sau đó, các nhà khoa học không công bố thêm thông tin gì về chiếc giếng này và đến nay nó vẫn còn tồn tại với những lời đồn kỳ lạ.
Thông thường, một văn bia sẽ được dựng trước lăng mộ của hoàng đế để ghi lại những thành tựu to lớn của vị hoàng đế trong suốt cuộc đời của ông. Ngay cả khi vị hoàng đế chưa có đóng góp gì cho đất nước, nhưng trên bia mộ vẫn sẽ được biên soạn, tạo khắc một số nội dung chính. Vậy nhưng không có gì được viết trên văn bia của Võ Tắc Thiên - điều này cũng khiến các nhà sử học bối rối.
Nhắc đến Võ Tắc Thiên, chắc hẳn mọi người không còn xa lạ. Đây là nữ hoàng đế kiệt xuất nhất Trung Quốc và cũng là nữ hoàng đế duy nhất của đất nước này. Võ Tắc Thiên sau khi mất được an táng tại Càn Lăng ở Lương Sơn, Hàm Dương. Hiện nay Càn Lăng đã trở thành một địa điểm thu hút rất khách du lịch. Tuy nhiên, khi đến thăm Càn Lăng, hẳn ai cũng sẽ chú ý tới tấm bia để trống ngay phía trước lăng.
Xung quanh câu đố này, trong dân gian đã truyền miệng nhau rất nhiều giả thuyết khác nhau. Người cho rằng, bởi bà có quá nhiều công lao, nên không thể ghi chép hết lại được trên bia mộ. Bắt đầu từ việc trở thành hoàng hậu vào năm 655 sau Công nguyên, Võ Tắc Thiên buộc phải thoái vị vào năm 705 sau Công nguyên, tham gia và nắm giữ quyền lực cao nhất trong 50 năm.
Giả thuyết thứ hai cho rằng, do bản thân biết những tội lỗi nghiêm trọng của mình trong quá trình cai trị đất nước, Võ Tắc Thiên đã dựng lên "tấm bia không lời" và cho rằng đó là cách tốt nhất để không bị người đời bôi nhọ. Nói về những tội lỗi tày đình bên cạnh công lao trị quốc của Võ Tắc Thiên, dân gian truyền miệng rất nhiều phiên bản, chủ yếu xoay quanh việc bà hãm hại hoàng hậu để tiếm quyền , thậm chí hại chết chính con ruột và tôn thất để leo lên ngôi hoàng đế, và kinh hoàng nhất là việc thảm sát những người tình của mình. Ngoài ra, sự phát triển kinh tế và xã hội trong thời kỳ đầu của nhà Đường như một hình yên ngựa, trong khi Võ Tắc Thiên ở điểm thấp nhất khi bà nắm quyền. Và trong thời gian cầm quyền, bà đã để mất bốn trấn An Tây, gây nguy hiểm cho sự thống nhất của đất nước. Võ Tắc Thiên không thể thiết lập một tiểu sử hào quang cho chính mình, mà chỉ có thể để trống bằng "tấm bia không lời".
Lập luận thứ ba cho rằng Võ Tắc Thiên là mẹ Đường Trung Tông, biết rằng mọi người sẽ có những đánh giá khác nhau về cuộc đời của mình, đặc biệt là sự việc phế truất Đường Trung Tông để cướp ngôi. Việc viết tốt hay xấu lên bia mộ quả rất khó, bởi vậy bà đã quyết định lập một "bia không lời" để người đời sau tự đánh giá.
Một điều nữa là sau khi Võ Tắc Thiên qua đời, chính sự rối ren không ai để ý. Đợi đến khi ổn định, mọi người chú ý lại thì đoạn lịch sử đó đã qua đi, qua nhiều người truyền miệng, khó phân biệt thật giả, bởi vậy không biết khắc gì trên bia mộ. Cho dù là giả thuyết nào, thì câu đố về bia mộ Võ Tắc Thiên cho tới nay vẫn chưa có lời giải chính xác.
Danh tiếng của Lâu Lan quốc cổ đại không chỉ được biết đến ở Trung Quốc, mà còn có ảnh hưởng rất lớn trên thế giới, bởi đây từng là một quốc gia cổ đại rất rộng lớn và giàu có, chiếm một vị trí vô cùng quan trọng trên con đường tơ lụa cổ đại.
Lâu Lan (Kroran) là một quốc gia cổ, tồn tại từ thế kỷ II TCN ở vùng đông bắc sa mạc La Bố, Tân Cương (nay thuộc Trung Quốc). Lâu Lan được biết đến với cái tên tiếng Nga là Krorayina hay Kroran.
Tuy nhiên, vào năm 630 sau Công Nguyên, nó đột nhiên biến mất một cách bí ẩn, và mãi cho tới sau khi giải phóng, mới được giới khảo cổ học phát hiện và nghiên cứu. Cho tới hiện tại, lý do biến mất của nó vẫn mãi là một bí ẩn lớn.
Một số giải thuyết cho rằng vì lý do thiên tai nên thành phố cổ kính huy hoàng này đã biến thành đống đổ nát. Một số cho rằng nguyên nhân là do chiến tranh. Một số khác lại đưa ra nghi vấn tất cả người dân của Lâu Lan quốc cổ đại đã bị nhiễm bệnh ác tính, lần lượt ra đi trong một thời gian ngắn.
Một giả thuyết được cho là có cơ sở khoa học tin rằng, Lâu Lan quốc do trước đây lạm dụng chặt phá rừng, làm mất một lượng lớn đất và nước, kết quả là đất đai bị sa mạc hóa và cư dân không thể sinh sống được nên họ đã chuyển đi nơi khác.Tuy nhiên, cho dù là lời giải thích nào thì cũng chỉ là giả thuyết chưa được kiểm chứng, và Lâu Lan quốc vẫn là một hòm bí mật chưa tìm được chìa khóa.

articles.title: Loài rắn hiền lành với con người, nhưng lại là khắc tinh của rắn độc
articles.text:
Tại Việt Nam có phân bố một loài rắn với lớp vảy bên ngoài hết sức đặc biệt. Đây là loài rắn rất hiền lành đối với con người, nhưng lại được xem là kẻ thù của các loài rắn độc.
Loài rắn được nhắc đến ở trên là hổ hành, còn được gọi là rắn mống, có tên khoa học Xenopeltis unicolor. Đây là một loài thuộc họ rắn mống. Họ rắn mống chỉ bao gồm 1 chi duy nhất với danh pháp khoa học Xenopeltis và 2 loài rắn, bao gồm rắn hổ hành và rắn mống Hải Nam.
Dưới ánh nắng mạnh, rắn mống sẽ tỏa ra ánh sáng óng ánh nhiều màu rất đẹp mắt.
Đặc điểm chung của 2 loài rắn mống này đó là lớp vảy có khả năng thay đổi màu sắc nhờ tác động từ ánh sáng bên ngoài. Đặc biệt khi dưới ánh nắng mạnh, rắn mống sẽ tỏa ra ánh sáng óng ánh nhiều màu rất đẹp mắt.
Các loài rắn mống được tìm thấy ở Trung Quốc và các quốc gia Đông Nam Á như Myanmar, Thái Lan, Lào, Campuchia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore và cả Việt Nam. Trong 2 loài rắn mống, rắn hổ hành phân bố phổ biến và dễ bắt gặp tại Việt Nam hơn.
Rắn hổ hành trưởng thành có chiều dài từ 1 đến 1,2m, đầu và cổ không phân biệt rõ với nhau. Đầu của rắn hổ hành thuôn và nhọn, giúp chúng có thể đào đất dễ dàng.
Do sở hữu lớp da óng ánh đặc trưng, rắn hổ hành rất dễ được nhận biết trong tự nhiên, ngay cả với những người không có quá nhiều kiến thức về động vật hay bò sát.
Rắn hổ hành non trông rất giống rắn trưởng thành, ngoại trừ việc những con non có một lớp vảy màu trắng xung quanh đầu, như một chiếc vòng cổ. Chiếc "vòng cổ" này sẽ mờ đi trong năm đầu tiên của rắn hổ hành non.
Rắn hổ hành non nổi bật với "vòng cổ" màu trắng trên cơ thể. (Ảnh: ThaiNationPark).
Bên cạnh đặc điểm nhận biết về màu sắc bên ngoài, rắn hổ hành còn có thể được nhận diện bằng mùi hương cơ thể của chúng. Loài rắn này tỏa ra một mùi hương không mấy dễ chịu, giống với mùi hành sống. Mùi hương này khá đậm khiến nhiều người có thể nhận ra sự hiện diện của chúng ngay khi chưa nhìn thấy. Có thể đây chính là nguồn gốc bắt nguồn tên gọi của loài rắn này.
Tại Việt Nam, rắn hổ hành thường xuất hiện nhiều ở khu vực Tây Nam Bộ. Chúng thường ẩn nấp ở nơi nhiều bụi rậm, ven hồ, nơi có nhiều có ếch nhái sinh sống, cung cấp nguồn thức ăn dồi dào của chúng.
Mặc dù mang tên "hổ", nhưng trên thực tế rắn hổ hành lại không thuộc họ rắn "hổ", họ rắn sở hữu nọc độc chết người, mà như trên đã đề cập, hổ hành là loài thuộc họ rắn mống, không có nọc độc.
Do không có nọc độc, rắn hổ hành săn mồi bằng cách sử dụng sức mạnh của cơ thể quấn chặt và giết chết con mồi trước khi ăn thịt. Cách thức săn mồi của rắn hổ hành giống với loài trăn và một số loài rắn không có nọc độc khác.
Rắn hổ hành sử dụng sức mạnh cơ bắp để siết chặt và giết chết con mồi. (Ảnh: ResearchGate).
Một điểm đặc biệt giúp tăng hiệu quả của rắn hổ hành khi săn mồi, đó là răng của loài rắn này không cố định, mà có thể linh hoạt gập lên hoặc xuống. Khi săn mồi, răng của rắn hổ hành sẽ cắm chặt vào con mồi và gập ngược về phía sau, điều này giúp giữ chặt con mồi, khiến chúng khó có thể thoát ra được. Ngoài ra, cấu tạo răng này cũng giúp hổ hành nuốt trọn con mồi dễ dàng hơn.
Một đặc điểm ấn tượng khác của rắn hổ hành đó là chúng có khả năng kháng nọc độc của một số loài rắn độc, trong đó có một số loài của họ rắn hổ như hổ mang, cạp nia, cạp nong… điều này cho phép hổ hành có thể săn và ăn thịt những con rắn độc mà chúng bắt gặp.
Rắn hổ hành siết chặt một cá thể rắn cạp nia, loài rắn sở hữu nọc độc chết người thuộc họ rắn hổ (Ảnh: TBH).
Dĩ nhiên, hổ hành chỉ có thể giết chết và ăn thịt những cá thể rắn độc có kích thước nhỏ hơn chúng. Trong trường hợp hổ hành gặp phải những con rắn độc có kích thước to lớn hơn, chẳng hạn như hổ chúa, hổ hành khó có thể đánh bại kẻ thù để ăn thịt mà ngược lại, có thể trở thành con mồi của rắn độc.
Nhiều chuyên gia cho rằng nếu bắt gặp rắn hổ hành trong vườn nhà, mọi người không nên giết chết hay xua đuổi những con rắn này, mà hãy giữ chúng lại để đóng vai trò như một "quản gia", khi hổ hành có thể giúp làm giảm bớt được số lượng rắn độc nếu có trong vườn nhà.
Ngoài rắn độc, hổ hành có chế độ ăn rất đa dạng, bao gồm cả ếch, nhái, thằn lằn và một số loài động vật có vú nhỏ.
Dù được xem là khắc tinh của các loài rắn độc, hổ hành lại là một loài rắn rất hiền lành và hầu như không tấn công con người. Thậm chí, ngay cả khi con người cầm con rắn này trên tay, nó cũng chỉ tìm cách để chạy trốn.
Một cá thể rắn hổ hành được bắt gặp tại tỉnh Kiên Giang. (Ảnh: Trần Trí Dũng).
Nhiều người cho rằng với bản tính hiền lành và màu sắc rực rỡ như vậy, hổ hành sẽ là một loài rắn được nhiều người yêu thích và chọn làm vật nuôi.
Tuy nhiên, như trên đã đề cập, hổ hành tỏa ra một mùi hôi đặc trưng khiến nhiều người khó chịu. Bên cạnh đó, hổ hành thường bị chết trong môi trường nuôi nhốt, do vậy loài rắn này không phải là sự lựa chọn phù hợp để làm vật nuôi.
Hổ hành là một loài rắn hiền lành và có lợi trong hệ sinh thái. Loài rắn này có thể dễ dàng được nhận diện nhờ vẻ bề ngoài đặc trưng, do vậy, nếu bắt gặp loài rắn này trong tự nhiên, bạn hãy để mặc và tránh xa chúng.

articles.title: Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
articles.text:
Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
Cedars-Sinai identified a protein that may allow harmful “zombie cells” to evade the immune system and accumulate as we age.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Cedars-Sinai Medical Center
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a protein that may help harmful aging cells hide from the immune system, allowing them to accumulate and fuel age-related health problems. Blocking the protein in mice reduced these cells and inflammation while improving blood sugar regulation and strength, offering a promising new direction for anti-aging research.
- Share:
Researchers led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University have discovered a protein that may allow harmful aging cells to escape detection by the immune system. By helping these cells remain in the body instead of being cleared away, the protein could contribute to their accumulation and the development of health problems associated with aging.
The discovery, published in Cell Metabolism, identifies PD-L2 as a potential target for therapies aimed at eliminating harmful aging cells. Scientists also believe the protein could serve as a blood marker, providing a way to detect and monitor these cells.
"Our findings suggest that PD-L2 may help aging cells stay in the body when they would normally be removed by the immune system," said Selim Chaib, PhD, research assistant professor of Medicine at Cedars-Sinai and first and co-corresponding author of the study.
How Harmful Aging Cells Escape the Immune System
As cells age or become damaged, some enter a state known as senescence. These cells stop dividing but remain alive, lingering in tissues rather than disappearing. Over time, they can accumulate and release substances that trigger inflammation and disrupt the normal activity of surrounding cells.
The buildup of these senescent cells has been associated with a range of health problems that become more common with age. Understanding why they persist, particularly when the immune system would normally remove them, could help scientists develop new ways to reduce their harmful effects.
The researchers found that PD-L2 may play an important role in this process by helping aging cells avoid immune clearance.
Blocking PD-L2 Reduces Aging Cells in Mice
To investigate the protein's role, scientists conducted experiments in laboratory mice in which PD-L2 was either removed or blocked. Both approaches reduced the accumulation of senescent cells and lowered levels of the inflammatory substances they release.
The benefits extended beyond changes at the cellular level. Mice with reduced PD-L2 activity also showed improvements in their ability to process sugar and demonstrated greater grip strength, suggesting that targeting the protein could influence physical functions affected by aging.
The team also examined human cells and tissues. They discovered that senescent human cells produced more PD-L2 than younger cells and that levels of the protein rose with age in certain human tissues. These findings suggest the mechanism observed in mice may also be relevant to human aging.
A Potential New Target for Age-Related Diseases
The results raise the possibility that blocking PD-L2 could help the immune system recognize and eliminate harmful aging cells, potentially reducing some of the health problems associated with their buildup.
"If we can find a way to block this protein, we may be able to help the immune system get rid of these cells and potentially improve health problems linked with aging," said James Kirkland, MD, PhD, director of the Center for Advanced Gerotherapeutics and senior author of the study.
Although the findings are promising, more research is needed before the approach can be considered for treating people. Future studies will investigate whether blocking PD-L2 is safe and can deliver meaningful health benefits in humans. Researchers also hope to clarify how the protein contributes to diseases associated with aging.
Additional Cedars-Sinai researchers who contributed to the study include Larissa Langhi Prata, Masayoshi Suda, Andres Sola, Jia Nie, Hyungsoo Kim, Tamar Pirtskhalava, Nino Giorgadze, Nicolas Musi, Ze'ev Ronai, and Tamara Tchkonia.
