articles.title: Apple updates App Store rules to ensure it doesn't offer AI nudify apps - Engadget
articles.text:
Apple updates App Store rules to ensure it doesn't offer AI nudify apps
Developers are now required to filter nonconsensual intimate imagery.
Apple has updated its moderation policy for the App Store to make sure people aren't using applications, including those that use AI tools, to "nudify" or turn normal images into sexually explicit content. The company has long prohibited pornographic materials in the App Store, and apps that were specifically made to generate sexually explicit imagery haven't been allowed for a long time. Now, Apple also wants developers to proactively police the use of their applications.
Developers with apps that host user-generated content are now required to filter nonconsensual intimate imagery, including those generated using AI tools. They must give users a way to report offensive content and block abusive accounts. They must also prevent users from being able to upload those kinds of images, and they must remove any that slip through their filters. If they fail to implement adequate safeguards of fail to remedy any violation after they had been notified, they risk being removed from the store.
In addition, it clarified its rules for apps that use bait-and-switch tactics on the company. If Apple finds that an app has misrepresented its purpose during review and that it actually has "nudification" capabilities, it will remove the app from the store and its creator from the Apple Developer Program.

articles.title: Why AI Isn’t Ready to Tackle Our Convoluted Genomes
articles.text:
The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
Since its molecular structure was deduced in the 1950s, DNA has been hailed by many biologists as the secret of life. They’ve read and studied the information stored in the DNA found in the cells of living organisms, known as their genomes, and claimed that this genetic database must be some kind of blueprint, code script, or computer. But if DNA really does harbor some greater secret about how life works, biologists have yet to find it.
In fact, the human genome is less a script than a puzzle that gets harder the closer they look. Knowing the entire sequence—the order of all 3 billion or so of our DNA’s chemical building blocks, nearly fully deduced by the international Human Genome Project between 1990 and 2003—hasn’t helped much. That investigation showed that barely 2 percent of the human genome consists of actual genes, the information-coding sequences of DNA.
It’s now clear that understanding the human genome is no longer a matter of figuring out what each gene does. The deeper and much harder question is how those genes are used, or regulated, a question that seems to involve some and perhaps much of the rest of the genome. By switching suites of genes on and off, the many different cell types in our bodies can all be created from the same material. Cells also regulate their genes from moment to moment in response to a constant inflow of signals from their neighbors and surroundings. But the processes that govern gene regulation are proving so complex that some biologists wonder whether a full understanding of it—of how the genome really works—will ever be within the grasp of our puny minds.
Some are counting on outsourcing the analysis to artificial intelligence. Genomic “foundation models” such as Evo 2, Genos, and Google DeepMind’s AlphaGenome are trained on vast quantities of genomic data, which biologists use to make predictions about how differences in DNA sequence affect biological processes and ultimately the traits (including disease risk) of a whole organism. These algorithms don’t worry about the complicated regulatory stuff going on. All of that is supposedly subsumed by the algorithm’s “training,” through which it deduces correlations from cases we already know about.
This approach is likely to be useful, but for those who crave real understanding of how the genome, and ultimately life itself, works, a computational black box will never suffice. And perhaps more to the point, the genome might not submit to the kind of straightforward input-output approach that such AI models ultimately assume.
That’s because the genome is no blueprint or algorithm. It’s something else.
Given that it’s the product of around 4 billion years of evolution, perhaps it’s not surprising that our genome is complicated. The surprise has been what those complications are. “Our genome is not what we might make it if we sat down at the drawing board,” said the biologist Karen Adelman, who studies gene regulation at Harvard Medical School.
The traditional view posits that a small proportion of our DNA holds the code for making the protein molecules that orchestrate our cells’ chemistry. Each instruction for a protein is held in a corresponding gene—we have around 20,000 of these—and gene sequences can range in length from a couple of dozen to almost 3 million DNA “letters” (representing molecules called nucleotides).
Making a protein from its gene is a two-stage affair. First the DNA is read, letter by letter, by an enzyme called a polymerase, which creates a copy of that code in a related molecule called messenger RNA (mRNA). This is called transcription. The mRNA is then read by a piece of molecular machinery called the ribosome, which constructs the protein—a process called translation. The proteins made by the ribosome then go off to do their jobs in making and sustaining the organism.
This picture is still more or less correct. But it turns out that “the genes are probably not the most interesting part of the genome,” Adelman said.
What matters more is how our genes, many of which we share with simpler organisms, are regulated—turned on and off. Which proteins a cell needs changes over time and according to cell type: muscle, brain, skin, and so on. How the genes that encode those proteins are regulated depends on some of the genome that doesn’t code for proteins.
Biologists have known about gene regulation, and the involvement of “noncoding” DNA, since the 1960s. But for many years, most of what they understood about this came from studies of simple organisms like bacteria, where the principles are generally straightforward. It has gradually become clear, though, that in complex eukaryotic organisms like us, gene regulation is far more complicated, involving overlapping systems of oversight and control, each with its own intricacies.
Transcription gets started by proteins called transcription factors, which are like the operations managers of gene regulation. These proteins stick to sections of DNA (typically close to the target gene) and recruit the polymerase enzyme to make an mRNA copy. In bacteria, transcription factors are rather like keys that fit the locks of unique binding sites on DNA. But that’s not how they work in complex organisms. In us, the logic of transcription factors is more difficult to parse.
For one thing, our transcription factors don’t show strong preferences for particular DNA binding sites. What’s more, they tend to work in pairs or groups. And a given transcription factor might have different effects in different contexts, such as activating gene transcription in one cell type but suppressing it in another, depending on which other transcription factors are around.
In bacteria, regulation tends to have an “OR” logic, Adelman said, whereby a particular signal turns a gene on or off: It’s either this or that. But in the human genome the logic is more like what computer scientists designate “AND.” Many signals are integrated to reach a regulatory decision: This and that and also that other thing. In this case, regulation can be more responsive to nuances of context, and the regulatory knobs are tunable rather than being just on or off. “This is part of the beauty” of our regulatory complexity, Adelman said.
When they interact with the genome, transcription factors bind to pieces of DNA called enhancers—which present a puzzle of their own.
Enhancers are gathering points for transcription factors, and they are thought to be the decisive influence on transcription: They deliver the “go” signal for a waiting polymerase to make an mRNA version of the DNA sequence. Seems simple enough, but mapping enhancers to their respective genes is far from straightforward. Our genome has hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions, of enhancers. That means we have many more of them than we have genes. Each gene might be influenced by many enhancers, and each enhancer might influence multiple genes.
“It’s embarrassing that 25 years after the Human Genome Project, we don’t know where all the enhancers are in the genome, let alone what they do when they act and which genes they control,” said Wendy Bickmore, a genome biologist at the University of Edinburgh.
Biologists do know that most enhancers won’t respond to a single transcription factor. Their activation “requires a cocktail,” Bickmore said. “That’s what gives [an enhancer] that exquisite specificity—because it’s only in a particular cell at a particular time that you have the right combination of factors to bind and activate that enhancer.”
Some enhancers are, as you’d expect, close to the genes they regulate, or even sit on DNA inside a gene. But others sit far away from the gene—perhaps millions of nucleotides away, with more genes in between.
The existence of such so-called “distal” enhancers “seems bonkers,” Bickmore said. “How do you get that information from over there to over here, to the gene that needs to be activated? That’s a largely unanswered question.”
One of the answers comes in the form of a loop.
Distal enhancers are brought to the gene they regulate on great loops of DNA or, more strictly, of chromatin, the combination of DNA and its packaging proteins that are unraveled as if from a ball of wool. The loops are created by a protein motor called cohesin, which runs up and down the DNA strand and extrudes it as needed.
Once cohesin has formed a loop to bring elements together, what then? It was once thought that they then stick together or assemble into a molecular machine, but they don’t. Rather, the components appear to form a loose but dense blob in which they interact rather weakly, fleetingly, and indiscriminately—a sort of committee, sometimes called a condensate.
These transcription hubs are extremely fluid and differ from one cell to another. “There’ll be a bit of loop extrusion going on over here, in the next cell it might be over here, and the whole thing is turning over incredibly fast,” Bickmore said. Even if the cells are notionally identical—both skin cells, say—exactly what the gene-regulatory machinery is up to at any moment is never quite the same in any two of them.
Chromatin loops are just one reason why a gene’s transcription depends on the shape and structure of the chromatin around it.
The textbook image of a chromosome—one of the 46 units into which our genomes are divided—is of a compact, X-shaped cluster of chromatin. But any time a cell is not actively dividing, its chromatin is unwound into what looks like a tangled mess. There is order to the chaos, however. Some parts of chromatin are densely packed into a form called heterochromatin. The compacted DNA there is relatively inaccessible to transcription factors; the genes it contains are typically silenced. Meanwhile, other parts are relatively loose, open, and accessible: This is called euchromatin.
There are special enzymes involved in packaging and repackaging chromatin, thereby controlling transcription. In other words, what matters is not just the encoded information in the DNA but also how it exists physically and dynamically in space. “We’ve stopped thinking about the genome as a linear piece of DNA code,” Bickmore said. “Thinking about this incredibly dynamic three-dimensional folding as absolutely inherent to regulation is a very exciting change.”
One aspect of this 3D organization is the clustering of segments of chromatin into compartments called topologically associating domains (TADs). Within a TAD, the genes seem to be coregulated: switched on or off in groups. Such groups keep suites of genes active or silent together to form and provide function in different cell types. Cohesin is also involved in the shuffling of chromatin to construct TADs—a dynamic process in which the chromatin is constantly rearranged in our cells.
Chromatin shape can also be influenced by chemical modifications called epigenetic marks: small molecules attached to DNA packaging proteins called histones or stuck directly to DNA. Some of these epigenetic modifications can alter the electrical charges on histones, which changes how the proteins attract or repel one another and so rejigs the chromatin packing. Epigenetic modifications to chromatin are like annotations of the DNA script that change its meaning in a given context. When cells divide, the epigenetic annotations are copied, too.
How and when the marks get added and changed, and what each type of mark means for gene activity, are complex questions with no simple answers. Some researchers talk of an “epigenetic code” governing this aspect of gene regulation, but it’s far from clear if anything so systematic really exists.
All of these processes and others can determine whether a gene gets transcribed into mRNA. But there are further layers of regulation that determine whether the mRNA is then translated into a corresponding protein—and which protein arises.
This post-transcriptional regulation is often controlled by RNA molecules that are said to be noncoding. These short-lived molecules aren’t templates for proteins, as mRNA is, but have other jobs of their own. While mRNA is produced from the protein-coding areas of DNA (so-called “coding genes”), noncoding RNAs are transcribed from other DNA regions now generally described as noncoding genes. These noncoding RNAs are versatile, taking on varied roles in a cell. Researchers are learning more about what they can do every day, and many if not most of them seem to be involved in gene regulation.
Small noncoding RNAs called microRNAs, for example, can silence mRNAs before they can be translated into proteins. They do this by guiding special enzymes to a particular mRNA to degrade or chemically modify it. The microRNAs don’t do this job alone but, not unlike transcription factors, act combinatorially, in groups, and in a rather promiscuous manner: A given microRNA might regulate many mRNAs, and a given mRNA might be regulated by many microRNAs.
Why make an mRNA only to stop it getting translated in a protein? This sort of post-transcriptional regulation is like having another checkpoint: Does the cell really need this protein? MicroRNAs can be mobilized to allow cells to adjust gene expression depending on the immediate context. In this way, the workings of the genome are less like a program’s inevitable progression and more like an adaptive and responsive process.
Another post-transcriptional complication is that mRNAs get translated to protein only after they have been reorganized. Fresh from transcription, an mRNA contains sequences that encode bits of protein, called exons, as well as sequences that shouldn’t be translated and need to be snipped out, called introns. (Strictly speaking, this pre-edited RNA is called pre-mRNA.) The job of editing introns out and splicing exons together is done by a molecular assembly called the spliceosome, which is made from several proteins together with various noncoding RNAs.
The spliceosome too can be sensitive to context, so that it might splice the pre-mRNA to encode one protein in one cell type and a slightly different protein in another. Sometimes these different protein “isoforms” can have very different roles. Transcription factors, for example, are often alternatively spliced in this way, and their isoforms can take on different regulatory tasks—some might activate gene expression, for instance, while others repress it.
All told, these and other regulatory mechanisms show that the genome is far from some automated program running in the background to build us and keep us alive. Our cells are, in effect, making complex decisions about how to use their genes—both the information they contain and the structure they assume.
Thus, cells need to assemble a rather loose and fuzzy committee of components, such as transcription factors and enhancers, to get transcription underway, which also depends on how the chromatin strand is shaped and molded at that moment. Then there are further layers of decisionmaking and action-taking in between mRNA and the final, functional protein.
Remember, too, that all the players—from transcription factors to noncoding RNAs—are themselves produced from the genome in the same kind of context-dependent process. That makes the genome rather like a recursive, self-referential system that the computer scientist Douglas Hofstadter dubbed “a strange loop.” It acts on itself, mindful of its own history—which determines chromatin conformation and epigenetic markings, say—and heedful of messages from inside and outside the cell. Not, then, a blueprint.
And for that reason, not at all easy to understand. “I wouldn’t have designed it this way if I was God,” Bickmore said. “But here we are!”
Why is gene regulation in animals like us so darned complicated? One potential answer is that evolution doesn’t have the foresight to design with efficiency and transparent logic, but merely tinkers with what it has already available. Maybe so—but eukaryotic gene regulation isn’t just a messy version of what happens in bacteria. It has different principles, and there’s surely a reason for them.
Bickmore suspects that the complexity of regulation and of genome organization might have been the only means of generating complexity in the organism. For example, organisms with many tissue types and varied lifestyles required more control over which genes were on or off in a given cell. One thing this demanded was more and more noncoding regulatory sequences in DNA. But then they couldn’t all fit close to the gene itself.
“As you get more complexity, you need to add more and more enhancers,” Bickmore said. “But where are you going to put them? You start to put them farther and farther away. Once they are [far enough], you start to need TADs and three-dimensional [chromatin] folding to allow those things to work.”
We also need regulatory complexity because, over evolutionary time, the human genome has accumulated DNA from parasitic viruses in the form of jumping genetic material called transposable elements. These sequences have inserted themselves all over our chromosomes and are good at replicating themselves. To sift the good DNA from the bad, we needed additional layers of regulation to ensure that cells weren’t translating RNAs they don’t really need or that could be actively harmful.
With so many context-dependent checks and balances in the workings of our genome, it is evidently not a program or algorithm that predictably generates the same outcome in every situation. It’s an open informational system that responds to external inputs and the genome’s dynamic internal conditions. This poses a challenge if AI relies solely on the genetic sequences within genomes to predict what genomes will do.
Researchers Developing AI-based genomic foundation models, such as AlphaGenome, hope that all these layers of regulation—transcription factors, splicing, epigenetic marks, loops, chromatin packing, and so on—will be implicitly included in the correlations that the algorithms learn between genetic sequence and organismal traits. They’re content for the complexity described above to be in a black box, so long as the model generates accurate predictions. But will that work?
“I’m sure [AlphaGenome] is going to be useful, but with limitations,” Bickmore said. “To me the big gap is in the complexity of the human body—in all the cell types and how they change over time in development. And all that data is missing.”
Fundamentally, the challenge is that the genome is not a set of static, linear instructions. It is highly dynamic, and it uses its information contextually, with combinatorial and promiscuous logic. “Whether we’ll ever be able to capture that aspect” in algorithms like AlphaGenome, “I don’t know,” she said.
Yet the problem goes even deeper because the functioning of specific organisms, including each of us, doesn’t just depend on genomes. Other factors, such as diet, environment, microbiome, and, for us at least, culture, can matter hugely, too—not just in terms of how we act and how healthy we are but also in the state of our genome itself. The biologist Adrian Woolfson, cofounder of California-based biotech company Genyro, which aims to use AI systems for so-called “generative biology,” calls this information cloud the “informiome.”
“While the human genome forms the foundation of the human informiome, other layers of extra-genetic information are equally important,” Woolfson wrote in his book On the Future of Species, published in April 2026. Genomic foundation models won’t even be able to predict all the consequences of genetic mutations, he argued, because the relevant information is not in the genome sequence in the first place.
So how should we think about the genome? Maybe the only metaphors that can capture the way the genome really works must come from biology itself. In 2020, the biological historian Evelyn Fox compared the genome to “an exquisitely sensitive reactive system.” Rather than a sequence of genes leading to the formation of traits, she said, it’s more of “a device for regulating the production of specific proteins in response to constantly changing signals it receives from its environment.”
That sounds close to the picture painted by the geneticist Barbara McClintock in the address she delivered upon being awarded the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for her discovery of transposons. The genome, she declared, is “a highly sensitive organ of the cell, monitoring genomic activities and correcting common errors, sensing the unusual and unexpected events and responding to them, often by restructuring the genome.”
Research since that time has fleshed out this image, revealing how the shape of chromatin can matter as much as the information its DNA sequences encode and how an army of molecules collaborates to reorganize it and make collective decisions about how to use its genetic information in context-dependent ways. There is no human technology that works this way, so metaphors such as blueprints, programs, or computers will always fall short.
Bickmore is optimistic that the workings of the genome are understandable, despite its complexity. “We’ve got a handle on it now,” she said. “We might not know the details, but I think the whole field is coalescing now into a framework where we’re thinking along similar lines.” AI can surely help with this sense-making, but in the end, human reasoning will be needed to discern the fundamental principles.
“McClintock was far more on point than people realized at the time,” Adelman said. “What she said was that the genome isn’t static—it’s living.”

articles.title: Bill Gates plans a bigger AI safety push and is leaning on CEOs
articles.text:
Bill Gates plans to widen his push on AI safety, Axios reported, citing unnamed sources. He is personally leaning on business leaders and considering a major deployment of his resources, according to the report.
“I can reach CEOs on this better than you can.” Bill Gates, to one person he consulted on AI safety, according to Axios
Associates told Axios the remark showed a return to “OG” form. Gates has yet to define the exact shape of his campaign, Axios said.
Why Gates changed his mind
Gates has grown dismayed by rising model capabilities, alarming security incidents and what he sees as weak regulation, Axios’s sources said. As he prepared his case for stronger rules, he spoke at length with AI executives, researchers and safety advocates. One of them was Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei.
That process led Gates to see containing AI risks as one of the most important issues of his lifetime, the people said.
In 2023, Gates wrote that “the risks of AI are real but manageable”. In August, he called for new institutions to coordinate AI policy, jobs reserved for humans and a tax on AI tokens and robots. Last month, he warned that AI could cause a billion deaths, and took the case to Ezra Klein’s podcast.
‘Comeback tour’
Some people Gates has spoken to called his advocacy a “comeback tour”, Axios reported. They described it as an attempt to rebuild a legacy hurt by his past association with Jeffrey Epstein. Gates has said he knows some people may dismiss his warnings because of those ties.
“What I did do, in some ways, was very limited, and it was motivated by my desire to raise money. But … it was a huge mistake.” Bill Gates, to Axios in August
A clash with Washington
His calls for strong regulation will put Gates on a collision course with the Trump administration, Axios said. The administration favours a lighter touch. It has organised a group of top officials to police the industry through a voluntary safety pact.

articles.title: How to check your Ethernet cable's speed - Engadget
articles.text:
How to check your Ethernet cable's speed
That 100 Mbps result doesn't automatically mean your Ethernet cable is bad. Here's how to narrow down the culprit.
You have gigabit internet and your wired-in PC is only getting 90 Mbps, so is that outdated Ethernet cable getting in the way? While running wired Ethernet connections avoids Wi-Fi interference and can lower latency, plugging in a cable doesn't automatically mean you'll get ultra-fast speeds. Even if your internet service is speedy, a slow Ethernet connection can slow down file transfers between computers at home.
Using an online speed test won't provide a definitive answer, as it measures more than just the cable. The first place to start is to check the Ethernet link speed, and you don't need to purchase a tester to do this.
Checking your Ethernet link speed
On Windows 11, go to Settings > Network & internet > Ethernet and check the Link speed (Receive/Transmit) field. Another method involves a shortcut that also works on Windows 10: press Windows + R, type ncpa.cpl, right-click your Ethernet adapter and select Status. The negotiated connection rate is displayed in the Speed field.
On a Mac, open System Settings > Network > Ethernet (or your USB Ethernet adapter), then go to Details > Hardware and check the Speed field. Keep the configuration set to Automatic, as manually setting a speed may result in connection issues.
There's a difference between seeing 1 Gbps here and actually downloading at 1 Gbps. The figure describes the connection between your computer and the router or network switch. It doesn't tell you your internet speed or the highest speed the cable can handle. The link-speed reading alone also can't confirm whether the cable is faulty.
While you're looking into this, take a look at the lettering on the jacket of the cable. Markings like Cat5, Cat5e or Cat6 are typically found there, as the connectors are virtually identical and don't tell you much. Both Cat5e and Cat6 support gigabit Ethernet, so Cat6 is more than sufficient for 1,000 Mbps.
The category isn't an absolute speed ceiling either. Older cables can sometimes support very high speeds for short runs, but a successful test doesn't mean they will perform the same way for longer runs.
How to tell if your Ethernet cable is actually the problem
If your computer reports 100 Mbps cable speeds when you expect 1 Gbps, verify the hardware on both ends. A 100 Mbps LAN port on a router, or a similarly limited USB Ethernet adapter, will limit the connection no matter how costly your Ethernet cable is. Even with gigabit-capable ports at both ends, a damaged wire or loose connector can still disrupt the connection or fall back to slower connections. Gigabit Ethernet utilizes all four twisted pairs of wires inside the cable, whereas conventional 100 Mbps Ethernet uses two.
Start by reseating the connectors, then swap in a short, known-good cable using the same ports. If the reading changes from 100 Mbps to 1 Gbps, the original cable or its connectors are strong suspects for what's wrong. If nothing changes, check the port specifications and adapter settings before spending money on a replacement.
For a more thorough check, you can use iPerf3 to measure real throughput between two wired computers without involving your ISP. After installing it on both computers, turn off Wi-Fi, run iperf3 -s on one computer and iperf3 -c SERVER_IP on the other (replacing SERVER_IP with the local IP address of the first computer). Compare the results after swapping cables, keeping the rest of the setup the same.
A multimeter or simple cable tester can determine some wiring faults, but neither can determine the maximum data rate that a cable supports. That requires specialized cable qualification equipment. Certification testers verify compliance with cabling standards.

articles.title: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
articles.text:
Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice?
Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen.
In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak, suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them.
Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup, raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.”
Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August. Amazon has since filed an amended complaint.
Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems
This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon, which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok, Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are.
“Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge. “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.”
Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents.
The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment.
Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.”
The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products.
While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.”

articles.title: Sergey Brin says Google’s AI now helps build its next models
articles.text:
Google is “starting to get onto that RSI treadmill”, cofounder Sergey Brin said in a roundtable on Gemini 4 Argon, Business Insider reported. Google shared the video on Wednesday. Brin pointed to the Flash models Google released before Gemini 4 as evidence.
“And now our researchers and the model work hand in hand to make the next version of the model.” Sergey Brin, Google cofounder
Recursive self-improvement, or RSI, means AI helps build better AI. That speeds up the pace of new models. Brin said Google would be a couple of models ahead internally by the time people watched the video.
Brin joined Google’s Josh Woodward, Tulsee Doshi and Melvin Johnson for the conversation. Google released Argon publicly this week. Brin has been working on Gemini since his return to Google.
What Google’s safety report says
Google DeepMind published a safety and security report for Argon this month. It finds “no significant end-to-end acceleration of AI R&D, AI-driven or otherwise”. It rates the risk from AI-driven AI R&D as “currently low”.
The report says AI now automates some parts of AI research. Google surveyed 12 senior leaders and researchers for it.
“AI agents now operate as high-leverage assistants that author a majority of production code and bug fixes, though code changes remain subject to human review before submission.” Gemini 4 Argon Safety and Security Report
Most production code at Google DeepMind is now more than 75% AI-written, according to the report. The share of fully delegated pull requests rose from 7.5% in April to 11.9% in September. About 88% still need repeated human steering or code written by a human.
Humans remain key to choosing research directions, designing new experiments and diagnosing training problems, the report says. Argon solves only around half of the challenges in Google’s internal test of AI research tasks. Full automation would need a near-perfect score.
A steady pace
Google tracks the rate at which Gemini improves with an internal index built from 92 benchmarks. Before 1 April 2026, it rose by 0.091 points a month. After that date, it rose by 0.118 points a month, a difference the report calls not statistically significant.
Argon sits above that trend. Google suspects this is due to more investment and more training compute, “rather than reflecting AI-driven acceleration”.
‘A new gear’
Vihan Jain co-leads RSI and AI for science for Gemini at Google DeepMind. On X, Jain wrote that the model is “embedded in its own evolution”.
“When your post-training demand shifts from asking for raw chips to asking for Argon quota, you know the RSI flywheel has reached a new gear.” Vihan Jain, Google DeepMind
Gladstone AI interviewed researchers at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind for a report published this week. Most believe RSI will start within three to 12 months. It could come sooner, they said, assuming no US government intervention or slowdown.
Last month, US congressman Ro Khanna said he plans a bill to ban self-improving AI. OpenAI has asked the US to lead global standards for it.

articles.title: More than Just Storage: 8 Ways To Repurpose Your Old USB Flash Drive - Engadget
articles.text:
More than Just Storage: 8 Ways To Repurpose Your Old USB Flash Drive
Smart ways to turn forgotten storage into something useful
Remember the days when USB flash drives were the greatest thing since CD-ROMs? Those were obviously many days ago, but when thumb drives hit the shelves of, um, RadioShack, they were pretty revolutionary. Saving and sharing files for school or work became significantly easier than file sharing with floppy disks — as long as your files weren't too big. But eventually those stick drives got bigger. 1GB, 4GB, 10GB. They got so big they became external hard drives.
And then the equivalent of an extinction event for flash drives hit. The cloud was born, and it was endless. Now we could upload unlimited docs, photos and videos of any size to the ether for pretty cheap. Predictably, USBs went the way of Maxwell floppy discs.
Post-cloud, most of our USB drives ended up in boxes and desk drawers next to our iPods, firewires and dial-up modems. However, unlike much of our museum-ready tech, you can actually use your old flash drives and portable hard drives for some pretty neat projects. They may even save you money and earn you a little more privacy.
Make Yourself a NAS (Network Attached Storage) Device
At some point in the past few years, Sonos, the wireless home audio system, stopped allowing users to point their speakers to music folders on their computers and external hard drives. Instead, Sonos users now had to share their music folder over their local network. This didn't mean you couldn't keep your library on the same old hard drive anymore. It simply meant your hard drive was functioning more like a Network Attached Storage (NAS) device, because the library was served over your network. The only downside was your computer had to be on to play your music. Normally, NAS drives don't have to be. But the idea itself sparked a few ideas.
Imagine if you plugged that same old hard drive directly into your router. As long as your family was on the same network, it would now show up on everyone's devices. You could share whatever you wanted this way. Pics, recipes, to-do lists, books, movies — anything really. It would be like your private family cloud. No need to imagine, actually. It's very easy to set up. Here's how.
Plug your external drive into your router's USB port, if you have one. Fire up your browser and open up your router settings. Check that file sharing is on. That's basically it. That drive should now show up on all your local devices like any other network volume or drive. If you're concerned about the steps you can take to improve online safety, as you should be, you can hand-pick the devices on your local area network (LAN) that can access your NAS. LAN, as opposed to WAN, is the network of devices that use your router to communicate with each other, which is important because only people on your network can access your files this way.
Create a Slideshow Without Google Photos
Okay, so you've turned your beat-up Seagate into a functioning NAS device running off your router. Anyone on your network can access those files now. But let's say you want to share pics when you're somewhere else without direct access to your network. You can do that too, with a little more elbow grease.
First, download and install the latest version (3.2.1 or later) of an application called HFS, short for "HTTP File Server," on your home computer. HFS works with Windows machines and Macs, and, best of all, it's free. In both cases, since you've already set up your NAS, your home computer should already recognize your USB device as a volume or drive. Copy the network path name or drag and drop the volume into your open HFS window. Now you're ready to share your files — with two important caveats.
One, HFS will need to be up and running for this to work, so your home computer will need to be on. Two, opening up local folders to the internet at large can get messy, to say the least. Especially if it isn't a photo of your Corgi you want to share, but an electricity bill or a copy of your driver's license. To secure your home file server, you'll want to grab a free program called ngrok. It requires the command line, but after you install ngrok and set it up, you shouldn't have to do anything.
Ngrok is critical because it gives you a secure web link you can access remotely. Have that link handy when you're ready to share your files and you're good to go. As with HFS, ngrok will need to be running on your home computer in order for you to share your photos.
Mission Impossible Your Windows Device with a Physical Login
Do you really think Tom Cruise uses a measly login to open his laptop? Ha! If Tom Cruise opens his laptop at all — that is to say, if Tom Cruise doesn't open his Chromebook using his mind alone — he definitely uses a USB pen drive for extra security. Now you can, too.
If you're running Windows, install a program like USB Raptor on the computer you want to log in to. Stick in your thumb drive. This will serve as your key. USB Raptor will lead you through the configuration process and add a tiny encrypted unlock file to your drive. When the USB drive is inserted, your computer unlocks. As soon as you remove it, it locks.
Another option is Rohos, which works on both Windows devices and Macs. The results are the same. Just keep in mind that USB Raptor is free and open source; Rohos requires a paid subscription.
The advantage of this approach is that no one without that key can get onto your device, not even Tom Cruise. Also, you don't have to remember a master password or risk using a weak one. On the other hand, carrying a flash drive around in your pocket isn't exactly 2026.
If you don't mind carrying around a second physical device to open your device, you may want to try Google Titan or YubiKey instead. These, or any other FIDO2 security keys, use a virtually unassailable cryptographic key to lock down computers, which may offer tighter security than an old USB thumb drive serving as a physical token. That said, a USB login is a step-up from the login setups most of us already have, and it's free if you're recycling an old thumb drive. Security keys will set you back at least $25 a pop.
Cure Your Sick Devices with a Portable Antivirus
Bad viruses are nasty. They can lock you out of your operating system (OS) so you can't get inside to root them out. Like bed bugs, evil malware can be very persistent. It can deactivate your native antivirus or meddle with essential system processes. It can even reinstall itself if you manage to find it and delete it. In the worst cases — ransomware being one of the worst and on the rise — it can lock your files down.
Typically, with invasive malware, a lot of us would just throw in the towel and take our device to a professional to clean it up. But you don't necessarily have to. Here's where your grungy old Verbatim 1GB might be able to help.
For Windows users, load a portable antivirus like ESET SysRescue Live or Kaspersky Rescue Disk onto your flash drive. Start your computer and boot up the antivirus. The antivirus will run independently of your OS and find the malicious code, which won't even realize you're there. You may be able to clean up your machine that way. If you're on one of the latest Mac devices, a bootable antivirus isn't going to be an option due to Apple's strict boot security protocols, but you should be able to run macOS Recovery and swat the bug that way.
Help A Kid Learn for Free
Sugar Labs wants our old USBs, and they aren't collecting them for a museum of vintage technology. They're putting learning software on them for free and giving them to kids in underprivileged communities to plug into their laptops and learn math, coding, and critical problem-solving skills.
For a bit of background, Sugar Labs has been around since 2008, and they claim to have served over three million young learners in 170 languages. Making a difference is easy. You send your spare flash drives (1GB minimum) to Recycle USB. They reformat them and load their super-light OS, Sugar-on-a-Stick. Then they send the sticks to young learners everywhere who plug them into their laptops and learn.
This isn't a Sunday tinkering project. But if you do have a drawer full of dusty thumb drives, it's a great way to give them a new life that can make a huge impact in the places that need them.
Host a Website off Your Old Sandisk
This is definitely more of a "two-Sunday" project, but if you're into the open web, like static websites (simple HTML and CSS, no backend), and aren't afraid to get your hands dirty, hosting your own website can be a lot of fun. Here's the basic idea.
Dust off your thumb drive and put all your website files on it. A lot of folks use Raspberry Pis for this because they're small and relatively cheap. Stick your drive into your router's USB port. Your router needs to be able to run a web server and serve files from a USB. If it can, you need to point the server to the website directory on your drive. At that point, you should be able to see your website locally at the corresponding IP address and port you've configured on your router.
Just to restate, this is not a piece of cake. Your router needs to have firmware like OpenWrt, which comes with a pre-installed web server, and setup will require the terminal and possibly some hair pulling.
To make your website public, you'd need to point your domain (mystaticwebsite.com, for example) to your public IP address and configure your router to accept incoming requests. Here's where it gets a little fuzzy security-wise. Ideally, you don't want people accessing your website via HTTP. HTTP is unencrypted, and browsers will flag your website as potentially dangerous. You want access by HTTPS only, and for that you'd need to set up an SSL/TLS certificate via a service like Let's Encrypt.
So, yes, a bit of a hassle (and subject to the whims of your ISP), but a lot of fun!
Carry Essential Apps Around With You
Laptops and tablets are made for portability, but you may find yourself in a situation without your go-to device, and hence without the apps you swear by. You're traveling and for some reason your work laptop is missing the latest version of Firefox and doesn't let you install it, for example. Or you're on a plane and your kids don't have VLC media player installed. Game of Doom, anyone?
In all of these cases, and many others, you can download a portable version of your favorite app directly onto your USB flash drive and launch it from there. This could be extra handy for devices with download restrictions like university or work laptops. Just be aware that not all apps have portable versions. LibreOffice does, for instance, but Microsoft Office doesn't. Similarly, you won't be able to launch iTunes or many antiviruses (see above) from your flash drive. To check if your favorite apps have portable versions, head to a site like PortableApps.com or PortApps.com. For power users, the Awesome Portable GitHub Repository is a gold mine.
If you want to go one step further, application launchers like PortableApps (Windows only) will keep all your portable apps in one place and organized. For Mac users, you can still load and run apps off your USB (or SSD for heavier loads). You'd just launch those apps from Finder, provided Apple's Gatekeeper and runtime protection don't block them.
Make a DIY Password Manager
While most of the best password managers are quite secure because they use Pentagon-grade encryption, there's always the chance that one day, your manager could get hacked. And not just by a rogue AI, like the OpenAI agents who hijacked a German coding forum. LastPass got hacked in 2022, including its customer vaults. Big outfits like 1Password and the open-source Bitwarden have also announced security vulnerabilities in the past.
Is this a reason not to trust them with your passwords and personally identifiable information (PII)? Probably not. But many password managers aren't free. So you may just want to save money. In that case, get your Lexar 512MB out and find some free encryption software like KeePass. Then put your passwords in a file and choose a master password so you can decrypt them.
The advantages of this old-school hack are that your passwords don't live in the cloud; they're physical. Just don't lose your master password or your logins are toast.
Is this a better solution than a traditional password manager? It's certainly better than keeping your passwords on sticky notes. Just be prepared to lose some of the time-saving features a good password manager provides, like auto-fill and the ability to create logins automatically while you're online.

articles.title: Wired earbuds are having a moment, and Bose is here for it
articles.text:
After Apple courageously removed the headphone jack from the iPhone in 2016, most people switched to Bluetooth earbuds and never looked back. But their wired counterparts have stuck around, and their sales even went up this year after five years of decline.
Bose’s new wired earbuds are simple in the best way
Wired earbuds are making a small comeback, and Bose is capitalizing on it — with ANC this time.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Part of the resurgence can be tied to the fact that they’re cool now with younger generations — following the revival of tape decks and vinyl. Celebrities have been spotted wearing them, and there’s even an Instagram account that follows the trend. Wired earbuds have real benefits. They don’t need a battery, so they’ll last longer than wireless ones that eventually die, and it’s a lot harder to lose a wired pair with a long cable than a single earbud.
Now, after more than a decade, Bose has returned to the wired world, but the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are no throwbacks.
The Good
- One of the few sets of wired earbuds with ANC
- Comfortable and secure fit
- High-res audio
- Simple to use
The Bad
- Call quality isn’t great
- Wind noise is distracting
The $99 Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds connect over USB-C, so they don’t need an extra dongle to work with current phones. That’s also how they can offer ANC. Because the 3.5mm or 4.4mm analog audio connector doesn’t provide enough power for active noise cancellation, most wired earbuds, from cheap off-brands to wildly expensive audiophile in-ear monitors, rely on passive isolation only. Bose’s last attempt at wired in-ears with ANC, 2013’s QuietComfort 20, had a 3.5mm jack, and their ANC relied on a rechargeable battery in the cable. The new Bose earbuds don’t need the battery pack; they can get the minimal power they need for ANC from the USB-C port.
There are a few other USB-C wired headphones with active noise cancellation, but not many. There’s also the $30 Belkin SoundForm ANC Wired Earbuds, which reportedly have weak noise canceling, and Audio-Technica released a pair in Asia earlier this year.
The best part of the Bose earbuds, or any wired earbuds, is that they’re simple. No need to worry about pairing them, no need to charge them, and no need to fiddle with an app. Plug them into the USB-C port on a phone or computer and they just work.
While the noise canceling performance doesn’t measure up to Bose’s Bluetooth earbuds (the wired earbuds have two mics per side, while the QuietComfort Earbuds have three), it’s still solid for the price. It does a great job blocking low-frequency sounds like air conditioners and low truck rumbles, but has difficulty muting conversation (with ANC on, I can’t hear our air conditioner at all, but can make out every word of my wife’s phone conversation as I write this). There’s a slight high-end hiss when the noise canceling is active, but it’s only noticeable when they aren’t playing any sound.
And they sound great. Vocals are clear and bright, and bass is punchy without overwhelming other instruments. I wouldn’t mind being able to cut down the high-end brightness a bit (mainly to tame cymbal ringing), but since these don’t use an app there are no EQ options. The wired connection allows for low latency, so there’s no worry about sound and video lining up, and they support high-res audio at 24-bit/48kHz. I went back and forth between CD quality (16-bit/44.1kHz) and high-res streams of the new release of The Beatles’ Rubber Soul on Qobuz, and the high-res versions sounded a bit more open and spacious. It’s not an enormous difference, but I’d listen to the high-res version on the Bose over the CD-level stream any day.
The in-line remote has three buttons that control volume, playback, and noise-canceling mode selection. They respond quickly when pressed and have a nice rubberized texture. The headphones come with three ear tip sizes and two sets of wings to find a good fit (you don’t even need to use the wings if you find them uncomfortable). I was easily able to find a comfortable combination and they stayed securely in my ears for hours. The earbuds are also IPX4 rated if there’s a light rain while you’re out or you want to use them on a run.
Even with the benefits of wired earbuds, though, nostalgia can’t wipe away the frustrations. If you don’t run the 4.2-foot cable under your shirt, or coil up the excess in your jacket pocket, it catches on everything. In my short time with the Bose, the cable caught on the handle of a kitchen drawer, the edge of my keyboard, the zipper of my sweatshirt, the strap of a bag I was carrying, my pocket (when I accidentally stuffed too much of the excess in with my phone), and even the hand of a stranger who got too close to me in line at Starbucks.
And as with any wired earbuds, there’s cable noise, as vibrations from rubbing or bumping against something travel up the cable to be heard in the earbuds. Although I will say the cable insulation is enough to minimize the effect better than cheap (and older) options.
The Bose struggle with wind. The microphones for noise canceling or transparency mode pick up the wind noise, and it’s distracting — with ANC on, it cuts out the low-end whoosh decently, but the high end is still incredibly present. I found turning it off was best when it was windy outside, although that meant compromising on the noise canceling.
Call quality also isn’t the best. The microphone is on the in-line remote, and it picks up a good amount of ambient sound during calls. If you regularly make calls while walking busy streets, these aren’t the earbuds for you.
I’m not ready to go back to 2016 and convert back to wired earbuds. In most situations, the benefits of wireless earbuds outweigh those of wired ones, and I don’t see that changing for me. But for the ease of use, convenience of a USB-C connection, lack of lag, high-res capability, sound quality, and the fact they include ANC, the Bose are unquestionably the best affordable wired option out there.
Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

articles.title: Anthropic’s Daniela Amodei warns against AI girlfriends and boyfriends
articles.text:
Anthropic president Daniela Amodei has warned that AI romantic partners risk driving people further apart, Business Insider reported. She spoke in a prerecorded interview with Arianna Huffington, founder and chief executive of Thrive Global. It was made for the Think Health conference in Bentonville, Arkansas, on Friday.
“I think that’s a terrible use of AI and people should not do it.” Daniela Amodei, Anthropic president, to Arianna Huffington
AI relationships, Amodei said, are “another step further down the road of disintermediation of humans being further from one another.”
What social media did
Amodei said her concerns come from what she sees as the damage social media has done to human relationships. Platforms like Snapchat and Instagram have increasingly replaced face-to-face contact, she said. Online arguments have taken the place of in-person communities.
“What it’s led to is a warranted skepticism from people that technology can be used to bring us closer together.” Daniela Amodei
It would “probably be a better world”, she said, if people spent less time with technology and more time with each other.
‘Claude can never be your partner’
Later in the interview, Amodei said some relationships should stay human, however advanced AI becomes.
“Claude can never be your manager or your therapist or your partner.” Daniela Amodei, on Anthropic’s chatbot
Those are “fundamental human relationships” that she thinks “will become more important”, she added.
She wants AI to take over repetitive or isolating tasks instead, leaving people more time for friends, family and partners. She gave healthcare as an example. AI tools could help doctors find medical information faster, she said, so they can spend more time with patients.
Companion apps and Claude’s rules
Apps such as Replika, Nomi and Character.AI let users build relationships with personalised chatbots. Character.AI filed for bankruptcy this week.
Last week, Anthropic updated Claude’s usage policy with new clauses on deceptive campaigns, weapons and surveillance, Business Insider reported. One new provision bans roleplay between the model and minors. The policy takes effect on 12 November.
Anthropic told investors this week that it made $16.8bn in revenue in the third quarter. It is preparing to go public, possibly as soon as November.

articles.title: The Tesla Roadster should go into production in 2028, but don't get your hopes up - Engadget
articles.text:
The Tesla Roadster should go into production in 2028, but don't get your hopes up
I drive upside down on the boulevard of broken dreams.
Tesla dominated the headlines on Thursday thanks to a very cool stunt. In announcing the redesigned Roadster at its October 15 event, the electric car company put some jet fuel in the mix. After driving up a C-shaped ramp on a suction rig until it was upside-down, the Roadster floated to the ground on rocket boosters. We also learned that the new sports car is targeting a 2028 production window and that it will cost $250,000 to reserve the "Thrust" trim level with cold-gas thrusters. "We enter production in 2028," Musk said during the event. "Actually, for real."
If you're feeling a bit of deja vu, don't worry — you're firmly within your faculties. This is not the first time Tesla has announced the second-generation Roadster, and the company hasn't exactly drawn attention to that fact with this re-announced version. Still, the question on many minds is whether this is another paper launch for Tesla's embattled second-gen sports car.
The first Roadster was a milestone for Tesla in its early days. Released in 2008 and produced in very limited numbers, the car was ideated by one of Tesla's original founders, Martin Eberhard, before current CEO Elon Musk had bought Eberhard and his partner, Marc Tarpenning, out of the company. It was the idea of the Roadster which initially drew Musk to the fledgling startup in 2004 and prompted his initial investment in the company. He would go on to oversee the production of that sports car. Crammed inside the chassis of a Lotus Elise, it was truly impressive at the time to see a battery-powered vehicle able to reach 244 miles on a charge.
The redesigned Roadster was first unveiled in November 2017, promising to be the apex of Tesla's innovations in electric vehicle manufacturing. Musk called it "a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars." Targeted for a 2020 release, it was shown off alongside the Tesla Semi, a Class 8 electric semitruck which also stalled in production. In Feburary 2018, Musk promised a "SpaceX" package that would "include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around the car" and would "dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking and cornering."
Then the delays began. With Tesla still accepting deposits starting at $50,000 and extending up to $250,000, the initial 2020 production window came and went. In a July 2020 earnings call for Tesla, Musk said production would begin within the following year to 18 months. With the globe engulfed in a public health crisis, the delay wasn't the most shocking of developments. Ironically, Musk noted in an interview with Joe Rogan that same year that he wanted to build the Cybertruck first — a mission accomplished after years of that vehicle's own delays.
But a year and a half after the initial delay, there was no Roadster in sight. Musk delayed the car to 2022 in early 2021, but by the end of the year, that projection had slipped to 2023. The CEO announced further delays in 2023 and 2024.
And those years have been bizarre for Musk and Tesla, to say the least. The CEO has undergone a public transformation from public environmentalist to far-right political kingmaker, a period which culminated in a slash-and-burn of the Federal government as he headed up president Donald Trump's newly formed Department of Government Efficiency. By July 2025, The Lancet had published a study projecting the cuts could lead to more than 14 million deaths by 2030. Musk has disputed those numbers, but the reputational damage his stint in government caused spilled over to Tesla, leading to widespread global protests against the company. As Musk stepped down from DOGE in May 2025, dogged by allegations of substance abuse and family drama, the Roadster may not have been near the top of the billionaire's priority list.
By the time Tesla recommitted to releasing the Roadster this past April, many had given up hope that the sports car would ever make it to market. Tesla's failure to deliver the vehicle had long ago become pop-cultural joke fodder, and even Tesla owners such as YouTuber Marques Brownlee, who had interviewed Musk multiple times on his MKBHD channel, fretted on his Waveform podcast in September 2025, "Tesla has been sitting with my 50 grand for eight years and hasn't done anything with it." Another high-profile figure to complain about their Roadster reservations included Musk's erstwhile business partner and current rival Sam Altman of OpenAI.
It's worth noting that a launch event without a firm launch date isn't much of a launch. Even after Tesla's impressive October event, Musk and company will need to convince potential customers that putting down a deposit for the Roadster is a better investment than burning a pile of money with a Boring Company flamethrower.

articles.title: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
articles.text:
When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions.
Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
Its simplified, hands-free instructions strip out much of what’s essential to online recipes.
The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. No distractions, no unnecessary text, and no need to deal with a touchscreen while you’re wrist-deep in a chicken carcass. The appeal is obvious.
There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. “Tools that just extract the recipe,” Eater senior reporter Bettina Makalintal says, “break apart that unspoken social contract with recipe developers and audiences.”
The online recipe landscape is a diverse place. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains.
The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. That’s welcome, but for website owners it’s still a lot less valuable than the repeated ad impressions that come from someone scrolling down the page and staying on it while they cook.
“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”
— Jaya Saxena
It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page.
And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. “So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”
Apple is far from the first company to attempt to streamline online recipes. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Bigger tech companies have been able to plow through that resistance. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all.
Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.”
Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. For them, the choice remains as it has for some time: Stick it out with ever-diminishing Google traffic and ad revenue; take on more sponsored content and paid-for recipes with big brands; or move to a paywall or newsletter business model.
Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.
Some version of paid-for content may be the only answer going forward, though, for creators both big and small. Tech companies like Apple will have to grapple with how their tools work when access to free content gets trickier, and the rest of us may have to get used to paying for recipes again.
“A good, creative recipe that has been tested to ensure it really works takes time and effort and money,” Saxena says. “It is a real skill to communicate how something is made when you’re not physically with that person, and buying all the ingredients needed to test things multiple times is expensive. People should probably be more comfortable paying for that.”

articles.title: Meta drops ‘train’ from website-crawling terms
articles.text:
Meta has rewritten new terms that would have let it crawl and train its AI on the websites of businesses that use its ads and tools. Critics say the change does not go far enough.
The company changed the terms late on Friday after complaints from business customers and the media, Gizmodo reported. The revised terms preview no longer uses the word ‘train’.
“We’ve heard you and want to clarify,” Meta said in a statement to the Mercury News.
The company said the crawling terms only ever applied to its ads and business products. It has now spelled that out in the terms.
What the terms said
The original clause let Meta use automated software to access, copy and re-crawl websites linked to its business products, PPC Land reported. It also covered using that content to train Meta’s own products.
The terms take effect on 30 October. Businesses accept them simply by carrying on using Meta’s commercial products.
The new wording focuses on advertising and business products. Meta also said it was not changing how its web crawlers work.
Publishers are not convinced
The News/Media Alliance, which represents US publishers, said the fix only limits what Meta can use content for.
Training was taken out of the listed uses but not expressly banned, spokesperson Sam Quigley told the Mercury News.
“It’s still potentially on the table,” he said.
Quigley also noted that the terms do not say Meta will respect robots.txt. That is the file sites use to tell crawlers which pages they may visit.
Why it matters
The terms cover data gathered by web scrapers, bots, spiders, crawlers and user agents. That wording lands as AI agents spread across the web and the old rules for bots come under strain.
Meta is pushing hard on AI after launching Muse, its chatbot. Startups such as Firecrawl are also building web tools for agents.
