articles.title: Semiconductor market to remain solid ‘at least through next year,’ South Korea finance minister says
articles.text:
The semiconductor boom will last at least through 2027, South Korean finance minister Lee Hyoung-Il said on Saturday.
"For now, our view is that we can sustain this growth at least through next year," Lee told CNBC on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "That's because the gap between demand and supply for semiconductors is still very wide, and supply is still being expanded."
His comments come after semiconductor stocks fell sharply this week, hurt by investor concerns about interest rate hikes and rising competition from Chinese companies. South Korean chip stocks like SK Hynix and Seoul Semiconductor were part of the sell-off, along with U.S. giants like Nvidia.
Chip stocks have fueled volatility in South Korea's stock market this year, Lee said. He attributed the market's wild swings to the semiconductor industry's larger share of the economy than in other countries. Despite the market swings, South Korea's economy is "solid," Lee said.
On Thursday, an opinion column in Maeil Business Newspaper, a prominent South Korean publication, urged the country's government to prepare for the coming slowdown in the artificial intelligence boom. The author said two experts expect a "flood of new supply" of semiconductors that will turn the memory market "into a red ocean" by 2029, according to a CNBC translation.
While South Korea's semiconductors may be driving volatility in its stock market, the industry has also fueled tax growth. Lee said the country expects to collect more taxes than initially projected this year.
South Korea will ultimately be in a stronger fiscal position because of the chip boom, he added.
WATCH: Don't overlook opportunity in South Korea, says Verdad Advisers' Rasmussen

articles.title: AI stocks plunge. Inflation heats up. Where we're still finding opportunities
articles.text: The sinking AI trade and hotter-than-expected inflation data rattled last week's stock market. But solid bank earnings and a rotation beyond tech gave us reasons for optimism. The Nasdaq's 4.5% weekly decline broke a four-week winning streak and marked the worst weekly decline for the tech-heavy index since June. The S & P 500 fell 2% last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average bucked the trend — gaining 0.7% as investors rotated into healthcare, consumer staples, and other sectors less dependent on the artificial intelligence boom. The sell-off accelerated Wednesday after hotter-than-expected consumer inflation data raised concerns that the Federal Reserve could keep interest rates elevated for longer. September's consumer price index rose 3.7% from a year earlier, above the 3.6% expected, while core inflation also came in slightly hotter than anticipated. Thursday's producer price index offered little relief, jumping 1.3% for the month and 6.3% annually, the biggest annual and monthly gains since March 2022 and December 2022, respectively. Higher inflation, fueled partly by elevated oil prices, threatens to push up borrowing costs and complicate the massive AI infrastructure buildout. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan warned Monday that access to capital could become the industry's next major constraint. Our cybersecurity stocks were crushed last week, while Meta Platforms and Microsoft had some of the week's rare bright spots in tech. Against that backdrop, we continued diversifying beyond the AI trade — adding to Kimberly-Clark on Tuesday as its Kenvue acquisition moved closer to completion. We exited our remaining Honeywell Technologies position on Wednesday to replenish cash. We trimmed Cardinal Health Thursday to lock in profits after its recent rally and bought more Bank of New York following strong earnings Here's a closer look at the three developments that shaped the market week. AI's sell-off makes the case for diversification The AI trade took another hit last week as investors grew concerned about rising borrowing costs and mounting competition in the semiconductor industry. Memory stocks — including Micron , Sandisk , Western Digital , and Seagate — fell after Chinese rival CXMT announced progress on a more efficient chip structure , raising fears of increased competition and a potential supply glut. The iShares Semiconductor ETF extended its losing streak to nine straight sessions, its longest in more than a decade, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF was down 10% for the week, its worst week since July. Concerns that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout sent neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its total debt rise to more than $51 billion , plunging 25% last week. Perhaps even more concerning than the stock rout has been the jump in CoreWeave corporate bond yields and spike in credit default swaps , a kind of insurance policy on debt. Our cyber stocks Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike were our worst performers of the week, losing more than 18% and 17%, respectively. Reports that OpenAI is in early talks to buy Trail of Bits hurt the cyber sector. An acquisition of this sort would expand OpenAI's cybersecurity aspirations. The cyber stocks were also caught in the AI trade crossfire. As investors rotated out of AI and into defensive stocks, Kimberly-Clark and Eli Lilly emerged as some of our portfolio's best performers last week. The sell-off reinforced the importance of diversification . "We don't talk enough about diversification, in part because it's no fun when one group keeps outperforming the rest of the market," Jim said Thursday on "Mad Money." "But when that group crashed to earth over the last few weeks, only diversification could save your portfolio." It's unclear how long the rotation will last, but concentrating too heavily in one investing theme leaves investors vulnerable to steep losses and panic selling. Diversification helps cushion those swings and makes it easier to stay invested. Meta and Microsoft prove why patience pays off Not every tech stock got slammed last week. Club holdings Meta Platforms and Microsoft showed why patience with high-quality companies can pay off. The Facebook and Instagram parent rallied after Monday's release of its latest AI models , Muse Wonder and the more advanced Muse Wonder Full, which Wells Fargo said ranks among the industry's best, behind only Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5. The launch could attract more paying users and create revenue opportunities beyond advertising, offering further evidence that Meta's massive AI investments are beginning to pay off. Microsoft closed at a record high Tuesday for the first time in nearly a year, completing a remarkable comeback after shares plunged more than a third on concerns about AI spending and Copilot's competitiveness. We stuck with the stock because we trusted CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood to turn things around. It's a call Jim reinforced during Thursday's October Monthly Meeting . Microsoft's efforts to expand Azure capacity, rein in spending growth, and revamp Copilot helped restore investor confidence. Both recoveries reinforce Jim's longstanding investing rules: own best-of-breed companies, do the homework and avoid panicking when a quality stock falls out of favor. Meta and Microsoft did finish the week down more than 1% each, but that was a far cry better than most of our tech holdings. Salesforce , our big tech standout for the week, gained 5%. It is another stock that Jim believed in when it was getting killed earlier this year. While still down 9% year to date, Salesforce is up 65% since its 52-week low of $146 in June. Bank earnings impress, but Wall Street isn't buying Third-quarter bank earnings gave us reasons for optimism, even as largely solid results failed to translate into stock gains. Jim said on Wednesday that investors appear more concerned about what lies ahead for the economy than what the banks just reported, given persistent inflation, rising interest rates, and pressure on capital markets. Goldman Sachs delivered a standout quarter Tuesday, with equities trading revenue surging 72%, investment banking fees rising 21% and asset and wealth management exceeding expectations. Despite the strong showing, shares surrendered an early rally. We viewed the weakness as a buying opportunity, upgrading Goldman to our buy-equivalent 1 rating while maintaining our $1,200 price target. Wells Fargo reported mixed results Tuesday, beating earnings estimates but missing on revenue. Encouragingly, net interest margin stabilized at 2.43% after four consecutive quarterly declines. We upgraded shares to our buy-equivalent 1 rating and maintained our $95 price target. Bank of New York also impressed Thursday, beating revenue and earnings expectations and raising its full-year outlook. Strong fee-based revenue reinforced our confidence in its custody-focused business model, which generates recurring income and is less dependent on traditional lending. And as mentioned earlier, we got bigger in the position on earnings day. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long KMB, BNY, CAH, MU, LLY, META, MSFT, GS, WFC. See here for a full list of the stocks.) Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. If Jim has talked about a stock on CNBC TV, he waits 72 hours after issuing the trade alert before executing the trade. articles.title: 'Dead money’ for a decade: Why this hedge fund approach may deliver an advantage over bonds
articles.text:
Investors may want to rethink their bond allocation and opt for managed futures exposure.
DBi's Andrew Beer suggests the popular hedge fund strategy could deliver a modern twist to traditional 60/40 portfolios.
"[Bonds have] been dead money for the entire decade," the firm's co-founder and managing member told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "I fell in love with a strategy called managed futures because tactical is really good. Be nimble when other people's [portfolios] aren't."
Beer contends the managed futures strategy, historically only available to hedge funds, could counterbalance stocks better than bonds during periods of volatility, which has been moving higher due to recent worries surrounding debt and the artificial intelligence trade.
His reason: Managed futures exchange-traded funds can go long and short across global markets to position early against turbulent market events.
"You want something that has low correlation to both stocks and bonds, and something that will do well in crises," Beer said. "It's very, very hard to find a better hedge fund strategy than managed futures to accomplish that."
He helps manage the iMGP DBi Managed Futures Strategy ETF (DBMF). The fund replicates the performance of leading managed futures hedge funds inside a low-cost, liquid ETF, according to the firm's website.
"There's an existential crisis right now in strategic asset allocation and the model portfolio world," Beer said about the 60/40 approach. "I love my bonds … [but] I'm not making it a 40% allocation for something that is not adding to the rest of my portfolio."
As of Thursday's close, Beer's ETF is up almost 19% so far this year, according to FactSet data.
However, managed futures may not be a replacement for bonds.
According to NovaDius Wealth Management's Nate Geraci, bonds still have a place for diversifying a portfolio.
"I call fixed income the most challenging area in investing right now," the firm's president said in the same interview. "[Alternatives] fit in the sleeve of a well-diversified portfolio that includes stocks and bonds. But I don't think you just give up on the bond side of the equation."
Geraci added that investors should understand how alternative investment strategies like managed futures ETFs could interact with the rest of a portfolio.
These funds can outperform during volatile markets, but they may also have periods of underperformance.
"You have to let that work out over the long-term," said Geraci, who is also an ETF Institute co-founder. "To me it's just a balance. It's all about diversification."

articles.title: Investors are buying up vast tracts of timberland across U.S. in one of market's longest-term bets
articles.text:
When the economy and the market look shaky, gold and government bonds are the traditional places to park money. Lately, some investors have also been looking at something more rooted: timber.
The pitch is easy to like: a back-to-basics, natural asset that grows on its own, matures into a harvest and can be cashed in all while you use it to hunt, pitch a tent, or forage.
Institutions have been buying timberland at a rate of one million acres per year, according to Bank of America, and some financial advisors say individual investors, including younger Americans priced out of the housing market, are also taking a look at the asset class. But it is far from a rush, and investors who already own timberland caution that it may not be very profitable in the short term.
"Timber is a very low return investment. I have curtailed my investments," said Pat Dorn, founder of Anchor Investment Management, a fee-only advisory firm in Columbia, South Carolina, and a former chairman of the South Carolina Forestry Association. Dorn owns 2,500 acres of timberland in South Carolina's booming upstate region. Dorn said the problem is that right now more timber is being grown than is needed in a sluggish housing economy.
"Supply beats demand, and that causes flat prices. Timber is not an investment I would make currently," Dorn said.
Nationally, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' producer price index for logs, bolts, timber, pulpwood and wood chips ticked up in September, but prices have been mostly on the decline since summer 2022. This measures prices received by producers for those products, rather than timberland values or investment returns. Over the very long-term, prices have climbed substantially.
Financial institutions point to the asset class as one of interest specifically for the long-term investor.
Ken Shepard, head of specialty asset management at Bank of America Private Bank said that timberland is not a tactical asset class that can be easily entered or exited in response to short-term market conditions. "We view it as a strategic, long-term investment supported by several favorable secular trends, including the continued expansion of the timber industry in the U.S. South and growing demand for wood products beyond traditional construction uses," Shepard said.
For example, he said, demand for wood pellets used in bioenergy, while controversial, has increased significantly. In addition, timberland values are benefiting from strong demand from recreational and lifestyle buyers, providing support for land prices beyond the income generated from timber harvesting.
The National Council of Real Estate Investment Fiduciaries' Timberland Property Index, which tracks privately held U.S. timber properties owned at least partly on behalf of institutional investors, posted a total return of 0.95% in the second quarter of 2026, comprising 0.34% income and 0.61% appreciation.
Timberland managers dominate acquisitions
Bank of America's 2026 outlook reported that the one-million-acre annual pace of buying is a three-year streak of dealmaking it expects to continue.
According to Bank of America, timber managers acquired 55% of all acres that changed hands in 2025 against just 15% sold. Institutions are playing the long game. Large timberland managers buy for pension funds and endowments that can wait decades, and that can make bets on a longer-term recovery in a currently slumping U.S. housing market that will be good for lumber pricing. But a private owner living through today's market sees things differently.
Dorn pointed out that timber companies buy less mature trees for pulpwood, which goes into paper towels or notebook paper, and those trees can take 12-14 years to mature. The chip-and-saw variety of trees take a little bit longer, while the big prize, timber cut for houses, can take 25 years. "That is where the top value is," he said.
According to Dorn, what landowners are paid for standing timber varies depending on what the trees are used for. Pine pulpwood consists of trees ground into paper and packaging, while pine sawtimber is made up of larger trees cut into lumber for homebuilding. Meanwhile, hardwood sawtimber, consists of oak and other big trees used in flooring, furniture and pallets. Each product feeds a different set of buyers, so one can climb while others fall.
South Carolina Forestry Commission data show statewide average pine pulpwood stumpage prices, what buyers pay landowners for standing timber, fell from $5.67 a ton in the third quarter of 2025 to $3.79 in the third quarter of 2026, a decline of about 33%. Pine sawtimber prices fell about 6% over the same period, from $22.78 to $21.47 a ton, while hardwood sawtimber prices rose about 40%, from $16.04 to $22.52.
Historically, pulpwood has been as high as $12 to $18 a ton, according to Dorn, and twenty years ago, soft timber was in the $35-$40 range. He said those prices could make a comeback if the housing market ever recovers, because pine sawtimber is cut into lumber for new homes, so its price tends to follow home building.
Strategically placed, timber may not be a bad investment, according to Dorn, though that would be because of the land itself more than the timber. "The return is in the land, not the timber," Dorn said.
He advises anyone thinking of investing in timberland to scout for prime parcels of land located outside growing metro areas that may be poised to pop as the local population keeps spreading. "If one hopes to buy land near growing metro areas and holds on to it, timber is a reasonable way to keep it earning something — a very low return — while you hold that land," he said.
Ownership risks are extensive
Michael Martin, a timber owner in western New York and vice president of market strategy at brokerage firm TradingBlock, says timberland can be a good long-term investment but the reality of being an owner belies the romantic image of acres of untouched timberland. It is not as passive an investment class as it may seem to be.
Direct ownership is highly illiquid and comes with management costs, property taxes, harvesting expenses, exposure to local timber markets, and risks including wildfire, pests, disease and trespassers hunting or cutting trees.
And when it is time to harvest timber, you need to make sure you are getting the best deal. "If you simply go with a small local outfit without getting competing bids, you don't always know if you're getting the best price," Martin said.
He also said timber prices are very local and can impact whether it's a solid investment.
"I am constantly checking stumpage reports because timber prices are extremely local. An oak tree in western New York may have a completely different value from one in the Adirondacks," Martin said.
In addition, partial timbering every ten years or so has barely covered the property taxes. "At the end of the day, I barely break even," he added.
Some in local real estate and investing markets say younger buyers are curious, though firsthand evidence is hard to find.
"As a millennial and a realtor, I understand the appeal. I've thought about buying timberland myself," said Jake Kennedy, a Nashville-based realtor, noting that his generation has lived through the dot-com crash, the Great Recession, a pandemic, huge swings in housing and now inflation. "One lesson from all of that we have learned is that scarcity matters when it comes to places to park your money," Kennedy said, adding as examples that more IPOs can be announced or new crypto created.
"But you can't manufacture another 500 acres of land," Kennedy said. "Timber itself is a resource that takes decades to grow. And there is something reassuring about owning an asset that is tangible," he added. But he also cautioned that timber's durability doesn't mean profitability. Trees can be temperamental and subject to many variables.
The people Kennedy has spoken with see timberland as a relatively safe place to park money, he said, because demand for timber products isn't going away. "In the meantime, yes, hunting is a common activity while owners are waiting for the investment to grow and mature, literally," he said.
"I don't think my generation is suddenly giving up on houses and becoming timber barons. However, I do think we are a lot more interested in alternative places to store wealth than previous generations might have been," he added.
Timber ETFs offer access to the asset class
For many millennials, homeownership has become increasingly difficult due to elevated home prices, higher mortgage rates, and limited inventory in many markets. "As a result, some investors are looking for alternative ways to participate in real assets and potentially build equity without purchasing a home directly," said Nadeem Kassam, chief investment strategist at Marnoa Private Wealth Counsel.
Outside direct or institutional fund ownership, there are timber ETFs and timber-focused funds that provide exposure to a theme that is closely tied to long-term housing demand and construction activity, though they remain highly niche investments in an ETF market now valued in the trillions of dollars.
Kassam pointed to the iShares Global Timber & Forestry ETF (WOOD), with roughly $260 million in assets, and the Invesco MSCI Global Timber ETF (CUT), which has roughly $30 million in assets.
"The investment case is supported by persistent housing shortages across many parts of the U.S. and growing bipartisan support for policies aimed at increasing housing supply and improving affordability. If these efforts lead to increased homebuilding over time, demand for lumber and wood products could benefit," Kassam said.
But he noted that investors should understand that timber ETFs are not a direct investment in timberland. Neither ETF owns trees.
"Most own publicly traded companies involved in timber, forest products, wood manufacturing, and other parts of the housing value chain," Kassam said, explaining the advantage is liquidity and accessibility, but returns will be driven by more than just timber prices.
WOOD's largest holdings include Weyerhaeuser, a major timberland owner, alongside Brazilian pulp maker Suzano, Nine Dragons Paper and West Fraser Timber. CUT is weighted toward paper, packaging and materials makers such as Svenska Cellulosa, UPM, Stora Enso and Avery Dennison. WOOD has drawn about $73 million in net inflows over the past year, according to ETF Database.
"For investors who are priced out of the housing market, timber ETFs may offer a way to participate in the long-term housing and construction story through a diversified, liquid investment vehicle. The key is recognizing that you're buying exposure to businesses that benefit from housing-related demand, not a direct ownership stake in land or residential real estate," Kassam said.
Junyi Liu, professor of economics at Soka University of America, who studies international and development economics, said he is not seeing evidence of a boom, but that timberland does have some unusual characteristics as an alternative asset.
"Returns can come from biological growth, timber prices, and land appreciation, and owners sometimes have the option to delay harvesting when timber prices are unfavorable," Liu said. But for retail investors, Liu added, it is quite different from "the simple 'trees grow while you wait' investment story."

articles.title: Trump's student loan overhaul could lead to more bankruptcy filings, former judge says
articles.text:
In Judge Sarah Sharer Curley's nearly three decades presiding over bankruptcy cases, some were especially painful to witness, she said — such as the 73-year-old woman who stood before her in 2012 with a student loan balance of more than $584,000.
The debt dated back to the 1970s and had grown throughout the woman's public sector career, Curley writes in her new book, "The Price of Forgiveness: Debt, Bankruptcy, and the Future of Fairness in America." She had "never made a lot of money," Curley said, and by the time she sought debt relief, the woman was living in poverty, with Social Security as her only income. Even so, strict bankruptcy laws can make it nearly impossible to discharge student loans.
Curley, the first woman appointed to the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Arizona, said it was a familiar story.
"We allow the financial markets to take innumerable risks, yet we refuse to allow an individual to be forgiven for choosing to pursue an advanced degree," Curley wrote.
Curley retired in 2014. CNBC spoke with her this month about her new book, in which she describes a legal system that often fails to give indebted Americans the second chance it promises. In 2025, more than half a million personal bankruptcy cases were filed — an almost 50% rise from three years prior, according to the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts.
The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
'People are subject to many unexpected events'
Annie Nova: What do people get most wrong about those who file for bankruptcy?
Sarah Sharer Curley: People assume that individuals who file for bankruptcy are committing fraud, trying to hide assets and cheating creditors. Nothing could be further from the truth.
AN: And so why did people end up in your court?
SSC: People are subject to many unexpected events. People can't always plan adequately for the next earthquake, hurricane or natural disaster. But usually, it's someone losing a job. It could also be an illness that becomes chronic with medical costs that increase dramatically over a short period.
Student loans is another area of concern. Universities are charging more for basic degrees, as well as graduate programs. The cost of medical school over four years can be more than $400,000.
AN: You write that many people who file for bankruptcy are not unemployed; they're just living paycheck to paycheck. What does this tell us about our economy and labor market?
SSC: Despite the increase in wages that most economists tout, many people are working as independent contractors. They receive few benefits and have few rights. The company is not responsible to them.
Other individuals may be working for a company but find the wages or benefits are insufficient. Many people are forced to work for several employers to meet their needs on a weekly basis.
Although unemployment may be low, the quality of the employment is also low.
'I found her credible'
AN: The story in your book about the woman in her 70s with the six-figure federal student loan balance really stood out to me. What happened in her case?
SSC: The federal government would not agree to any settlement. I was the one who would have to decide whether her debt would be discharged or not. But the case law I had to follow was not in favor of discharging student loan debts. So, I didn't have a lot of flexibility in granting her relief.
However, I gave her credit for seven years of public service helping out troubled teens in San Diego County, since people who are in certain types of public service only have a 10-year repayment period. That meant that she'd need to repay the debt for just three more years.
AN: Wow. Why wouldn't the federal government agree to any settlement with her?
SSC: The federal government retains law firms to represent it in bankruptcy court, allowing the law firms to have a certain amount of discretion as to how to proceed. As a result, some law firms are aggressive in the positions that they take.
In the case of the woman in her 70s, the law firm attorneys didn't believe her when she said she had no assets and was on Social Security. But the law firm did not do an adequate investigation. I found her credible.
'Harder to reach a settlement' on student loans
AN: Under President Joe Biden's administration, it reportedly became easier for federal student loan holders to get their debt discharged in bankruptcy. What's the current situation like?
SSC: There were attempts by the U.S. Department of Education to work out repayment plans for student loan borrowers who could not repay their debts. There was also the possibility that the Education Department would agree to forgive at least a portion of the student loans.
However, once the Education Department was gutted in 2025, there were few, if any, employees who could approve the debt modifications through one of the offered programs. As a result, it has become harder to reach a settlement with the Department of Education.
AN: In your book, you describe President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill," which passed in July 2025, as an "attack" on student loan borrowers. How so? Do you expect the new law to drive up bankruptcy filings?
SSC: The bill created unrealistic federal loan caps for students. As a result, if a student takes out a loan from a private financial institution that's not federally guaranteed, that loan will often be provided at a higher interest rate.
Let's say the student needs a $300,000 loan to go to medical school. If the individual has a lower credit score, their interest rate may jump to 16%, leading to a payment of $5,017 per month over 10 years, or $302,040 in interest.
These expenses are not sustainable for most individuals. The rate of bankruptcy filings will most likely increase.
Many bankruptcy filers 'feel they have failed'
AN: You write that medical debt is another major reason people need to file for bankruptcy. Can you say a little more about this?
SSC: There were many individuals who appeared before me who had chronic illnesses. Chronic diseases are a problem because the person can only discharge the debt they owe at the beginning of the bankruptcy case. As with any chronic illness, the debt continues to mount day by day for years to come.
Many individuals are traumatized when they file a bankruptcy case.Sarah Sharer CurleyFormer U.S. Bankruptcy Court judge
AN: You write that the bankruptcy process is "tortuous" for most individuals. How so?
SSC: Dramatic changes were made to the bankruptcy law in 2005. People are required to jump through many hoops to get relief now.
There was no evidence to support certain beliefs that individuals were engaged in fraud or filing bankruptcy cases every few months. But the creditor lobby pushed to make the bankruptcy law more pro-creditor. The many forms that need to be filled out and the hearings that need to be attended usually keep the individual in a perpetual state of stress.
AN: How does filing for bankruptcy affect people emotionally?
SSC: Many individuals are traumatized when they file a bankruptcy case. They had believed if they just work harder, they could solve their debt problems. However, when they're about to lose their homes, their cars or their businesses, they turn to bankruptcy.
Many see their inability to solve their financial problems as a moral failure. They feel they have failed.
AN: What was it like for you, day after day, seeing people under the pressure of insurmountable debt?
SSC: At times, at the end of the hearing, after I had rendered my decision, I would let the individual know that under the current law, I couldn't provide them with what they really needed. I told them that the law needed to be changed. We give a break to large financial institutions and corporations, and it's time that we do so for individuals, too.

articles.title: 'Everyone laughed' when he started a pumpkin farm—now it brings in $2 million a year
articles.text:
Three decades ago, when Kelly Schultz announced his intention to start a pumpkin farm, "everybody laughed at me," he says. Schultz, a second-generation antique seller, had no prior experience with farming when he bought a small farm in Clarence, New York, in 1993.
Nobody thinks he's out of his gourd now.
Schultz, 74, is the owner and operator of The Great Pumpkin Farm, a seasonal attraction about 15 miles northeast of Buffalo that draws over 100,000 visitors each fall.
The Great Pumpkin Farm brought in $2 million in annual revenue in 2025, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It — and it's open just seven weeks a year.
This year, the farm is open to visitors between Sept. 19 and Oct. 31, and they're not just coming to buy pumpkins. With a $20 weekend admission ticket, fall enthusiasts can ride the farm's pumpkin-themed train, explore its giant corn maze and compete in pie-eating contests, among other attractions.
Halloween is big business for Schultz and other seasonal business owners. Halloween-related spending is expected to reach $13.5 billion in the U.S. in 2026, according to a consumer survey by the National Retail Federation published in September. Among the 74% of Americans celebrating the holiday this year, 42% said they plan to carve a pumpkin.
At The Great Pumpkin Farm, "attendance is increasing just about every year," according to Schultz.
During the fall, "there are people that come here almost every weekend," he says. "They love it so much, they just keep coming back."
A giant pumpkin put them 'on the map'
Schultz, who runs an antique store and an antique auction business year-round, says he was inspired to start his farm after visiting a pumpkin patch in upstate New York in the early 1990s. That farm had "muddy parking lots and not a whole lot of restrooms," he recalls, but there were "a zillion people" walking around and buying pumpkins.
"I looked around and I said, 'I could do this, better than this,'" Schultz says. So when the old cow farm next to his antique store went up for sale, he bought the 85-acre property for approximately $650,000, he says.
With the help of other local farmers, Schultz learned how to grow his own gourds, and The Great Pumpkin Farm officially opened in 1996. But Schultz had even bigger plans for his farm. That same year, he asked Ray Waterman, founder of the World Pumpkin Confederation, an organization dedicated to growing giant pumpkins and squash, to host his annual World Pumpkin Weigh-Off at The Great Pumpkin Farm.
Schultz bought prize indemnity insurance, which covers the cost of contest and promotion prizes, and offered $50,000 to anyone who brought in a pumpkin that weighed 1,000 pounds or more. He took out ads in papers "across the country" to promote the weigh-off. The winning pumpkin, grown by a couple from Lowville, New York, broke the world record at the time at a whopping 1,061 pounds.
"We were in magazines and newspapers all over the world," Schultz recalls. "That put us on the map right off the bat."
The Great Pumpkin Farm still hosts a weigh-off event every October, and this year's heaviest pumpkin weighed a whopping 1,908.5 pounds, almost double the weight of the 1996 winner.
Hay rides, pumpkin cannons and more
These days, Schultz focuses less on growing gourds — to keep up with demand, he purchases most of the farm's pumpkins from nearby farms. But The Great Pumpkin Farm's 50-foot pumpkin pyramid, which is visible from the road, is still the first thing that incoming visitors see. According to Schultz, the farm stocks over 25,000 pumpkins each year.
Weekend visitors pay $20 per ticket, which covers admission for both days. They can access a vast range of activities including hayrides, pie-eating contests, magic shows, a giant slide, live music, train rides, a kid-friendly "boo barn" and pumpkin pedal kart rides, just to name a few.
For an extra fee, visitors can try the farm's amusement rides, pumpkin cannons, zombie paintball train, carnival games and Buffalo Bills-themed corn maze. Alongside the farm's bar and bakery, Schultz hosts festival food vendors whose offerings range from barbecue to specialty grilled cheese sandwiches.
"You can come out here and spend the day and still not have done everything," he says.
Weekdays require no admission charge, and are more low-key. Visitors can purchase pumpkins, visit the Halloween store, bar and bakery, and enjoy the outdoor playground, petting zoo and hay maze.
Creating this fall festival requires a huge amount of labor, according to Schultz. He employs over 100 seasonal workers during the seven weeks the farm is open each year, and their job duties range from driving tractors for hay rides to serving pumpkin donuts.
Rising gas costs are another major expense, Schultz says: It takes "lots and lots of gallons of fuel" to maintain the grounds and operate tractors for the hay rides. Since Schultz tries to avoid raising admission costs, he predicts that the business will "make a little bit less" in 2026.
"The business has been profitable, but we generally take most of the money and try and put it back into it," Schultz says.
Because Schultz owns the land surrounding the farm — approximately 300 acres in total — there's always room to expand, he says. Each year, he aims to add "something new, something fun, or upgrade what we already have."
Creating a 'generational business'
The farm has grown into a family operation: Schultz's son Ben has helped him run it, and his antique businesses, for the last 25 years.
"I just like hanging out with my dad, so that's how I got involved in all this," says Ben Schultz, 45. "I'm very proud of what he created here, and I'm just happy to be a part of it."
Their shared goal for The Great Pumpkin Farm, according to Ben Schultz, is to "continue the momentum." From the farm's simple beginnings, "it's hard to imagine that it's gotten as big as it has," he says.
Kelly Schultz's grandchildren have also started to help out around the farm, he says.
"They love coming here," he says. "They all want to be here all the time, every day."
"I'm sure that the pumpkin farm will be a generational business," he continues. "It's definitely a family event."
Throughout October, the farm is buzzing with activity, but after Halloween, everything shuts down, according to Schultz. The petting zoo animals go back to their original farms; the amusement park rides are packed up and removed, and pig farmers pick up the remaining pumpkins to use for feed. Putting everything away and cleaning up the property takes approximately a month, Schultz says.
For the rest of the year, around 20 full-time staff help maintain the Great Pumpkin Farm's old barn buildings and keep the grass mowed.
Otherwise, it's back to selling antiques for Schultz and his family — at least until next fall.

articles.title: These tech stocks are a buy ahead of their earnings reports, Bank of America says
articles.text: Bank of America says there are several technology stocks that have more room to run heading into their next quarterly results. The investment bank sees companies like Spotify Technology offering plenty of upside. Other buy-rated stocks that Bank of America recommends and that were screened by CNBC Pro include: Amphenol, Box, Camtek and Coupang. Box Don't sleep on this undervalued AI winner, according to analyst Matt Bullock. "We think Box is one of the most underappreciated AI beneficiaries in application software," he wrote recently, calling the stock a top pick. The bank also raised its price target on Box shares by 19%, to $50 from $42, and said the company is too attractive to ignore ahead of its next scheduled earnings later this quarter. "It's in the early stages of a multi-year growth acceleration, and trading at a significant discount to peers," he said. Box shares are up 32% this year, and 66% in six months. Amphenol Another robust quarter ahead, analyst Wamsi Mohan, wrote earlier this week ahead of the electronic connector manufacturer's quarterly report. "We continue to see APH as a beneficiary of AI infra investments across both GPU- and custom-accelerator-based architectures," he wrote. Mohan also says IT data demand remains robust, which benefits Amphenol. "Beyond AI, we expect most end markets to remain healthy & see continued room for upward estimates revision," he said. Shares are up 17% this year. The company will report its results on October 28. Spotify Technology Analyst Jessica Reif Ehrlich said tune out the "noise" and buy Spofitfy now. "We firmly believe that Spotify has a long runway for growth, including ramping advertising, subscriber growth, pricing and new products," she recently wrote. The stock is down almost 9% this year, but the bank says AI fears are overdone. "In addition, while AI-related narratives may be difficult to disprove, we continue to view Spotify's scale, engagement, and ecosystem advantages as enviable and difficult to replicate," she went on. Spotify will report quarterly earnings on October 22. Camtek "Reiterate Buy, $200 PO, now on 29x CY28E PE given CAMT's leverage to multi-year AI advanced packaging growth where it is gaining share, and diversifying product/market drivers ... We like Camtek's strong product portfolio, share gains, and exposure to key growth markets across advanced packaging for AI-driven high performance logic and memory." Box "We think Box is one of the most underappreciated AI beneficiaries in application software ... It's in the early stages of a multi-year growth acceleration, and trading at a significant discount to peers ... Box's AI capabilities transform enterprise content from a passive asset into a critical input for enterprise AI systems, agents, and tooling." Coupang "We expect Coupang's 3Q revenue to be slightly better than consensus estimates, at US$10.18bn, mainly as we marked to market the sharply strengthening KRW in Aug Sept. We estimate adj EBITDA of US$151mn, slightly softer than consensus estimates of US$157mn." Spotify ""Tuning out the noise ... In addition, while AI-related narratives may be difficult to disprove, we continue to view Spotify's scale, engagement, and ecosystem advantages as enviable and difficult to replicate ... We firmly believe that Spotify has a long runway for growth, including ramping advertising, subscriber growth, pricing and new products." Amphenol "We continue to see APH as a beneficiary of AI infra investments across both GPU- and custom-accelerator-based architectures ... Beyond AI, we expect most end mkts to remain healthy & see continued room for upward estimates revision."

articles.title: Berkshire shares buck market sell-off, rally to highest since Buffett said he would step down as CEO
articles.text:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire Hathaway shares closed Friday at their highest level since Warren Buffett told shareholders at the May 2025 annual meeting he planned to step down as CEO at the end of that year.
The day before that Saturday surprise, both the Class A and Class B shares had closed at all-time highs.
Over the next three months, they lost more than 14% of their value as investors worried a "Buffett premium" was dissolving.
It's been more than a year since their post-meeting low in August of 2025, and the recovery has not been a straight line, but BRK.A ended Friday at $798,000, just 1.4% below its all-time closing high of $809,350.
The B shares finished at $532.02, also 1.4% under their all-time closing high of $539.80.
A loss Thursday broke a 10-session winning streak that added 5% to Berkshire's stock prices but they rebounded with gains of more than 1% Friday.
CNBC Pro thinks investors may be happy Berkshire is spending some of its big cash pile under CEO Greg Abel, with $4.5 billion of buybacks in Q2, investments in Alphabet, Taylor Morrison Home, Lennar, (although there haven't been any buys of that stock since October 2), and now, Bending Spoons. (More on that below).
It also notes Keefe, Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields believes higher short-term interest rates are helping to lift the shares.
Berkshire still has roughly $360 billion in cash, "a good symbol of continued patience under the new CEO," and those higher rates mean "they'll be making more money" on that money.
In addition, its insurance operations have benefited from a quiet hurricane season so far.
Higher oil prices are good for its $19 billion stake in Chevron, which closed Friday at an all-time high after gaining almost 36% since the start of July. Berkshire's energy-related subsidiaries are also getting a tailwind.
And recently, Berkshire may be getting a boost as investors shift away from high-flying AI and tech stocks and turn to "old" economy names.
For example, Coca-Cola, a long-time Buffett favorite and now a $37.6 billion holding, also closed Friday at an all-time high, perhaps with some extra help from KFC's switch from Pepsi to Coke. It's up 34% year-to-date.
Berkshire's position has gained $2.4 billion since last Friday, overtaking Alphabet to become the third largest stake in its portfolio. (See the full top 10 below.)
Berkshire's B shares have cut their June 1 deficit of 17.5 percentage points versus the S&P 500 by almost two-thirds.
They are now 6.0 percentage points behind the benchmark for the year.
Atypical bet on 'buzzy' Italian tech company is big win ... so far
Berkshire Hathaway's surprising bet of close to $1 billion on Bending Spoons is paying off big, at least in the short term.
The Italian company, which began trading on Nasdaq in the U.S. in July, buys cast-off internet names like AOL, Evernote, and Vimeo, uses AI to cut costs, and deploys the savings to make more acquisitions.
In late July, CNBC Pro said, "Wall Street is buzzing," and "analysts ... see big gains ahead."
The tech stock is decidedly not a typical Berkshire value play, trading at a large multiple to its earnings.
But before Wall Street's open Wednesday morning, a Bending Spoons news release revealed Berkshire is investing a "further" $330 million in the company by purchasing 10 million newly issued shares at $33 per share in a private placement.
That was already an almost 12% discount from Tuesday's closing price of $37.86 and the news sent Bending Spoons shares even higher.
They hit an intraday high of $58.56 before closing up 41% at $53.46 on Wednesday.
Bending Spoons shares are up 24.3% over the three trading days since the revelation, after giving up a chunk of their earlier gains in Friday's tech sell-off to end at $47.07.
That's a solid 42.6% higher than Berkshire's $33 purchase price for a profit, on paper, of nearly $141 million.
But what's that "further" in Bending Spoon's statement?
The release also disclosed, apparently for the first time, that Berkshire invested $600 million at Bending Spoon's IPO more than three months ago.
The release doesn't specify how many shares Berkshire bought in July, and Bending Spoons wouldn't confirm my math, but assuming Berkshire paid the $29 per share IPO price, that initial purchase would have been almost 20.7 million shares.
That puts Berkshire's holding now at close to 30.7 million shares, which would be worth more than $1.4 billion at Friday's close, a gain of 55.3% for its overall investment of $930 million.
Bending Spoon's release also says the "new investment brings Berkshire Hathaway's ownership to 4%."
The company told me in an email it hasn't "specifically disclosed" how many outstanding shares it has now, "but we had 635 million fully diluted weighted average shares outstanding in Q2, we issued 34 million shares as part of the IPO, and we will be issuing an additional 10 million as part of this transaction."
Using those numbers, Berkshire's presumed 30.7 million shares are a 4.5% stake, and that's what I've put in the Berkshire Portfolio Tracker for now.
We may learn more next month about exactly how many shares Berkshire bought in the IPO when its portfolio snapshot as of September 30 is due to be disclosed.
Another unknown: who at Berkshire made the call to take a stake in Bending Spoons.
Bending Spoons CEO and Co-Founder Luca Ferrari shares Wall Street's enthusiasm about Berkshire's investments, saying in the news release the Omaha company "has been among the finest and most respected capital allocators in the world, and is a longstanding inspiration for Bending Spoons."
Morningstar's Greggory Warren (who was one of the designated analyst questioners at Berkshire shareholders meetings from 2014 to 2019) writes the Bending Spoons buy, along with Berkshire's now $36 billion stake in Alphabet, show "the firm is finally moving out of its comfort zone to find places to put capital to work, which should be viewed as a positive for long-term investors."
At Barron's, Andrew Bary says, "Many Berkshire holders would like to see the company invest more heavily in stocks given the company's $350 billion-plus in cash, but Bending Spoons was a surprise" given its high valuation.

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah well — people have been drinking Coca-Cola since 1886, so I imagine that there's been some —
I don't know of any study that's been made on the lifetime of heavy users of Coca-Cola versus people who drink nothing but water.
But speaking for myself, I'm 84, literally one-quarter of all the calories I've consumed in the last 30 years have been Coca-Cola. And I don't see how anybody can feel any better than I feel.
I am one-quarter Coca-Cola, and I can tell you, I haven't missed a day of work, you know — since I had the prostate cancer — radiation — three years ago. And I don't think the prostate cancer was caused (laughs) by Coca-Cola.
So — I — and all my friends drink it like crazy.
So there's 1.9 billion eight-ounce servings of Coca-Cola products sold around the world today, and there will be more than 1.9 billion a year from now, and more than that five years from now, and more than that ten years from now.
And that's been true. And some people will like other things, and — and if they like broccoli and Brussels sprouts, God bless them, you know, but don't invite me for dinner. (Laughter)

articles.title: Software’s new consolidator gets big vote of confidence from Berkshire
articles.text:
At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July, Bending Spoons was a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote.
Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway.
Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion.
"Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement.
The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio.
For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the "SaaSpocalypse."
Shares of Intuit, HubSpot and Adobe are all down at least 30% this year, and a long list of private SaaS companies that were once venture darlings are now struggling to find capital, with the public market showing no appetite for IPOs. Last month, Bending Spoons agreed to buy collaboration software vendor Miro, once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion.
"You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore."
An app turned acquirer
Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus.
Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning with Evernote in 2022, followed by Brightcove in 2024, and Vimeo, AOL and Eventbrite in 2025.
The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07.
Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade were private equity behemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price.
Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions.
Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied."
"They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020.
Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years."
As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar.
"Unfortunately, a lot of my friends in that game are stuck," Mehta said. "Investors want out but there are no buyers. Anything pre-ChatGPT is legacy now."
Lloyd Walmsley, an analyst at Mizuho, said Bending Spoons' model is distinct from the older buyout approach.
"I think there aren't a lot of people that do what these guys do in terms of the depth of operations and the willingness to make substantial product changes," Walmsley said in an interview. "It's not typical of traditional private equity firms to make anywhere near this level of change."
For customers of the companies that Bending Spoons buys, sudden price hikes can follow.
In April 2023, months after the Evernote acquisition, Bending Spoons lifted the annual personal subscription price to $130 from $70. Later, the company changed its offerings, charging $100 for its so-called starter plan and $250 for "Evernote Advanced," compared to the $170 it had been charging for the pro plan.
"My first reaction was like, Oh man, I guess I have to switch to OneNote," said Walmsley, referring to Microsoft's notetaking app. But he said he stuck with Evernote.
"They're really savvy at finding these things that they provide a lot of value, and the switching costs are really high," Walmsley said. "The price isn't that high relative to the switching cost."
Bending Spoons uses the profits from its portfolio companies for future growth, the "overwhelming majority" of which comes from doing more deals, Ferrari told CNBC in an interview on Thursday.
"There are certain opportunities for improvement we can unlock over the first few years, and then the business will have whatever organic growth is intrinsic in that market," Ferrari said.
For Berkshire and its fellow Bending Spoons investors, the bet is still unproven.
The products have to remain desirable enough that customers are willing to pay up at a time when AI is squeezing margins across much of the software sector. In its first earnings report as a public company in August, Bending Spoons said revenue more than doubled from a year earlier to over $700 million, with growth almost entirely driven by acquisitions, while net income climbed 171% to $177 million.
That was before the Airtable deal had closed and Miro had yet to be announced. In the coming quarters and years, Wall Street will get a clear picture of whether the firm's structure can revive software.
On the earnings call in August, an analyst asked whether Airtable represents a long-term shift in the M&A strategy towards enterprise.
Ferrari said that about half of Bending Spoons' revenue already comes from professional businesses, largely through Brightcove and Vimeo, which has an enterprise component. The focus on software of late, he said, has more to do with where he's finding value after a hefty selloff.
"Most enterprise SaaS businesses were valued at irrationally high levels until somewhat recently," Ferrari said. "We never saw those prices making any sense."
— CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions, Zelenskyy condemns it as 'wrong'
articles.text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday condemned the White House's waiver of key provisions of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine.
"... The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskyy said in a post on X. "And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people."
President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving key parts of the new U.S. sanctions on Russia.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States," Trump wrote in Friday's order.
The House passed the Russia sanctions bill on Sept. 16, and Trump signed it into law two days later. The bill was introduced over a year ago, and its primary backer was the late Lindsey Graham, a veteran Republican senator who represented South Carolina.
Titled the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, the legislation targeted Russia's economy, intending to penalize the country over its continued full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The act required the president to increase duties on all Russian goods imported into the U.S. by up to 500% no later than 30 days after enactment. It also required Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries including China and India that are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas.
Trump's latest order waives these two parts of the Graham Act and comes two days before the law's implementation deadline. However, the order preserves existing sanctions on Russia under earlier executive orders.
Zelenskyy said he expects Trump to waive other sanctions on Russia, too.
"Sanctions relief will continue," he posted on X. "I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately."
The law could also sanction Russian leaders, officials, and financial institutions, and expand sanctions on Iran.
Oil sales revenue is critical to funding Russia's war effort.
The move also comes a week after the Trump administration temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027 to ease a supply crunch caused by the war in Iran.
High fuel prices are a sensitive issue for voters ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
A 'historic moment'
"The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's economy envoy, said in a post on X.
"The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," Dmitriev added.
But Trump's opponents have criticized the move.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who also drafted the Graham Act, condemned the latest waiver.
"Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug & the enablers of Russia's war machine & against the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, & our European allies," Blumenthal said in an X post.
Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Zelenskyy had warned that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives.
"Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry."
Earlier this week, reports emerged that Ukraine has restricted SpaceX's Starlink military application, Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network.

articles.title: Trump's Russia diesel deal may offer Putin more than money — and spell trouble for Ukraine
articles.text:
Ukraine is facing increasing uncertainty over its ability to sustain the war against Russia as a series of moves by U.S. President Donald Trump has raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner.
Trump's agreement with Putin to ease sanctions for Russia to provide global markets with diesel, as well as restrictions on U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukrainian forces, has put President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a difficult position as winter looms.
Higher diesel prices – essential to transporting goods and agricultural production – tend to drive up costs across the wider economy and fuel inflation. With November's U.S. midterm elections approaching, Trump is under pressure to bring fuel costs down.
But experts told CNBC that the diesel deal would deliver only a marginal financial benefit to Russia, and not move the needle much on global energy prices. Its wider political implications may be more significant, potentially reinforcing the Kremlin's belief that it can secure concessions from Washington without making compromises over Ukraine.
"Russia's main gain is political: Trump's decision eases sanctions pressure and undermines Western unity," Sergey Aleksashenko, senior research fellow and head of economics at the NEST Centre, told CNBC.
Diesel deal
Trump's agreement with Putin was for Russia to supply the global market with 4.8 million metric tons of diesel, the equivalent of about ten days of U.S. domestic demand, or about a single day of global demand. Experts say it will do little to affect prices.
"It does not even touch the sides – it is very, very small," Neil Atkinson, former head of the IEA's oil industry and markets division, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.
Aleksashenko estimated that the initial part of the phased agreement that covers 1.8 million metric tons of diesel could generate up to $1.25 billion in additional export revenue over three months, equivalent to around 1% of Russia's commodity export revenues during that period.
However, the benefit to Russia's federal budget would be substantially smaller, at less than $30 million per month, or under 0.07% of monthly federal revenues.
The deal was therefore unlikely to meaningfully strengthen Russia's war finances, Aleksashenko said. Instead, its main benefit to Moscow is political, because it eased sanctions pressure and undermined Western unity without requiring Putin to make concessions over Ukraine, he told CNBC.
The research fellow also argued that the additional Russian diesel entering global markets is not sufficient to produce a noticeable reduction in consumer fuel prices in the short term.
"Funding the war is currently Putin's priority, and he is prepared to increase that funding even if it means cutting all other expenditures," Aleksashenko added, pointing to Russia's draft budget for 2027.
The bigger problem for Ukraine
"Rather than encouraging compromise, the [diesel] deal likely boosts Moscow's belief that continued pressure will eventually yield further Western concessions," Maria Snegovaya, senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CNBC.
Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Zelenskyy also warned that the diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives.
"Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry."
Earlier this week, reports emerged that SpaceX's Starlink military application Starshield has been restricted in Ukraine. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network.
The order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, according to a Reuters report citing three officials familiar with the matter. CNBC has contacted the White House for comment.
The consequences were felt sharply in Ukraine. As Starlink's speed limits were lowered, Ukraine became incapable of shooting down some Russian drones. This week, Ukraine also did not receive advanced warning from partners of incoming ballistic missiles, resulting in civilian deaths, according to Ukrainian officials.
According to Serhiy Derkach, Ukraine's first deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure and transport, Starlink restrictions emboldened Russia to intensify attacks on Ukraine.
"With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Derkach told CNBC on Friday.
Russian authorities didn't respond to multiple CNBC requests for comment.
A political blow
The diesel deal was a political and moral blow to Ukraine and the Western coalition, according to Snegovaya. The U.S. sanctions exemption, which runs until April 2027, could facilitate Russian diesel exports beyond the initially announced shipment, potentially increasing Moscow's economic gains, she warned.
"If [the] White House uses its military and intelligence support as leverage to constrain Ukraine's strikes, the implications could become far more significant," Snegovaya said, adding that Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries have inflicted substantial economic costs on Moscow.
Such a move could have far greater consequences for Ukraine's efforts to weaken Russia's war economy, she added.
The diesel deal further undermines Washington's credibility as a mediator in the eyes of Ukraine and its European allies, as it appears to reward Moscow without securing concessions while increasing pressure on Kyiv, she said.
The problem, Snegovaya said, is that achieving military autonomy for Europe and Ukraine is extremely difficult in the short term, and Europe has been slow to develop the necessary capabilities.
"Almost five years into the war, Ukraine and its European partners remain heavily dependent on the U.S. in critical areas, like intelligence and missile defense. These dependencies are unlikely to be overcome during the remaining years of the Trump administration," she told CNBC.

articles.title: Some companies give AI to everyone. This CEO is doing the opposite
articles.text:
At London-headquartered payments technology company Paysend, access to artificial intelligence tools has to be earned.
CEO Ben Chisell told CNBC he is a “very cynical man” about the hype around the technology, though he still sees value in it. 
Chisell, who previously worked at Amazon, eBay and Starling Bank, estimates that Paysend can now deliver around 25% more engineering work with the same-sized team, but argues that getting results isn’t as simple as handing everyone the latest tech.
I know it sounds very unglamorous and unsexy as an approach given the world of tokenmaxxing and AI, but I think it’s really, really importantBen ChisellPaysend
Instead, he limits AI tools to his highest-performing employees, often only after they’ve proved what they can do with them. In the wrong hands, he said, AI can magnify bad habits such as laziness and poor judgment.
His broader rule is to resist the “fear of missing out” and focus on customer problems.
“I know it sounds very unglamorous and unsexy as an approach given the world of tokenmaxxing and AI, but I think it’s really, really important,” Chisell said.
Companywide AI rollouts
The pressure to demonstrate AI’s value is growing, from the legal sector to software engineering and finance, and many companies are responding by putting the technology in as many hands as possible.
London-based Lloyds Banking Group has rolled out 40,000 Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses, with 97% of employees who have one actively using it, the bank said. Newcastle-headquartered software company Sage said its AI coding tools had saved hundreds of thousands of work hours, while London-based professional services firm Grant Thornton UK has encouraged all of its staff to use Anthropic’s Claude as part of a £500 million ($660 million) investment in AI.
These figures do not necessarily translate into gains on the bottom line, however. U.K. government research published in January found that three-quarters of businesses using AI said it had improved workforce productivity, but 77% said revenue had not changed.
Read more from CNBC Work
Like Chisell, Lokdeep Singh, CEO of British enterprise software company Unily, sees AI as a “superpower” best reserved for high-performing employees. He is also wary of companies giving it out to everyone as a way to reduce costs.
“I personally believe you should use it to expand your ambition rather than make the team smaller,” he told CNBC. “But the reality is that in many industries, again, because of the macro environment, it is being thought as: ‘OK, can I cut costs? Can I cut employees?’ The truth is probably somewhere in between.”
Measuring AI value
At Paysend, Chisell wants employees to demonstrate what a tool actually contributes. New hires get a month to experiment with AI tools and explain what they have achieved.
He recently put that policy to the test with a new search engine optimization lead who requested access to Claude. A month later, the employee told Chisell he no longer needed it. All he found it useful for, he said, was producing briefs more quickly. So instead of a general-purpose AI tool, the employee suggested building a dedicated content-brief agent, which he is now working on.
At software company CoreView, the approach has been different. London-based CEO Simon Azzopardi told CNBC the company was initially “very gung-ho” on AI, initiating a widespread rollout for its software engineers. They first used AI to investigate problems by correlating logs, events and data, as well as to produce technical documentation and onboard new engineers faster.
You feel more efficient, but you actually aren’tSimon AzzopardiCoreView
Now, he said, developers increasingly coordinate teams of AI agents handling tasks including back-end and front-end coding, quality assurance and documentation. Azzopardi said work that previously took weeks could now take days.
However, AI-generated work isn’t necessarily productive if employees use it to build things outside their expertise, Azzopardi warned. “You feel more efficient, but you actually aren’t,” he said.
Still, when onboarding a major customer in the U.K.’s National Health Service, CoreView only needed to add one engineer while continuing to deliver its other projects, he said. The company has been hiring rather than cutting staff, using the extra capacity to take on more work.
Jobs after automation
As AI takes on more of people’s existing responsibilities, the question is what happens to the employees who used to do these tasks. Chisell believes companies will thrive if they help employees move into new roles, rather than replace them once their work is automated.
Customer-service workers, for example, have spent years resolving complex issues — a skill that’s valuable across a business, he said. For Chisell, technology should never replace human responsibility.
“Having a human in the loop shouldn’t mean human CC’d,” he said. “It should mean human ownership.”

articles.title: Loại quả "khó chiều", giá rẻ và rất quen thuộc với người Việt Nam lột tả áp lực của cuộc chiến Iran lên vai người dân Mỹ
articles.text:
Bấm vào quả chuối để cắt · kéo để xoay

articles.title: Nàng thơ H.T giấu cả nước sinh con cho chủ tịch showbiz bị "đế chế nội y" Victoria's Secret từ chối phũ phàng?
articles.text:
Nàng thơ H.T giấu cả nước sinh con cho chủ tịch showbiz bị "đế chế nội y" Victoria's Secret từ chối phũ phàng?
Trước đó, cặp đôi gần như giữ kín toàn bộ quá trình yêu đương lẫn mang thai, chỉ đến khi "ván đã đóng thuyền" mới chính thức công khai với công chúng.
Vào ngày 16/10, nhiều blogger Trung Quốc tung tin siêu mẫu Hà Tuệ đã bị show diễn Victoria's Secret Fashion Show từ chối. Trong bối cảnh thương hiệu tung ra nhiều video giới thiệu, dàn người mẫu nô nức lên đường đến Mỹ và chỉ còn 2 ngày nữa là đến show diễn, sự im lặng bất thường của Hà Tuệ làm dấy lên nhiều đồn đoán.
Chủ đề này đã làm cư dân mạng xứ Trung xôn xao bàn tán. Nhiều người cho rằng trong thế giới thời trang, việc người mẫu bị thương hiệu từ chối là rất bình thường. Nguyên nhân có thể đến từ không phù hợp với chủ đề của show diễn đó. Năm nay, Victoria's Secret thậm chí còn gây ồn ào khi loại bỏ thẳng tay cựu thiên thần Romee Strijd.
Tuy nhiên, cũng có rất nhiều người tỏ ra tiếc nuối cho siêu mẫu sinh năm 1989. Hà Tuệ bắt đầu trình diễn cho Victoria's Secret Fashion Show từ năm 2011, sải bước trên sàn diễn của thương hiệu này tổng cộng 8 lần. Đây là quãng thời gian gắn bó không hề ngắn ngủi. Ở tuổi 37, Hà Tuệ vẫn duy trì được phong độ visual, body đỉnh cao, đặc biệt là càng thêm "gái 1 con trông mòn con mắt" sau khi sinh con cho tài tử Trần Vỹ Đình.
Hà Tuệ là gương mặt quen thuộc của sàn diễn Victoria's Secret. Clip: YouTube
Còn nhớ trước đó vào tháng 10/2025, Hà Tuệ bất ngờ thông báo đã sinh con trai cho tài tử Trần Vỹ Đình. Trước đó, cặp đôi gần như giữ kín toàn bộ quá trình yêu đương lẫn mang thai, chỉ đến khi "ván đã đóng thuyền" mới chính thức công khai với công chúng. Chính vì vậy, tin vui năm ấy từng gây chấn động mạng xã hội và khiến nhiều người hâm mộ "đứng hình", không tin nổi vào tai mình. Do đó, kể từ sau khi lên chức mẹ, cuộc sống cũng như sắc vóc của Hà Tuệ luôn nhận được sự quan tâm đặc biệt từ cư dân mạng.
Trần Vỹ Đình - Hà Tuệ dính tin hẹn hò vào tháng 8/2021. Khi đó, nam diễn viên bị bắt gặp đưa đón Hà Tuệ trong nhiều ngày. Cặp đôi được công chúng ủng hộ nhiệt liệt vì kín tiếng, không sử dụng đời tư để PR tên tuổi và có ngoại hình lẫn sự nghiệp "xứng đôi vừa lứa". Tới tháng 3/2023, cặp sao bất ngờ gặp trục trặc và chia tay nhau 1 thời gian. Đến cuối năm 2023, họ mới cho nhau cơ hội, hàn gắn mối quan hệ tình cảm.
Trần Vỹ Đình sinh năm 1985, ngoài là tài tử hàng đầu showbiz Hoa ngữ, còn là thiếu gia của 1 gia tộc giàu có bậc nhất đất Hong Kong (Trung Quốc). Cha nam diễn viên Cổ Kiếm Kỳ Đàm là trùm bất động sản, anh trai Trần Vỹ Đình làm trong ngành vận tải biển, còn chị gái điều hành 1 doanh nghiệp may mặc có nhiều nhà máy ở Dubai.
Bản thân Trần Vỹ Đình nắm giữ gia sản lên tới hàng trăm triệu NDT (hàng trăm tỷ đồng) và là chủ của 1 thương hiệu thời trang có tên tuổi. Nam diễn viên có 2 biệt thự trong The Leighton Hill - khu dân đắt đỏ nhất thế giới. Anh cũng từng khiến dân tình "lác mắt" khi xuống phố với những chiếc xe đến từ các thương hiệu hàng đầu như Rolls-Royce, Lamborghini, Audi, Mercedes-Benz, Maserati... trong đó có những chiếc là phiên bản giới hạn hoặc được sản xuất riêng.
Trong khi đó, Hà Tuệ sinh năm 1989, là người mẫu hàng đầu Trung Quốc, được mệnh danh là "Hà tiên cô" vì sở hữu vẻ đẹp ngọt ngào, gương mặt đậm nét Á Đông. Cô là 1 trong số ít người mẫu Trung Quốc từng biểu diễn cho show thời trang nội y của Victoria’s Secret. Hà Tuệ cũng là người mẫu xứ tỷ dân sải bước nhiều nhất ở "đêm thời trang sexy nhất hành tinh".
